Charlie Holmes (10/9/82):
You could start by saying who you are, and the date and place of birth.
Should I start saying "My name is..."?
Yes, why not?

I should think that they would know. Okay. My name is Charlie Holmes, born January 27, 1910. Mmm! Boston, Massachusetts. Seven o'clock in the evening -- so they tell me. Now, you've got to ask me some questions.
You were what position in the family?

I don't know. It was a pretty large family. There was children all over the house at the time, and I was somewhere in the middle. They told me at one time there was thirteen children in the family, but never all at one time. A lot of them died in their infancy.
Can you remember older brothers and sisters?

Yeah, I remember my oldest brother. His name was... We used to call him Buster. My sister's name was Alice. I had another brother, Phil. And then I appeared on the spot. After me was a sister... No, another brother, named Shirley, and a sister named Lucille. Now, I've left one of them out. Now, after me, my sister Helen. She was after me, and then Shirley come into the picture, and then my sister Lucille.
Now, you lived on Tremont Street?
Holmes (10/9) - 2

No. Never lived on Tremont Street in my life. My family lived in... Well, in Boston we lived on Warwick Street. Then we moved to Marble Street. And after Marble Street, we moved out in Roxbury to Harrishaw(?) Street.

Now, while I was on Warwick Street, that's when I was going to grammar school, the Sherwin Grammar School. Around about that time... This was, oh, let me see, in the years... Quite a few years back there. Anyway, that's when I met Howard Johnson, Johnny Hodges, Harry Carney. Harry and I were in the same class in school
Now, Harry is supposed to have lived on Cunard Street.
Can-ard Street.
That's right. And Johnny Hodges lived on Cambridge Street, and then he moved to Hammond Street.
Well, I knew him when he lived on Hammond Street. I don't know if there is a Cambridge Street. He lived in Cambridge.
Oh, he lived in Cambridge. That's right. You're right. He lived in Cambridge, and moved to Hammond Street. Then, just around the corner from Hodges, on Shumond(?) Avenue...
Shawmet(?) Avenue, it should be.
On Shawmet(?) Avenue was Howard Johnson.
Holmes (10/9) - 3
That's right. He's from a big musical family, too.
Was Howard in any of your classes, too?
No. Howard was ahead of me at school. There was two years difference in our ages. Naturally, age will make you... A two years difference, you know.
And Hodges was ahead of you, too.

No, Hodges was... He's three years older than I was. But see, by changing from school to school, he was a little bit behind, I think. I don't know... He might have been ahead of me in school. But I don't remember him being in school too long, because he was in Cambridge most of the time. He lived in Cambridge. Just before he started coming to New York, he moved to Boston -- Hammond Street. He lived on Hammond Street quite a while, but I mean, he was...
That's when you knew him, though.
Yeah. He was traveling back and forth.
And that was your neighborhood.
Yeah.
Where was that in terms of Boston? South Side?
No, that was in what they call... Well, that was called Roxbury. That was Roxbury.
Have you been back to the neighborhood at all?
Holmes (10/9) - 4

Well, I went back quite a few times after I came to New York, when my family was living. When my mother and father were alive, I'd go back to visit them and the family, and I'd go around to all the neighborhoods, one thing or another... Yeah. I went back quite a few times.
The neighborhood has changed a lot, or has it stayed the same?

Well, now I wouldn't know. Because the school burned down. I don't know if it was ever rebuilt or not. As all neighborhoods change, I imagine they had their changes, too. Of course, we're going back about sixty-some years now.
And this was a predominantly Black neighborhood?
No.
Mixed?
Mixed. Because the house I lived in on Warwick Street, we were on the ground floor, our family, and right above us was a White family, and above them was another Black family.
So you went to an integrated school, actually.
Oh yeah.
Did you have White and Black teachers?
No. At that time there weren't any Black teachers -- when I started in school. But they had Black
Holmes (10/9) - 5

teachers before I had finished grammar school. They had integrated the school as far as the teachers were concerned. Because one of my best friends, his sister was a teacher there. For years she was a teacher. In fact, two of my friends, their sisters were.. One of the first Black teachers in the system, you know.
What about your parents or anybody else in the family? Were your parents musically inclined?

No. No music in the family, except I. And I don't know how it got to me, how I became musically inclined. Well, I know how I become musically inclined. Because I heard Johnny Hodges play, and it was just something about his playing and the tone of his instrument that just appealed to me. And I had known musicians, plenty of musicians. Because at that time there was nothing else... Well, I don't mean nothing else. But I mean, that was about the main thing that Negroes could venture into. Because Big League ball wasn't open to them, and there so many things... So many doors were closed to them at the time. So anybody who was playing music, they were supposed to be something, you know.

I don't know, it just appealed to me when I heard him play. And I said, 'Well, gee, I want to be a saxophone player.' I didn't know him, you know what I mean, on
Holmes (10/9) - 6

speaking terms, but I sure made myself acquainted with him. Of course, he was about 13 years old the first time I heard him play. Of course, I was about ten years old. But he appealed to me at that age. I mean, I thought, oh, he was the greatest thing I ever heard in my life!
Before that, though, had you been interested in playing anything at all at school or anything?
Not in music. Nothing. I played baseball and games, and one thing or another.
You had a piano at home?
Oh, there was always a piano there. My Daddy tried to start the kids off musically, you know. Because at that time, practically all homes had a piano in it.
Piano in the parlor.
There was no radio or television or nothing like that. But practically in all the homes there was a piano.
In your home did anybody play it?

No. I played about as much as anybody in the family. He started my two oldest brothers and my sister with lessons on the piano. But nothing ever happened. My brother, he'd be out in the street playing ball or something. They cared nothin' about the piano. And then I
Holmes (10/9) - 7
would come along, and I would play by ear, you know. I'd be trying to pick out something.

They started me with piano lessons, but I didn't keep them up, because I wasn't interested in the piano then. I wanted a saxophone! Well, my Daddy... Pianos were never cheap. Pianos were always expensive. And with the salary that he was making, how he could ever afford to buy a piano I don't know!
What did your father do?

He was the chief of the what would you call it...? The maintenance... That's what they would call them today. In them days he was just a chief janitor. He was the head janitor at South Station, where the trains come in. He was the head janitor there, up in the building. He had two floors up there. He was the Boss Man up there. And salaries was no big deal in them days. I mean...
Did your mother work?
She did a day's work. Not wholly. But she had a family to raise. Every time you'd turn around, Mama was... You know what I mean? The family was getting bigger. All right?
Yeah.
So I don't know, well... I forgot where I was at...
Holmes (10/9) - 8
[PAUSE]
We'll now take you back to Boston again and continue where we left off, and discuss Howard Johnson, who was perhaps the most...

Well, Howard was a very serious musician. He started playing fife in an aggregation of Miss Smith's... a lady named Smith. She got a bunch of kids together in a fife-and-drum corps, and he started playing fife in that band, and flute also. He was a very good pianist, piano player.
Did his mother teach piano?
His mother taught him.
Did she teach other students, too?

Oh yes. She was a great piano teacher. And his older brother was a great pianist. He was really great. He was very outstanding all over the City of Boston. He played all the Society affairs and one thing or another, and he had four or five different combinations working on the same night -- all the Society affairs. That was his oldest brother, Walter Johnson. But he was a great deal older than Howard was.
And Walter Johnson was a pianist.
He was a pianist, yeah. Very good.
No relation to the Walter Johnson, the drummer.
Holmes (10/9) - 9

No. None whatsoever. No, his brother was... He was really something. He was really a big attraction, his brother was, his oldest brother. Well, the whole family was musical. And they were good musicians. Bobby, his brother Bobby Johnson, he played guitar and banjo and banjoreen(?) and this-that-and-the-other. He worked with Charlie Johnson's band for years. Then he went with Chick Webb's band. He was very good, very outstanding.
Now, he at one time got a saxophone.

Yeah. Well, he bought a saxophone, because he thought he could learn how to play it. You know, saxophone was getting to be kind of popular up there in Boston after Johnny got one. And everybody was talking about Johnny Hodges. So he thought he would get a saxophone too.
No, no, no, he got his before Johnny had one. Because at that time when Johnny got one, Howard was playing saxophone...
Because Bobby got it...
Because Bobby got the saxophone...
And didn't like it, and gave it to Howard.
That's right. Well, he had left the horn at home, and Howard started to playin' around with it and learning how to play it. And Bobby came home one day and
Holmes (10/9) - 10
saw Howard with the horn, and listened to him, and he said, 'Well, you keep it.' So Howard, he starts playing saxophone. He could play, too -- very good.

So it was a toss-up between him and Johnny, you know, who could play the best. But Johnny had a different kind of tone, a different kind of sound. Now, you could hear the two of them play the same thing, but there was a difference in Johnny's playing. And it was in the tone, you know. But the two of them together, they were really something else. A friend of mine whose name was Don Donaldson, he had an orchestra, and both of them were in the band. They used to rehearse at Don's house -- Don was a piano player. And we would stand outside in the street and listen to them play, you know.
This was also in Boston?
Yes.
Don Donaldson was also from Boston.

Yeah, it was still in Boston. And we'd stand outside the window and listen to... Well, we'd make comparisons between Johnny and Howard, you know. But both of them were even-up to me, at that time. But of course, Johnny had a different tone. But Johnny was the favorite. I don't know, some people just followed him, you know. Johnny was the favorite all over Boston.
Holmes (10/9) - 11
And you first heard him at a dance because your older brother came home and said he'd heard him.

Yeah, he came home... Then I met him around what they call house rent parties. Up there they have a different name for them; they call them totes. But in New York they called them house rent parties. It was parties in the house. I'd go around to these different little gatherings with other kids and one thing or another. And Johnny would always be around somewhere, because he loved to blow his horn, you know. So he loved to blow, and I liked to listen. And I'd always try to find out where he was going to be at, and I'd go by there and listen to him. I mean, we became acquainted that way, you know.

Then he found out I was interested in saxophone, but he didn't let me play his horn. Well, I wasn't trying to play, because I didn't have none. I didn't know anything about it. But I just admired the way he played.
But in the back of your mind, you now wanted to play saxophone.

Oh, yeah, yeah. It was in my mind the first time I heard him. But my Daddy couldn't afford to buy me a horn. I think at that time saxophones cost seventy-five dollars. Now they cost seventy-five hundred!
That's right! Anyway, tell me about the Doctor Holmes,
Holmes (10/9) - 12
no relation, who got together and had a brass band. Tell me about that.
A Good Samaritan.
I see.

He was a Good Samaritan. He made his money, he had his money. I don't know anything about him personally, if he was married or single or anything. I never heard anything about a wife, because I wasn't interested -- I wasn't interested in his wife or anything like that, if he had one.

But all I know, he was outfitting a band for children... And grownups! He wanted a band. He wanted a brass band. And he would front us the estimates. And he had a director that could play all of the instruments in the band, and he would teach. He would teach anybody in the band that wanted to learn how to play.
Now, with the kids, he didn't want nobody that could play anything, that could play an instrument. He wanted to start you off fresh. And he would teach you, and you'd come around that way.
But you had to say that you would stay with the band, didn't you, for about a year...
Well, yeah. I mean, you stayed...
You had to promise to stay with the band if they were
Holmes (10/9) - 13
going to teach you.
Everybody promised to stay when they joined. But he would give you your instruments while you were with the band.
Now, do you remember the name of the fellow who could play all the instruments and who gave tuition? Who taught?
Mmm, he was an Italian. Right now I can't remember his name.
Dr. Holmes was White?
No, no.
He was Black?
He was Black.
Now, you mentioned that Buster Tolliver was part of that group?

Yeah, he was one of the members of the band. Harry Carney got his clarinet there. Buster Tolliver got his clarinet there. Buster Tolliver was known as a great pianist, but Buster Tolliver played a lot of clarinet, too. He was a great clarinetist. But he went to piano like... Well, him and Howard were... Howard's first instrument was piano, and Buster's was, but he liked clarinet.
Now, you and Harry went to Dr. Holmes almost at the same time, and they gave Harry a clarinet. And what did
Holmes (10/9) - 14
they give you?
An oboe. A beautiful oboe. And promised me if I made any improvement on the oboe, in a year's time they would give me a saxophone.
Now, when we're talking about saxophones, we mean alto sax, right?
Yeah, that's all that I was interested in. Of course, tenor in them days was not... It wasn't a popular instrument. Tenor was not popular at all.
When you first heard Johnny Hodges, he was playing an alto?
Mmm-hmm. He might have had a soprano. But he was playing them dances with an alto. Because he had the soprano there, too. He was playing both of them.
Now, how did you learn the oboe? Did you have a teacher?

Yeah, I went to a teacher. He used to work in the State Theatre Orchestra. His name was Trogliano(?). He was a very good oboe player himself. I didn't think much of his teaching, because he didn't teach me much. He taught me very little. In fact, he had me on the C scale for six months, and I wanted to learn how to read fast, because I was playing with the school symphony, and then the kids in them bands, they had been studying for years on them violins
Holmes (10/9) - 15

and things, since they were little kids, and put a piece of a symphony or something up in front of, the conductor come down with this hands...I mean, they were right with it. Well, I wanted to learn how to read fast. I could read. I had a good idea, you know, a knowledge of music, but I couldn't read fast.
Now, were you getting any instruction in music in school, too?
Oh yeah.
At the same time.

Sure. Well, we didn't get no instruction. I mean, we were playing in the school... I was playing in the school orchestra. They didn't teach you nothin'. You were supposed to go there... They'd make up a band or an orchestra; you were supposed to sit down and play. But they didn't... You weren't being taught.
So you brought your skills to the band.
Mmm-hmm.
Now, I understand you were paying for these half-hour lessons.
Three dollars a half-hour.
That's a lot of money.
It was in them days. It was a hell of a lot of money.
Holmes (10/9) - 16
Especially if you felt you weren't getting anything out of it.

And that was thirty minutes. That was not thirty-one minutes. He was never a minute overtime. I mean, you know... Boy, that was the quickest half-hour. And he'd just keep you on one note, one note and blow, crescendo and diminuendo and all of this, that and the other. After six months (that was on the C scale), then he raised it up to the D scale. I said, 'Well, at this rate I'll be a hundred years old, and I might not even be able to play a song!' So I just put him down.
But you must have done a lot of practicing at home.

I practiced four and five hours a day by myself. I was interested, and I wanted to learn. At that time, we lived in a house that was three stories, and I was up in the attic -- my room was up in the attic. And I'd go up there, and I'd practice four and five hours a day. I just lived for music at that time, that's how inspired I was. I wanted to be good, man.

I just imagined that oboe was a saxophone. I just imagined that it was, you know! So I played the oboe. I studied and I learned all the music I could with it, you know...
Now, in these dances that you went to, did you ever
Holmes (10/9) - 17
bring your oboe and try to sit in or anything?
No! It's not a dance instrument.
No, I understand that.
No, definitely not.
But if your desire was so great, maybe you would try, even on the oboe.

No, no. I was ashamed to let people around Boston know I played oboe. The first thing they wanted to know was, 'What is an oboe?' They was just like I was. I never heard of an oboe until Dr. Holmes gave it to me.
Now, later on you must have studied with a Joseph Wagner in Boston.
Well, he was the conductor of the school symphony. He was the conductor.
I see. So he didn't give you any private tuition.
No. No private tuition.
He gave tuition to the whole band.
The only private tuition I had was with Trogliano(?). That's the one who kept me on the C scale.
Then through Joseph Wagner and playing with the school orchestra, you played in the Boston Civic Symphony Orchestra in 1926.
Yeah, that's right. But I don't remember the conductor's name of that.
Holmes (10/9) - 18
Were you part of that for a long time, then? You must have been going to rehearsals and things with the symphony orchestra. You didn't just sit in there.
Yes, I did.
For just one performance?
No-no-no, I was going to it.
So you attended rehearsals?

I was associated with it. But not for long. Maybe one season or something like that. Because let me see... In my third year in high school, my Daddy decided to buy me a saxophone. Well, I was never a Grade-A student. I would pass, my marks... I was a passable student. But when I got the saxophone, then my marks flopped, because I was out at night playing any place I could for nothing, and running around different places, you know, with my horn under my arm, and get home at 2-3-4-5 in the morning, and then be in school at 8 o'clock in the morning. Well, I'd go to school to sleep. Because you have to sleep sometime!
Do you remember the first horn you had? What make it was?
The first horn I had?
Yeah, the first saxophone.
A Pan-American. A Pan-American horn. Yeah, I remember it. It didn't have any pearl where the
Holmes (10/9) - 19
keys are. No pearl. Plain metal.
A silver or a gold color?
No, it was silver. There was no gold in them days.
Was it brand-new or second-hand?

Are you kiddin'? Brand new?! It was brand new to me, but it was not brand-new. Second-hand horn. Well, I did very good with it, I think. I played around at house parties and one thing or another, and then word got around Boston about some kid around the corner playing saxophone who sounded just like Johnny Hodges. Because you see, Johnny's name was very big. It got very big. And he was known not only all around Boston; all the bands that had come from New York were trying to get him to join their band.
You mean, all the bands that came through Boston wanted to take him with them.

Yes, of course. Eddie Haywood's daddy, he was playing a show that was a burlesque show, and he tried to get Johnny to go with him. But see, Johnny didn't read music at the time. Naturally, Johnny was... He was kind of shy, and he wasn't thinking about leaving town with no band and he didn't know anything about them, one of them things. So Johnny asked me if I wanted to go with him. I said, 'No,
Holmes (10/9) - 20
I won't go nowhere." One of them things. But I remember it was Eddie Haywood's daddy...

But I hung around Johnny, and I got to meet a lot of big-time musicians. And then the word got around that I could play, and I'd go from one to another. This is all in Boston. This all happened in Boston.
Once you got the saxophone, I guess you gave the oboe back to Dr. Holmes?
Oh, no. I gave him his oboe back before I went in high school. After the year was up and he told me after doing so good on the oboe, he decided to keep me on it, then I gave it back to him.
Because you were so disappointed.

But when I went to high school, they heard that I played oboe and they needed oboe players in the school orchestra. And I told them I didn't have an oboe. I said, "I don't mind practicing with the band and one thing or another, but I don't have one." "That's no problem. You just go to this address here, and they'll have an instrument for you."

So okay, I went and I got the instrument. It was a Lorais(?) oboe, brand-new. That's just like somebody gives you a car, and they come up and give you a Rolls-Royce. You know? It was about the best of the oboes; the Lorais(?)
Holmes (10/9) - 21
was the best. And brand-new. And I couldn't believe it. So I played it. I was glad to play it, you know. Oh, it was beautiful.
And that was the instrument that you played in the Boston Symphony with?
Yeah. Yeah, it was a beautiful instrument.
You never thought of later on buying an oboe for yourself?
I did buy one later on.
You did buy one.

I bought a Lorais(?) oboe later on. I kept it... That's after I came to New York. And I kept it and kept it, and I never played it, and the thing was just deteriorating in the case. And I finally sold it during the Depression for twenty-five dollars. Not that I needed the money. I was just tired of seeing it sitting around. I sold it for twenty-five dollars. It was worth about two-hundred and fifty then. And now, I don't know what... I guess you can buy a home cheaper than you can buy an oboe. They're very expensive things. Well, with this inflation and everything, you know...
You said around 1925, Fletcher Henderson's band came to Boston.
Yeah. Louis Armstrong was in it.
Holmes (10/9) - 22
And you went to hear the band.
Yeah. Louis was really blowin' something like I never heard before. But I didn't appreciate him, because he didn't look nice. But I didn't know... I shouldn't put this in there.
You mentioned it was unusual for a band of that size, first of all.

Oh, it was remarkable. Everything was precision. They was right together. Everything. Even that little sign-off they had. When they'd get through playing a set of dances, they'd go LUP-LOOP and everything would be right on the head, you know. LUP-LOOP. They were really sensational. Yeah, and Louis was blowing, too. He blew.
And repeat the personnel of that band that you heard then.

Well, in the reed section was Don Redman, Buster Bailey, alto saxophones, and Coleman Hawkins, tenor saxophone -- three reeds. Then in the trumpet section there was Elmer Chambers, Joe Smith, and Louis Armstrong. And the trombone was Big Green, Charlie Green. There was Kaiser Marshall on the drums. I think it was Escudero, I think that's his name, on the bass.
Yes.
And who else?
Holmes (10/9) - 23
Probably Dixon.
Oh, probably Charlie Dixon playing banjo.
And then Fletcher on the piano..
Fletcher on the piano, yes.
No vocalists or anything.

I didn't pay attention to the vocalist. Oh, Louis Armstrong was the vocalist. And he had a little megaphone -- because there was no microphones in them days. He had a little megaphone, singing through it, scattin'. He was scattin', because he didn't know the words. But he was sensational...
Did you go to that thing...? Was Carney there? Was Howard Johnson there? Johnny Hodges? Everybody went?
Well, I don't know if anyone of them particularly were there. But all the... You know, musicians and everybody else went. Yeah, I guess...
And it was a dance?
No, we didn't go with no band. No.
It was a dance that they played?
It was a dance, yeah. And we went as...
And there was no segregation at that dance or anything?
It was a Colored dance.
Oh, it was a Colored dance.
Yeah. See, they had played a White dance
Holmes (10/9) - 24

for about four hours before. And this dance, I think they came in around 1 o'clock, 12 or 1 o'clock. That other dance was out in the country somewhere, but this dance was in the city. They only played one hour.
Then before that, Hodges was playing with a little group, so that the people there had...
As a fill-in, yeah. He was with a pick-up band.
So that must have been one of the first times for Hodges, too, to hear Armstrong.

Well, I can say so. Well, I don't know. Because see, at that time Johnny was back and forth into New York and back. See, his family was still in Boston, and he'd run over here and he'd play with Bechet in different clubs and things for a few weeks and so, and months; then he'd run back to Boston. He was back and forth.
So chances are he'd already been to the Roseland.

I don't know if he went to the Roseland. He was working uptown in Harlem then. I don't know whether he went downtown or anything like that. But he was interested in blowin' his horn. And he loved to blow it! He played at practically all these clubs around there. Bechet had a club, and then there was a place called the Garden of Joy on Seventh Avenue. Oh, there was a lot of
Holmes (10/9) - 25
clubs around then.
Did any of the saxophonists in Henderson's band impress you at the time?

Yeah, Don Redman! Oh, Don I thought was great. He was. And I didn't know him before, you know. And Buster Bailey with the clarinet, oh...! Hawkins was a sensation, you know. Yeah, the whole reed section impressed me. And then when they'd play together.
And they doubled on everything, too.

Everything, oh yeah. Well, everybody doubled the clarinet. He had a sensational band at the time. Well, you didn't hear no bands that size. But as time went by, other bands come up, and Duke's band come along, and I started changing my ideas about who I liked and who I didn't like. Oh, there were a lot of bands...
What other bands did you hear, then, before you came to New York? What did you hear in Boston?

Well, they had Boston bands, you know. They had bands up there. But I can't remember the name. There was a band that did the most work, that was the most popular amongst the Colored people, was George Tines(?). He was a popular band. But there were a lot of bands...
What size was that band?
Oh, I don't know. Let me see. I'd say
Holmes (10/9) - 26
about 8 to 10 pieces, something like that.
And what did he play?
George Tines(?)?
Yeah.

I think he played piano. He played piano, and he had a very good drummer with him -- I'm trying to think of his name. Because I used to get them mixed up when I was a kid. I thought the drummer was the leader! I thought he was George Tines(?). But George Tines(?) was the piano player. He was a kind of quiet guy, but the drummer, he was the kind that would attract attention.
What kind of music were they playing primarily?
Oh, they were playing dance music.
Stocks? Straight things?
Stocks and...
Was there any Jazz at all to it, would you say?

Sure, it was. Sure. That's what killed me about this thing, talking about Jazz from New Orleans. It might be from there, but they were not the first ones to play it. Jazz has always been played amongst Black people. It's always been. Because I could... Man, when I was a little boy and my Mama would be ironing clothes or something, you know, and I'd be crawling around the floor, and she'd be ironing her clothes and just humming one of
Holmes (10/9) - 27
them spirituals or something. You talk about your Jazz! You would have to tap your foot. And she was just hummin' a spiritual. But I mean, the Jazz was there.

So I mean, you can't... I don't see how they can pinpoint it to one particular area in the country, when the same thing was happening all over the country! Any place you go where there were Black people, they were singing and doing the same thing. And it was not a whole lot of communication in them days like there is today. But that stuff got around. Yeah, it got around all right. I don't know...

It's very convenient. So we're all sittin' around. And I'm waiting for somebody to say somethin'. I was not an instigator of this idea. You know, I had no part of it. So I said, "Well, I'll start the ball rolling, then somebody else will pick me up." I just know somebody's going to pick me up. So I said, "Well, Mr. Mills, we decided with the crowd that we're getting on the road, that we're not making enough money, and we deserve a little bit more than what we're getting."

Well, Dillard, I mean, he exercised. He showed it. You know what I mean? Those big arms and big legs. He looked like a Greek goddess (sic). He looked like one of them weightlifters and things -- you know what I mean? He had the body to show it, too.

Yeah, Blanchard figured...he taken his family and went down to Florida. I don't know what year that was, but...

His son is a concert pianist right now. I don't know where he's playing, because I don't keep up with Classical music. But Blanchard, I don't know if he ever come back to New York or not. I never heard nobody say anything about him.

Now, tell me about Bingie Madison, because he was apparently quite an unusual musician.

Yes. He was an extraordinarily good musician. He could write... Oh, I mean, he could write fantastic things. The only trouble about Bingie's arrangements, they were written too hard. He had the brass on top of one another, reaching for the sky or something. And all the stuff was fast and very difficult. Very difficult stuff. When you'd be rehearsing and you couldn't make it and one thing or another, he'd sit back and laugh. he got a big kick out of the guys scufflin'. They'd be scufflin' trying to play it.
He could play his own music, though.
Oh, he could play it. Yeah, he could play it. But everybody else, they had to do what you call

Like, if you go to a place to hear a band play, you don't want to hear a band up there scufflin' over the music and it soundin' bad. You want it to be just right and nice. This guy, we'd be spittin' and carryin' on and one thing and another. The music was tough. It was really hard.
So in other words, it wasn't just tough for the sax section. It was tough for everybody.

Yeah, it was tough for the whole band. And that's for makin' a good band, you know. Who am I to say? I don't know about musicians, but I know it don't for makin' a good band. People pay their money, they want to hear you at your best, not at your worst.

Mmm-hmm.

Well, that's the way it was operated. The band would play... They would have what you call stock arrangements. You know what a stock arrangement is.
Yeah.

And they'd have a book about that thick with music. The way they used to play... The girls would get you a ticket. You'd play one chorus, and stop. She gets another ticket. When you stop, every time you stop they get a ticket. Maybe they play two choruses.
And this is what comes from that "ten cents a dance."
That's what it is! That's what it is. They called them "dancing schools" and then they called them

"taxi dance halls" and "ten cents a dance" -- they had a lot of names. The band would play... In fact, we were finishing up a number now, [DUH/DUH-DE-DUH-DE/DUP-DUP], one-two, into the next number -- here comes another ticket. And that's the way they played. Fifty-five minutes continuously, five minutes rest out of an hour. And they would work. I don't know how many hours they worked in them places, but they worked hard. I mean, you know...
So most of the time there was no original music. It was just stock after stock after stock.

Stock after stock, or anything they wanted to play. One of them head numbers, something like that. They'd make up something, 32 bars, and get it...so she could get a ticket for the dance. And I mean, you're playing the music, so you're playing fifty-five minutes of music each and every night. And say, it's nobody on the floor -- nobody dancing. You still have to play to an empty place. Well, you know how much inspiration you can get out of an empty ballroom, nobody on the floor, the girls are down on the other end there talking about this-that-and-the-other and one thing or another, and nobody on the dance floor -- and you're playing. So I mean, where is the inspiration? You know, there's nothin' then. Well, I mean, you got so you'd just automatically make some noise on ...(?)...

That's why I always tried to stay away from them. There was no inspiration for me. And I had to be inspired when I played. That's why I never went in too much for playing clubs and things where they sit down and drink and look at you. That to me was for the birds. I like to see people dancing, payin' attention to each other. Don't pay no attention to me. Pay attention to each other, dance and enjoy yourself. That's the kind of playing I like to do.

No.

Yeah, he would be in the studio. I mean, he wasn't doing anything. He was just there. He had nothing to say. If there was anything said, he would say it to Russell or the technicians or something. He had nothing to say to the band or anything.
You never saw him with a trumpet.

Oh, no. He didn't blow the trumpet. He was a sick man then. Too bad, too, because I always wanted to hear him play. Now, I mean, I wasn't too enthused about it. I mean, I'd just heard that he was a hell of a trumpet player, and naturally you'd like to hear him as much as you can. And to see the man and not to hear him, you know, it's kind of a letdown. But that's the way it was. I mean, I worked under his name, but I never heard him play.
Now, he, as you know, was offered the job to go into the Cotton Club.
Well, that was years before. Not years, but I mean...
A little while before.
Before that, yes.
Because presumably...

When I met him, he was at the end of the line. His teeth was bad, his gums or something -- he had pyorrhea. He couldn't blow his horn or anything. He was just at the end of his rope. He had a good-sounding band at the Savoy, but I don't know what happened between the business and why the band broke up. Then he went back to Chicago, and that was the end of it. He came back here and made some records, you know, and picked up whoever he could to make records.
Well, now, Russell's number, "Call of the Freaks" -- let me play you that. I think you switched to another instrument here.
[PLAYS "CALL OF THE FREAKS"]
You can make comments as you hear it.
Nice, nice, nice. Theme song.
Was that your theme song?
That was the theme song.
Actually. it was written by Barbarin.
He takes the credit for it?
Yeah, Barbarin has got credit for that.
Mmm-hmm. It's not his, though.
No?
No.
Who do you think?
Russell.
It was Russell's.
Yeah. Of course, Barbarin wrote a lot of numbers, though. He did write a lot of the songs. But that's not one of them. He might take the credit for the number. He really wrote...
Because there was a lot of "freaks"... Later on it was recorded as "The New Call Of The Freaks"...
Yeah. Well, we recorded it three or four different times.
Then later on, into the Thirties, it was "The Ghost of the Freaks."
No, I never heard that.

Then it was recorded the next day, actually, under...it was issued as a King Oliver thing. And it's on that one that you actually play soprano saxophone. But you felt it was a bit of a monotonous number?

Well, no. I mean, it was all right at the time, you know. It was a theme song, calling all the freaks together, you know... Heh-heh. No, it was all right, the number was all right. Just one of them things.
Now, did you rehearse for these recordings? Or was it material...? Obviously, you knew your theme song.
Well, I mean, numbers that we weren't

playing... See, while we was on the job working... You know, like, when we was workin' in a club a nightclub or something, boy, we rehearsed...we played the numbers during the night, and be rehearsing them while we're playing them. Then when we get to the studio, we'd know what we're doing. But sometimes, you get to the studio, there's... In them days, your numbers had to be under three minutes, two minutes and something. So the numbers we played were always longer than three minutes, and they would have to be cut down. Yes, we had to do a lot of cut-off here, and jump over to there, and one thing or another, and take out this and take out that. Yeah, there was a lot of... We had to rehearse most of the numbers because all our numbers were over three minutes long.
It's amazing what was compressed in under three minutes.
Mmm-hmm. See, now, today, you can record a half-hour one number, you know what I mean?
You can splice and do everything you want.
You can go ahead and play until. Record a whole symphony and anything. But we had to cut it to three minutes.
Well, now, most of the arranging was Russell's?
Well, at that time, for his band he did
most of the arranging.
But you could all chip in with ideas.
Well, we all had ideas. See, we had a lot of numbers that weren't even... They weren't written down. But most of them were written down. There was a lot of what's called head numbers.
I remember you used to say that Metcalf was full of ideas.

Oh yeah, he was full of ideas. Everybody had some kind of ideas. Some wasn't so good and some wasn't...one of them things. But who knows what's good or bad? But Metcalf, he was the lively one in the band. You know, he always had ideas and he was always playing this, that and the other, and jokin' and carryin' on.

It was always something going on in the band. It was a young band. Everybody was young in the band, and they behaved just like young people should. You know what I mean? We wasn't just sittin' up on the stand lookin' dead. There was something goin' on... We were the happiest people in the place!
Well, did you have any sense that you were creating music that was important to you and maybe to others?
It was important to everybody that heard it! Ha-ha. People were out there to have a good time, and
we were there to have a good time! And naturally, your music brings it out. Yeah, the band had as good a time as the public did.
What kind of audiences came?
Well, any kind. Any kind that wanted to come. We had all kind of audiences. Black audiences, White audiences...
What about age group?

Well, the age groups were young and.... We got up until 85 years old. Seen them out on the floor dancing. Yeah, there some old folks out there, too. Them old ones could dance just as good as the young ones. They were dancin' and cuttin' up.
But what I wondered is, was it the music of the young people? Because for instance...
This was the young people. We were the young people.
I know. I know.
Heh-heh-heh. Yeah, it was their music.
It was their music.
Oh yeah. Because when we went to work at the Savoy Ballroom, at that time they had a dance which was just created called the Lindy-Hop -- you know?
Mmm-hmm.

Boy, they were cuttin' them rugs, and one thing and another... Because you know, Lindbergh had just made his flight to Europe, and they had taken the name Lindy Hop, and it was this dance... And boy, the way they was throwin' their partners around and lifting them up in the air, and doin' all that gymnastics stuff and one thing and another...
You had to be young for that.

Oh yeah. Only young people could do it. The old ones do it and break their neck. All the young ones couldn't do it -- because I didn't want to do it. Yeah, it was strictly young people's music. That swinging music, that's strictly for young folks. At the Savoy you had that bright beat. You didn't have nothin' to worry about in the (?). Because if you have the right, by the time you finish your number, boy, that applause is going to bring you back again. But if you don't have the right beat when you finish your number, you just go into your next number. And when you sometimes get off the stand, they let you just get off the stand. The other band take over. But if you got the right beat on them now, in your last number, you don't get off the stand. They're not going to let you off. The applause is going to keep you right up there. And then all the bands started to do the best they could up there, get as

much applause as they could get.
That's why I worked in the Savoy so many different times. Russell's band was in and out of the Savoy just like he was the house band in there. So many, you know, different times... Because they knew the beat, what the dancers wanted. Like when we would have a battle of music there, nobody outshone Luis Russell's band. Because when he got through certain numbers...well, I mean, that was all she wrote.
I remember one flagwaver, I've forgotten the name of the thing, that you never recorded.
Yeah. Yeah...
That really brought the house down.

Well, we had about seven or eight house-breakers. Well, his "Old Man River" was the first one we had. And I attribute the idea to Louis Metcalf, his "Old Man River," because... It was just an arrangement gotten together from the band. But most of the ideas was Louis Metcalf on "Old Man River." And as we went along, we changed it four or five different times. And they even had a vocal in there on it, as part of the arrangement.
Yeah, Sonny Woods recorded it.
Yeah. Rex Stewart was in the band then.
Yeah, that was much later. Then, what about "Ease On
Down." Wasn't that a big number?

That was a... Well, I wouldn't say that was a house-breaker. Oh, it got its applause, all right. But we used that mostly when we played in theatre for the chorus girls to dance by. That was a chorus number, you know. That's the way we used it most of the time. That was a swingin' number, yes indeed. "Ease On Down." It was "Case On Down" on the record.
Well, they couldn't read Russell's handwriting, which was very small.
Well, yeah, it was misspelled "E-a-s-e" when it should have been "C-a-s-e."
No...
It should have been "E-a-s-e" but it was "C-a-s-e."
Well, it looked like a "C" apparently, and the people who did the graphics put it out as that. But it was really "Ease on Down."
Yeah, "Ease On Down."
Because it came out as "Case On Dawn." Which meant, obviously, nothing. Whereas "Ease On Down"...
Yeah.
...was a meaningful title. Do you remember any other numbers that would break up the house?
Well, there were quite a few of them. I don't remember the titles on anything. I was very poor on names and titles.
How about something like "Saratoga Shout"?
That's a good number, but that wasn't... "Saratoga Shout." Was that my number? No, my number was "Sugar Hill Function." "Saratoga Shout," that's my number.
Yeah, I think so.
Oh yeah. Yeah...I don't have much to say about that.
Okay.
No, that was a good number. A good dance number. A good arrangement, too. That was Metcalf's number.
What about "Panama"? You did that as an up number.
That was one of the top ones. [INAUDIBLE SENTENCE]
It's a shame I can't remember what that flagwaver was.
"Panama" was one of them.
Yeah.
I can't recall them numbers and things -- the names. See, if a bunch of us get together and get to talkin'... That's not being taped, is it?
Yeah, we're taping now. It doesn't matter.
All right. Well, I won't say what I was going to say. No, I was going to say if a bunch of us got together talking about different things that happened, then things would come to you..
Right. We should have Greely here. Now, in the Russell band, you mentioned you liked it because you could play either soprano or alto, as you pleased.
Yes.
So there was never any need to feel a constraint.
No...
If you felt like picking up the...
I enjoyed working in Russell's band more than any band I ever worked with. At ease, you know what I mean? No restraint there at all or nothin'.
And you always played a straight soprano.
Always. I never could play the other. I don't know if I could or not. I never tried to play the other. The curved?
Mmm-hmm.
I never had one of my own, and I never attempted to blow anybody else's.
Was it a Selmer?
No. Are you kiddin'? The soprano?
Yeah.
No. C.B. Conn. Selmer to me in those days was...that was a saxophone for somebody else. I didn't want to see them. And truthfully speaking, I never cared too much about it.
Was your alto also a Conn?
Yes.
Were most altoists playing Conns there?

Conns and Bushes. Plus other makes. But there wasn't too many Selmers in those days. Not around, you know. Tenor players liked the play the Conn tenors, because the tenor had a big bell to it. You know, they'd get a big sound out of it. But then Selmer instruments began to get popular, and everything turned Selmer. But I never cared too much about a Selmer. I had two, two Selmer horns -- it was all right. You know, I didn't take to them. Now, maybe I just couldn't play it. But I liked the Conn. Everybody had a quirk that they (?).
Now, you also mentioned that you tried to play flute later on, but that was...

Oh, yes. I had a flute of my own. And I always figured there was something wrong with the flute, because I couldn't play it. So I sold the flute for ten dollars. And then years later, Greely Walton loaned me his flute, which he had been playing and there was nothing wrong

with his flute; I still couldn't play that one. Then he taken his flute back, after he saw that I wasn't doing anything with it, and Howard Johnson, he loaned me his flute -- he had two. I couldn't play his flute either.

So I guess I just wasn't meant to be a flute player. And I love the instrument. I love flute. Like they say, I'm just a one-instrument man. Take me away from the alto, and I'm lost with everything else.
Not with soprano.
Well, I don't know if I'd be...how I would sound on that now.
No. But at the time you could double.

At the time, I loved soprano. I think I liked it better than I did the alto. I think I liked the soprano better than I did alto at the time. But I had my soprano stolen from me, and that was the end of the soprano. I wouldn't buy another one. Because it wasn't my fault it was stolen. It got stolen from a club we were workin' out in California, you know -- taken off the bandstand. I know the house was insured for instruments and things. But nothing was ever done about it. That was the end of that.
During these days you were in and out of the recording studios quite a bit.
Yeah, back in the Thirties, in the early
Thirties, the Twenties -- late Twenties, early Thirties.

My experience has been that most musicians didn't bother with their own records? Did you...? I mean, it seems to me you'd want to hear what you sound like. Didn't you buy your own records and have them?

Buy 'em? I didn't even want to hear any of 'em! You played some records for me i never heard that I had recorded. I had never heard some of the records that I heard; you know, that you played for me...
Yeah.
No, I don't want to hear them.

In other words, it seems like you mostly tossed these things off, it was another thing to do, and nobody ever collected their own records or anything. Although I've noticed that many musicians kept scrapbooks.

Yeah. Well, they would go in for scrapbooks and things like that -- which I never did either. I don't know. I didn't think too much of the music business. I mean, I was having a good time, that's all. Everything was good. Have a good time. That's one of the memories of it. You know, I didn't keep anything.
Like, I worked with a lot of celebrities. Big people. And now that I have become an old man, you know, out of the business...now I'm sorry I did not have my picture taken

with some of these celebrities that I have worked with and know -- I knew 'em on a first-name basis. I can't come up to the children nowadays and say, "Well, I know so-and-so-and-so. I worked with him," and this-that-and-the-other. They'd say, "That old man is crazy. He just said he knows so-and-so..." Well, that's the way they think of you.

No, I never thought about getting together with them and having my picture taken, and this-that-and-the-other. The nearest I come to anything like that, I worked the Palace Theatre...oh, this is way back in the Thirties. Edward G. Robinson was on the bill and Kate Smith was on the bill, and Bessie Love -- Bessie Love was a movie star. Well, Edward G. Robinson at that time, he was just starting in pictures. He was a big man, he was a big star. So I went to Edward G. Robinson in his dressing room, and I asked him for a photograph. And he gave it to me. And I went into Bessie Love's room, and she gave one to me -- an autographed photograph.

But I mean, I had never did anything like that! And all down through my career I never did it no more. I got Edward G. Robinson's and Bessie Love's -- Kate Smith didn't have any photographs of herself. I didn't get none of her anyway, and I worked with her twice. I didn't ask her for one the second time. But Bessie Love I got. And I got 'em,
I still got 'em, and I cherish them.

But I worked with, oh, hundreds of big stars. Nothin' to prove it. Now, I worked with Louis for five years. I don't think there's a picture where I'm even shakin' hands with Louis or anything, just the two of us. Never. Nothin'. Same with Duke Ellington I have nothing to prove that I even know him. And so many of the others. Not to go that far back, but even... Well, anyway...
What are you thinking about?
Down at the Empire... Not the Empire Room, but the old ...(?)...
What do you mean? The presence there of Sy Oliver?

Sy Oliver. Even Sy Oliver. He was crazy about me, believe me. I was one of his favorite saxophone men. I don't even have a picture of anything with him. And a lot of people, they don't know I even worked with the man! I worked with him plenty. Sy Oliver... I don't have a photograph or anything. So many of them I worked with. I didn't think of it. Now I'm kind of sorry. You know, I'm up in age, and I don't have nothin' to prove to anybody that I ever did anything.
What really kind of woke me up to that was years ago, a fellow I used to work with who used to be in Claude Hopkins' band, a trumpet player...
O.B. Olsten.
No, it wasn't O.B. Sylvester Lewis.
Oh, Sylvester Lewis.

Sylvester Lewis was his name. He was very much a part of Claude Hopkins' band, you know. And down through the war years, the broke up, he came out of Claude's band, and he was the manager of a USO show that went overseas -- and I was with the band; I was with his show. Oh, we had a wonderful trip over there. It was only... We were there six months. But it was wonderful. And he was a really good manager.

Well, he stopped playing his horn... After he came back, he stopped playing his horn altogether, and he got a job in the subway. He was working in the subway. He had been working there for years, you know. And one day him and I, we had a... He had a gig, he had a little dance to play, and at that time I had got my first tape recorder. So I came with the tape recorder on the job. And it was his band, you know. And I taped it on the job.

So a few years later, he comes by the house and says, "Charlie, you still have that tape of that job?" And I said, "Yeah, I still have it." He said, "Well, can I borrow that tape?" I said, "Well, what do you want to borrow it for? For what?" He said, "You know, up there where I'm

working, the fellows up there, they don't believe I'm a musician. And I want to prove to them that I had a band, and I was a musician." I said, "If they don't believe you was a musician, what they think you were?" I just taken it for granted; he'd been a musician to me ever since I knew him. But the people he was working with then, the guys that he was working with, they didn't believe he was a musician. I said, "Well, how can that be? Everybody knows you're a musician."

Well, see, as you get older and you get away from things, then you start thinking back on what you should have done -- should have done. To me, that sounds ridiculous. To me, because somebody did not know he was a musician. I knew he was a musician.

Well, the same thing happens to me. Now, I've gotten older, and people meet me, they've never heard of me. See, I've never been a leader, and I've always been a sideman. And I was never a big star or anything like that. I wasn't out on my own. I always worked as a sideman for somebody else. So my name was not in the public's eye. The public didn't know nothin' about Charlie Holmes. Certain ones in the public did.
But nonetheless,, you are still well-known the world over through your recordings, through your life, and because
of that Rutgers is now interested in doing this...
Yeah. Well, through the recordings... I've recorded with some pretty big people, you know; pretty nice stars and one thing or another.
And we mustn't discount the fact that you are a superb saxophonist. I said that.
Ah-ha-ha. I know you did. I know you did. And I like to hear that. Now I like to hear it, because now I'm not in the business. Yeah, I'm glad somebody thinks I was.
Well, I think you never really had any trouble getting jobs, did you?

No, no, never. That's right. I think I lost more friends by not taking jobs than I...you know, because I wouldn't work certain places, with certain conditions, or this-that-and-the-other. In other words, I was kind of hard to get along with.
And during your career, there was no lack of saxophonists.

Oh, there was always plenty of saxophonists. Always. Good ones, too. Well, there's always plenty of musicians. Yeah. It's been a good business. I just don't like the music business. The life is beautiful. But when you get old, you get out of it.
Then you grow up, you know. That's for young people. It's really for a single man...
