[TAPE III, SIDE 2 STARTS WITH "TIGHT LIKE THAT"]
That's you on clarinet.
Mmm-hmm.
Do you remember that vocalist?
Oh, yeah. That's Bichon(?).
Was he around New York then?

No, he come in... Well, I mean, he was trying to make it, but he didn't last too long. He didn't stay around too long. You know, he didn't get no breaks. I worked with him at the Chez Florence downtown, as part of a nightclub act. I think I was telling you about it.
Yes.
He was one of the entertainers down there. He was working down there.
Now, he was New Orleans.
He was from New Orleans. He came in... Russell brought him in, and then he was working around, making records, one thing or another. Then he got this job
at the Chez Florence... You know, at that time I had left Russell's band again, and I was at the Chez Florence. Good job all my good jobs blow up. I think it lasted two weeks.
Now, "It's Tight Like That," the title, that must have been an expression.
Yeah...
[PAUSE: TELEPHONE]
[MUSIC PLAYS]
The band had changed now, because now you've got Pops Foster on bass...
Well, he had (?) in the band ....(?)....
[DURING TRUMPET SOLO] That's Red Allen. [THEN DURING CHORUS, A LEAD VOCAL]...
That's Metcalf.
Metcalf. [ANOTHER RED ALLEN TRUMPET SOLO] [AS MUSIC ENDS...] I had forgotten all about that recording. Yeah, I forgot all about that.
Now, there it appears, at the end, that there's piano as well as chimes going at the same time.

Well, I wasn't paying particular attention. But it could have been that after the piano finished, then you hear maybe the chimes. Maybe he just picked up and hit the chord. Maybe. I wasn't paying attention to when the chimes were. Maybe that was Paul Barbarin...
On the chimes.
...on the chimes.
I think so.
Because he had chimes of his own. He had bells or whatever they called them that he used to it. He used to play 'em pretty good, too.
Yeah, I think it must have been Barbarin, because they were too much together.
Yeah. I wasn't particularly paying attention to it.
Metcalf told me when I played it for him once, that although he was out of the band, Russell called him up because he said, 'We're going to record your number.'
That's possible, yeah.
And he came down, and he didn't bring his horn, but he was just there to do the vocals.
Yeah.
The vocalists on that are Henry Allen, J.C. Higgenbotham and Louis Metcalf.
Louis Metcalf, yeah.
You can clearly hear him on there.
Well, it's his... They're his lyrics. You know what I mean?! Heh-heh. Yeah, they are his lyrics. He contributed sayings and things to a lot of little numbers
that didn't stay in the book. Because he was a fun guy, you know. He was always sittin' on the bandstand playin'. I mean, you know, crackin' jokes and one thing or another. Yeah, he loved fun.
Now he at that time was probably the trumpeter in New York.
No, they had a lot of trumpeters in New York. But he wasn't the trumpeter.
I mean, he was one of the top.

He was a good trumpeter. He was one of the good ones. And there was a lot of them, a lot of good ones. There was never no shortage of trying to find a good trumpeter. There was Bobby Stark, we had what's his name, who used to be with Fletcher, the fat....
Joe Smith?
No-no.
Russell Smith?
No. A short, fat one. He was with Fletcher, he was with Chick, he was with Russell's band -- he was with the band playing "Old Man River."
Oh, Rex Stewart.
Rex Stewart. There was a lot of trumpet players. But they was all in the same classification. One was no more outstanding than the other.
But at the time you were at the Savoy, wasn't...?

Louis had a crown made. Louis Metcalf had a crown. He was the king. That's because Russell had so many show-stopping numbers we used to play, and naturally, we'd finish one of them numbers and the applause would bring the house down, as they say. Well, naturally, the trumpet player, he'd take the bow, you know -- because they played louder than anybody else. So that made him the King. Metcalf was the King, you know. He had his crown and everything.

So Louis Armstrong comes to New York for a two-day engagement at the Savoy, and he was playing in front Russell's band. So when Louis played his first number, he opened up and played the first number...
What was it? Do you remember the number?

I don't remember the opening number. But I know on the end of it he played a high F, which in them days, that had never been heard of before. And Louis hit that F, big and broad and loud and clear. And the house did come tumblin' down. That's when Teddy Hill got'up and turned around to Louis Metcalf, with that crown on his head, and snatched the crown off and threw it out in the audience! -- and said, "The King is now dethroned." Heh. "There's a new King. Long live the King." He was talkin' about Louis
Armstrong.
And on that two-day visit that Armstrong made to New York, that's when you went in the recording studio.
We went in the recording studio the next day.
And that actually, according to Rust, was on March 5, 1929.
Yeah. And we started making a series of records and things. I don't know, I think we was makin'...I think was makin' "I Can't Give You Anything But Love."
Yes, that's correct. You recorded that.

I know it had taken us the whole session to make one side -- "I Can't Give You Anything But Love." We came back to the studio again, I think it was the day he finished, the next day after he finished at the Savoy. He was only there two nights. And the day after, when he finished at the Savoy, we was back in the studio again makin' some more records.
In fact, Louis kept us pretty busy there the short time that he was in New York.
Now, why it took so long to do "I Can't Give You Anything But Love" was because they really were trying to feature Louis, or...?
Oh, it was Louis. Everything was Louis.

Everything had to be perfect for him, according to the technicians. They were the ones back in the room with the stuff on their ears, and this-that-and-the-other, placing him here and placing the horns there. In them days, you didn't have no microphones up there. It was strictly a thing with a whole lot of horns, and you'd play into the horns.

Recording was very hard in them days. It was very tough. Because you weren't allowed to use drums, so you had no drums. You had a brass section, and the brass would way back in the back someplace. The reeds would be up in the front by the horns, and the brass would be someplace. and Louis might be blowing out the window somewhere! You know what I mean? Everything was disruptive. Not like the recording is today. A band goes in today, and they play just like they're on the bandstand, at ease; I mean, they play the same way. But not in them days. You just barely whispered into your horn. You could just barely hear it, you know. I don't know how they got such good recordings as they did, because they got some wonderful recordings, under the systems that they were using. But it was tough, it was tough.
Now, you said they had no arrangement or set routine for this "I Can't Give You Anything But Love," so they kept
trying new things...

Oh, no. There was no arrangement. I mean, there was nothing written out for it. They had no music whatsoever. The first thing, they had to get the time on the thing. It had to be under three minutes. So they had to figure how many choruses, how many interludes, bars you could put in there to fill out the time or something, and this-and-the-other. Time you'd get one thing straight, there'd be something else to figure out. I don't know, the big mechanical heads which were running the thing, they had all the say. We were just... The musicians, we were just there. We had nothing to say whatsoever. Just do as you're told. One of them things.
So you remember, then, that nothing more was accomplished that day than that one number.
That one number. That one side.
And then later on, you came back and did "Mahogany Hall Stomp."
Yeah, that's right. Which it could have been the day after...
Which was a completely foreign title to you. You didn't know anything about...
Well, I mean, it was really... That's all it was, was a title. Because he come in with a lead...
Hoagy Carmichael come in the studio; we were recording something else when he come in. And he come into the studio with this lead sheet in his hand, a lead sheet... You know what a lead sheet is.
Yeah.

One sheet of paper with the melody on it. He asked Louis would he record this number for him. And Louis said, "Sure Pops. Anything." And he didn't even look at the paper. He didn't know what was on it. So they went to the piano, and asked Russell if he'd play it, so they could, you know, hear what it was. So after Hoagy put out...played the music, you know, then Louis Armstrong said, "Yeah, we can make this. Can't we, Pops" -- talkin' to Luis Russell. He said, "Can't we, Pops." Russell said, "Mmm, yeah, I'll make a little arrangement for it."

So he sat over in a corner and wrote up some notes for the introduction, with different instruments, and then ...[SINGS OPENING]... He wrote {SINGS} for the instruments, then Louis made it ...[SINGS ARMSTRONG'S LINE]... -- all right, that's the introduction. "Now, Louis, you play the melody," and Louis played the melody or the verse or whatever it's called -- I don't know. And Russell made like a little organ background for the band. "Now, after so-and-so-and-so, then you play this chorus," and he'd pass out the
choruses who was to play this-that-and-the-other. And when he got through, he had an arrangement.

Well, so much for "Mahogany Hall Stomp." That was my version. Do you know what I mean. "Mahogany Hall Stomp," forget it. All right, let's get on to something now. Let's get back to the recording. Because I mean, to me it was nothing. It didn't mean nothin'. So we finished recording what other numbers we had to do, and the session was over that.

Well, when the numbers came out... They didn't come out quick in those days. Records taken a long time to come out. Almost taken a little bit longer than...almost as long as the money forthcoming to you. And when did come out, what we find out was the biggest hit of all of 'em, the one that we're talkin' about was "Mahogany Hall Stomp."
And that's the one that was spontaneously created right in the studio.

Yeah. And it was nothin'! I said, "Oh, that ain't nothin'. Get through with that." And that was the hit. That was really the hit. The ones that we did have real written-out arrangements for, and one-thing-or-another, they were all right, they were good. But "Mahogany Hall" was the... That got the big writeup. I couldn't believe it. I said, "Well, I'll have to get this record and
see what makes it so good." I didn't believe it was the same recording that we'd made, according to the writeups. The writeups was out before the record was. So much for writin' a hit!
How much did you get paid for recording, and...?
Well, we won't go into the pay now. No-no-no, don't go into that. I can't have my feelings hurt again.
And from whom did you get paid? Usually from the bandleader?
Well, the money I think was paid by the studio, the company you worked for.
But you didn't collect then and there?
Then and there?
Yeah.

It would be from three to six months gettin' paid. Three to six months later. No, you didn't get it then and there. But I think we did get paid for "Can't Give You Anything But Love." We got paid right away for that. I think so, yeah. But the rest of the numbers, we had to wait until they did the rest of the recording. You had to wait in them days for your money.
And Russell handled all the business, right?
He taken care of the business, yeah.
So as long as you were in his band, you got then a bonus for the recordings later? Or how did you know what was for the recordings and what was your salary?

You got paid whatever you were promised. Sometimes you got it, sometimes you didn't. But what you got, that was for your record. And that was the end of your record, as far as you were concerned. You got paid for making a record and that was it. No bonus, no nothin', no... Now, the rest of it, that's between the leader, the leader of the band or the star or the big-shots, between them... It had nothing to do with the musicians. The musicians just made the date, and got their little salary, whatever they was promised to get, and that was the end of it.
Now, in the discography, it's mentioned that Eddie Condon was on banjo and Lonnie Johnson was on guitar on this "I Can't Give You Anything But Love" session. Do you remember Eddie Condon being there?

Yeah, he was... Well, he was in the studio every time Pops was. He was in the studio. You know what I mean? Yeah, he was the studio every time Pops made a record. Not only him, all his boys. Oh, there was a bunch of them. Mezz Mezzrow, you know, the Reefer King? Yeah, he was there. All them boys. They used to follow him around
like he was a (?)sea dog(?) or something.
Well, now, the studios didn't have a limit on how many people could come?

Not as far as he was concerned. Not as far as Louis. Louis was the King. They were trying to make them some money. Oh, he was a big asset to any company was goin' for. Oh, he had all his boys down there, all or any of them. The studio be full of more bystanders around there than there was in the band. Sure. That's why half the time I can't remember who was in the band or who was just lookin' on.
Yeah, he had his boys. Well, they was behind him, because they was... They was followin' him around like a (?)sea dog(?).
I see. Well, while you were with Russell at the Saratoga Club, you have mentioned that Hodges used to come in sometimes and sit in for you...

No, not often. He did come in. He come into the matinee on Sunday. That was the only time they had a crowd in there. They had a matinee on Sunday' which was leased out to a private club. And they'd run this Sunday matinee dance with younger people, you know. That's the only time we had a crowd in there.
So naturally, Hodges would come in. All different musicians would come in. And Hodges, naturally, I'd ask him to come up and play for me. And he'd be glad to. He loved to blow anyway.
What I'm leading up to is the one time at least when his first wife was having a baby, and he asked you to sub for him.
Yeah. Right.
And you made a broadcast.
Yeah, Duke was broadcasting. I didn't make the broadcast. I broadcast in the band, with Duke Ellington's band. It was Duke's band.
And that was at the Cotton Club.
At the Cotton Club, yes.
And on one number you took a solo.
Yeah.
Duke turned around and said "Take it."
Yes. Well, I went out there and played what I knew -- a little bit.
Do you remember what number it was?
No, I really don't. I don't remember the numbers. But it was somethin that I was familiar with. I mean, it didn't mean anything to me then. I knew everything that was being played.
Is that the first and only time that you were with Duke?
That's the only time I sat in his band...
And actually played in the band.
Actually while he was working. This was on a broadcast. Yeah, that's the only time.
And then, the next day, you and Johnny were walking down the street...

Yeah. Johnny and his brother-in-law, Kirkpatrick. The three of us were walking down Lenox Avenue, going around to the Bandbox, the musicians' club. And Kirk and Johnny were talking (Kirkpatrick and Johnny), and Kirk was saying, "I caught the broadcast last night. It sounded damn good" -- telling Johnny how good he sound. And Johnny looked at me and smiled, and Johnny said, "That wasn't me, that was Charlie."
So you had a good laugh at that.

Well, it made me feel good, you know, to have somebody else compliment somebody like Johnny Hodges to tell them they sound good, and he knew himself it wasn't him! [LAUGHS] One thing, he give me the credit for it. "It wasn't me; that was Charlie."
Now, Russell made some recordings with Bill Coleman in the band. Was he ever regular in the band?
Bill, he was in there regularly.
So he wasn't just added for the recordings.
No. He was in the band later. But he stayed on. I don't know how long he stayed. Well, I don't know what recordings he ever made. But he made some. But he wasn't in a lot of them.
[PAUSE]
"Feeling The Spirit" and we'll spot the... [PLAYS "FEELIN' THE SPIRIT"] Higgy.
Higgenbotham. Albert Nicholas, clarinet. [TROMBONE SOLO] J.C. Higgenbotham, trombone... [TRUMPET SOLO] Bill Coleman, trumpet... [ENSEMBLE]
Are you reading?
Oh yeah. Yeah, we're reading. Some of us are reading. [SINGER] J.C. Higgenbotham, scat-singing. [TENOR SOLO] Teddy Hill... [CLARINET OVER ENSEMBLE] Red Allen.
[MUSIC ENDS]
I'd like to do the same for "Josie Lightning," which was another flag-waver.
[PLAYS "JOSIE LIGHTNING"]
[CLARINET OPENING SOLO] [THEN PIANO] That was Russell.
Oh, Luis Russell, piano. [AFTER BASS SOLO
AGAINST ENSEMBLE, THERE'S A TRUMPET SOLO] Red Allen. [FAST ENNSEMBLE]
Reading again?
Yeah. [TROMBONE SOLO] J.C. Higgenbotham. [ALTO SOLO 8 BARS]
Charlie Holmes.
[TROMBONE, 8 BARS, THEN TRUMPET SOLO] That's Red. [CLARINET SOLO] Albert Nicholas. ["JOSIE LIGHTNING" ENDS]
On those parts where you're reading, that wouldn't have been the first time you were seeing that music, was it?
No, that had been played many a time before we recorded it.
But you brought the music in with you and had it...

Oh yeah. They carried the music like you carry in your saxophone. Because they had a whole thing full of books, and everybody... Each book was about that thick with music. They had plenty of music to read. And it was tough reading, too, in them days -- tough arrangements.
Now, with Pops Foster on the string bass, that was somewhat unusual, because weren't most of the bands still playing tubas?
They were playing tubas. In fact, the only
band at that time that was using a string bass was Duke Ellington.
With Wellman Braud.
With Wellman Braud.
Well, Foster was also from New Orleans. So the New Orleans basses were usually string.

Well, when they had a bass, it was a string bass. In fact, Pops Foster changed the style in New York. See, they didn't change... See, Braud had been playing here for years, string bass, with Duke, and even before Duke. He didn't need nothin'. Soon as Pops Foster come around with the bass, then they all started to change it around, playing his style(?) on the bass.
Would you say at about the same time the banjo was fading out in favor of the guitar, or...?

No, it was before that. The guitar... It was all right; the banjo was all right in the band. Well, I guess... Well, I would say around the same time. But neither one of them was too popular in bands. They were being used in some bands, and some bands they weren't. But guitar had a hard way to go. They were usually the last ones to be hired in a band. They would even come behind the trombones; they would hire the trombones before they could have a guitar!
Well, it was hard for a guitar to be heard.
It would, yeah. But then they come into their day... They're in their day now. They're havin' their day now. They really got it now.
Well, then, did a lot of bass players come around to listen to Pops?

Everyone in New York come to listen to Pops. I don't know why, but they did. Yeah, he was very popular. Very popular. And he was a nice guy. Pops was really a nice guy. And I could understand why he become popular, because he was very nice.
And he was a very good bassist, too.
He was a very good bassist, and he loved to play his instrument.
Would you comment on the Luis Russell rhythm section? A lot of people have said it's one of the best rhythm sections ever.

Well, for what they were playing, the style of music they were playing, it was the best. Because they had a beat. I mean, you can't get away from it. They had a beat, you know. Strictly their own style.
And that must have helped the front line.
You had to pat your feet. What they say, if you can't pat your feet, it's not Jazz.
Well, now, would you say you were inspired by this kind of a rhythm section?

Oh, I loved it. Yes, indeed. Paul Barbarin. Boy, he... Nothin' flashy about it. But see, with a rhythm section, you're not supposed to hear it... Like drums and all of this technique... You're not supposed to hear the rhythm section. You're supposed to feel it. You're supposed to feel that rhythm. You're not supposed to hear it, a whole lot of bangin' and this-that-and-the-other. That's not a rhythm section. But it's supposed to inspire you, make you want to dance or do something, make you pat your feet, do something, move your fingers -- but move something. That's a rhythm section. Yeah, he had a wonderful rhythm section.

That's one thing I used to like about Duke's band, when Sonny Greer was in the band. Sonny was never acclaimed to be what you call a real star drummer, you know. But when he was with Duke's band, I don't care what other drummer Duke had or used in his band. None of them fit in the band like Sonny Greer did. Sonny had an old-fashioned beat, [SINGS IT], real jungle effect music. And it fit right into Duke's band. It just fit there. And when Sonny left the band, Duke tried out a whole lot of drummers, a whole lot of drummers, but none of them fit in the band like Sonny did.
It just didn't sound the same.
Well, that's the same way with Russell's rhythm section. The style of music he was playing, it couldn't be beat.
Were there any other drummers at the time that you thought were very good?

Oh yeah, a lot of drummers around. Big Sid... Oh, a lot of drummers around. Some of them made a big name, some of them didn't. But all of them made a living. Some of them didn't care to make big names. That's just not...not only drummers. I mean, any instrument you can name. They had all kind of instruments in New York City, and players and one-thing-or-another. Everybody didn't get a big break, or this-that-and-the-other.

Now, there's a man today like...name... Because you'd know him. But he's been around here for years, too. He's never been a big name on his own, but today he is. And this goes from way back. A marvelous trumpet player, one of the best in the business. And he just worked from this place to that place, to this band, the other band, the best of jobs, the best of bands or the worst of bands -- it didn't make no difference. It was work. And that's Doc Cheatham. Do you understand what I mean? He was always a sideman, or working for somebody else. He was never up-front as a leader,

trying to get it on his own.
That's why some people that you've never even heard of, they be in the business fifty or sixty years, and they work all the time -- nobody ever hears of them. They don't try to front anything on their own, but they're working all the time with the best attractions, and so forth and so on. And they are good musicians. Doc is one of the best trumpet players in the business, and he works with the best... You name anything and he can play it. I mean, any kind of music, any kind of show. He does the job.

And there's a lot of musicians around just like Doc. I wouldn't say they're as capable as he is, not trumpet players... But there's a lot of good trumpet players, too, in his classification. Nobody ever hears of 'em. Some of them work all the time, just go around mindin' their business, doin' the work, getting the money...
Now, in these early days, was there a Rhythm Club then where everybody collected? Or was it the Bandbox?

Well, they used to collect around the Bandbox, and then the Bandbox was... The Rhythm Club was opened by a fellow who come from Chicago. He opened up the Rhythm Club right around the corner from the Bandbox, the next corner. And it was a better-looking place, it was a larger place -- it had a pool table there. So naturally,
the fellas went around the corner. And that kind of taken all the crowd away from the Bandbox.
Where was it? Do you remember the street?
The Rhythm Club?
Yeah.

Yeah. That was One Hundred Thirty-Second Street and Seventh Avenue. The Bandbox was One Hundred Thirty-First Street and Seventh Avenue. So it was right around the corner. But it was a better place, it was a newer place, and it was a lively place. All the musicians talkin' and hangin' in there. The Bandbox finally faded out.
And where did you first run into Jelly Roll Morton? Was it at the Rhythm Club?

No, it was the Bandbox. He come in the Bandbox, and he was playing piano in there. Somebody said to me, 'That's Jelly Roll Morton.' I said, 'Jelly Morton? I never heard of him.' He was sittin' down there playin' the piano, Mister Jelly Lord. Mister Jelly Lord! I don't know what the hell can I say about him. Mister'Jelly Lord, don't come up with that old-time stuff! Heh-heh. After that, I met him, you know, and I found out who he was. He was all right. But he'd stand out on the corner and give all the musicians hell -- give everybody hell. He was a
loud-mouthed guy, you know. But he was all right.
Happy Caldwell told me he used to always have a crowd around him and...
Oh, he would always have a crowd.
...they'd egg him on and tell him 'You can't play piano' and...

Oh yeah, he would talk... Oh, he loved to play. Play and sing his numbers. Sure. Jelly was all right if you knew him. Yeah, Jelly Roll contributed a lot to music. Good guy. No dummy. He was not a dummy at all.
Now, you recorded with him at one time.
Yeah. Well, I recorded with... He was on the same record I was on with Wilton Crawley(?). Boy, that was somethin'.
Tell me about that.

I don't know how to even start that, because I don't know what happened. Russell was supposed to get a group to record with Wilton Crawley, and Jelly Roll was supposed to play piano. And Jelly Roll walked in there with his group. And there was a big conflict right there, because Wilton Crawley wanted Russell's group and Jelly was going to have his group -- he got his band with him. So I don't know, we compromised. Some of the guys played some of the records and the rest of them played on the other ones --
the rest of the record. Split it up, one of them things.
Because I remember once you told me it was like two prima donnas walking in, and...

Oh yeah, yeah! It was somethin' else. And they was at one another's throats all day long, making cracks at one another, you know. Yeah, Wilton Crawley had just finished playing the Lafayette Theatre, a Black theatre, and he had just finished playing a week there. So Jelly Roll is sittin' at the piano, makes a smart remark. He says, 'Well...'
[END OF TAPE III, SIDE 2]
...Wilton Crawley, and Jelly looks up from the piano.
"I dug you at the Lafayette Theatre" -- the Lafayette Theatre was in Harlem. So Wilton looks back at him and says, "Well, now you can dig me next week at the Paramount Theatre" -- downtown.
Keep on.
That's it.
Oh, I see! Anyway, as I understand it, they squared off, because Jelly thought that the records would sell because he was on them.
Well, Jelly heard a little part on the
piano. He had a little break in the number. And Jelly said, 'This is gonna sell the number.' BRR-RUMMPH. Wilton said, 'Wilton Crawley's name is on the record. That's what's gonna sell the number.'
So anyway, you got through the day.
Well, we finally made it.
Now, did Wilton Crawley do any of his stunts while in the studio?

Not while he's recording. Who's gonna see it? Nobody but us, and we didn't want to see it. Throwin' his clarinet and slap-tonguing on his clarinet and one-thing-and-another. He was quite good on that clarinet. I was actually surprised.
Well, the records to me show he had a lot of drive.

Yeah, that's what I say. He was very good. And I liked him now that I've heard him...you know, now, than I did then when I was recording with him. I couldn't stand him then. Well, I mean, i don't want to say I couldn't stand him. It was just a date, just another date, you know. But now that I can sit back and listen to the records, and... I mean he amazes me now. His tone is beautiful on them. I mean, for an...he's what you would call an unrehearsed musician. He just picks up the clarinet and starts doing funny things with it, and gets a wonderful
tone for...
Now, when he did his show, he was like a solo performer.

He was a solo performer. He'd come out and do his act. He had an act. And he'd come out there, and he'd take the clarinet all apart until he was playing nothing but... He'd take the bell off first, and he's playing the clarinet, then he'd take off the first joint, and then he'd take off the second joint, and then he'd take off the tuning barrel -- until he's left with nothing but the mouthpiece, and he's blowin' that. Then he comes back on the stage with the clarinet put back together again, he comes up and he's blowin', blowin'-blowin'-blowin', and he goes into some gymnastic turn or something, and the first thing you know, he's blowin' the clarinet and he's standin' on his head. His head is on the floor and he's still blowin' the clarinet.
You saw his show at the Lafayette?
Oh yeah. Many a time. Sure.
He was a popular performer.
He did all right. Oh yeah. He was very good. Very good with the clarinet.
I guess he traveled, then. He came in and out of New York?

Oh, yeah, he was... It was like he played what they called the TOBA circuit. I think there was about forty-some theatres in this circuit. They worked something like forty-some weeks out the year, from one town to another, all over the country.
So actually, he wasn't living here.
I don't know where he lived.
In other words, he sort of came into town, and...
Well, you know how everybody comes into New York. But I mean, he didn't live here.
No.
But he was a hell of a performer, and a hell of an act, anyway. But he was a little flaky up at the top.
And you were there because you were with Russell at the Victor recording.
Yeah. I was part of Russell's band. That's what I was.
So do you remember who Jelly brought in with him, any of the musicians?
I don't know, because we were all there together. See, all us musicians knew one another. Now, see, just like I know you and...
Yeah.

Well, I come with my band and here you come in with somebody else's band, but we all know one another. So it's hard to distinguish who come with who, or what, you know. But we're all playing together. Some numbers I played, some numbers the other guys played. I know there was a bunch of us around in the studio that morning. There was a bunch of us. There had to be. There was a string bass and a tuba on one of the recordings. We were so many that sometimes, you know, they would be recording, and Russell would tell me, "All right, Charlie, you're in this number," you know, and I'd go up there and play...
You remember that Barbarin was there, I suppose.
Yeah, sure.
Do you remember any other drummer?
Oh, I don't know.
Well, it's hard to...

Usually I wasn't thinking about what instruments they were playing, unless I actually heard them or saw them or one of them things. It's just like you'd meet a bunch...like you go around to a club meeting, and you meet a bunch of the guys that you don't know what they're playin', but you talk to 'em anyway. You know, they know you, you know them -- you talk. You don't stop to think of what instrument he's playin'. Music was the last thing we
thought about. That's the only reason we were there, was the music. We were there to socialize (?) a little bit(?).
As far as Morton was concerned, this was the only date you actually recorded with him.
That's about the only time I recorded with him, yeah.
Did you gig with him at all?
No.
Because he was always getting bands together.
I know. He had bands. In fact, I think he used Chick Webb's band sometimes. And other little bands he'd play around with. I don't know, did Clyde work with him?
With Morton? No.
No. He never said anything about him. He didn't work with him... He didn't say nothin' about it.
He used Bill Benford's band, so Tommy Benford was with him.
Tommy Benford's brother?
Yeah.
Yeah, I know Jelly Roll. He used quite a few bands, you know. At that time, anybody who had a job had a band.
With Russell, you went in and out of there several
times. And you could more or less come and go as you pleased, right?
Yeah. I did. He was always glad when I come back. And usually I was glad to get back, too. They say the grass is always greener on the other side of the street -- until you get there.
At this point, Louis must have returned, because didn't he end up fronting Russell's band and going out on the road?

In 1935. In 1935 he was (?). Because I worked with him from 1935 to '40. Then I couldn't take it no longer. Five years of hard work. The man was... He had too much stamina for me. And I couldn't take it no more.
When you first went out with him, did you find that exciting to be part of a group that Louis was...?
Louis was nothin' but another trumpet player to me. There was nothin' great about Louis to me. He was just another trumpet player and had some work, that's all. He was no different than nobody else.
But I mean, didn't you find him... You've said other times that there's nobody like him as far as... I mean, he was the greatest...
He could blow his horn, but he didn't excite me. I wasn't interested in trumpet music. He didn't excite me.
I see.
I mean, he was good, just like you'd see a whole lot of good piano players. But if you're not interested in piano, it didn't mean nothin'.
Saxophonists was what you were interested in.
Just one saxophonist I was interested in.
Your own.
No.
Hodges.
That's the only one. Even Benny Carter, great as he was -- and I admire him to the utmost. He's a real artist. He didn't excite me.
Well, what about somebody like Willie Smith?

Oh, he was in my classification. I class him down there with me. There wasn't but two...you know what I mean, two tops, and that was Johnny and Benny -- in my classification. Everybody else, they were down there with me. Yeah, Willie was a great musician. And there was a lot of others. But there was not one, but two at the top, and that was Johnny Hodges and Benny Carter. Johnny was playin' things, he didn't know what he was playin', and Benny was playin' everything, and he did know what he was playin'. Yup, there were some great musicians back in those days...
Do you remember anything about a record that you made called "Song Of The Islands," where they brought in three violinists?
"Song Of The Islands"?
Yeah.
Oh, that was with Louis.
Yeah.
Mmm-hmm.
Do you remember anything about that in the studio, how that came about?
No. What was it? Just they come in with some violins and started to playing. What's so great about that?
Well, it was just unusual for violins to be added.
Not necessarily.
No?
No.
Because Louis didn't at that time record with violins. It must have been somebody's idea to bring them in...

Well, now, I guess everything is somebody's idea, you know. Maybe it was as big a surprise to him as it was to me. I mean, you know, it was nice... But it didn't make no records...it didn't break any records for makin' records. Just another nice (?).
Well, tell me something about those road trips that you took with Louis in fronting the Russell band.

Well, with the Russell band we did a lot of hard playing. We didn't draw many people. Consequently, we didn't make much money. And with Louis, we drew a lot of people, but we wasn't gettin' much salary! But the salary we was gettin' was much more than we ever made with Russell's band, because with Russell's band it was a hit and miss thing.

See, with Louis' band it wasn't...you weren't gambling. You got so much a night. I mean, when you worked, you got paid so much a night, and you didn't have to worry about your money if the people come in or not. Which the people were always there. In fact, they had... The band's salary meant nothing. It was absolutely nothing, what they had to pay for the band to come into the place. Oh, they cleaned up some money, Joe Glaser and whoever was with him. They cleaned up oodles of money. Joe Glaser got rich off that band. Because the salaries he was paying were pathetic. And it wasn't pathetic at that time. I mean, comparatively speaking to other bands, we were getting more than the average bands around here. But even at that, I mean, the money that the attraction was drawing, which it was Louis Armstrong's name -- it was Louis Armstrong drawing the
people... The money that they were paying the men, I don't ...(?)... What could we do?
Where did you go?
All over the country. All over the South. All over the South. All over the West. The Midwest. The Far West. The Northwest. The Northeast. All over. Everywhere in the country.
How did you travel?
Bus. We had our own bus. We had a nice bus. There was nothing wrong with the bus.
Everybody was in one big bus.
Yup, one big one. Everybody was there. I think Louis had two...two Boston Bulldogs -- they was in there, too.
And his wife Alpha?

Alpha. Oh boy, it was somethin' when they come in the bus, with the two dogs and one thing and another. I think they had a maid, too. He had a maid and a chauffeur -- Louis had a chauffeur. Because Joe Glaser bought a big red Packard, a beautiful car, and had this chauffeur to drive for Louis, and he'd go on the road with Louis. Louis wouldn't ride in the car. He wouldn't ride in the car, I don't know why. He got in the bus; he piled up in the bus.

Now, that don't make too much sense to me, because if you... Say, like, you're leavin' anywhere... Say we're leavin' here and we're going to Washington. Well now, with a bus, it'll take four hours to get down to Washington. Well, in a car, you could at least save an hour -- at least an hour; maybe even more time than that. And they could get in the room or wherever you've got to go, and stretch out and get that much more rest.

With a bus, you've got a bus full of people, and they always have to be makin' stops for this-that-or-the-other, and you can lose a lot of time in a bus. And Louis wouldn't ride in a bus. He'd be with his band, his show, his people. So what happened to the bus...?
You mean to the car.

To the car. Bob Smiley had to drive the car, and Sonny Moore, vocalist, and myself, we rode the car with Smiley. We rode with him. I wasn't too ashamed to ride with him -- a great, big, beautiful red Packard. And brother, when we ride into any of them towns, well, you thought we were somethin'. And we'd get there ahead of time. We could get to the hotel and get rooms -- there's no trouble gettin' rooms. We'd be the first one in town, get our rooms -- and when they comin' down, we'd be in bed sleeping.

Oh, brother. We were somethin', this big red Packard would drive into town, and who would step out but little-bitty me and Sonny Moore -- Sonny was no taller than me. But Louis wouldn't ride in it; he wouldn't ride in that car. And I told him, I said, "I don't blame you."
Now, did Glaser go on the trips? Or did he stay...

No. He would come around. The first year he went out with us. The first year, he was in the bus with us. He was a forty-year-old manager, you know; he was forty during them days. He was good in this kind of way. We'd be in place where we couldn't get served, and he would, like, get out of the bus and he'd go and come back with all kind of food and stuff, and give it to us -- you know, come in the bus with it.

And then, like, we'd be playing a dance at night, and there would be a...we were gonna lay over or something, and there's a nightclub or something around there that had shows in the back, an (?)all-farmers'(?) club, out to have a little sport, see what's going on. Well, we fallen in the club, and some of these guys, they pick up their chicks or something, one of them things, you know, and be in the ..(?).. Joe Glaser would fall in the club: "Any of my boys in here from the Louis Armstrong band, give 'em anything they want." Oh, he liked that. He was loud, you know.
"Give 'em anything they want."

So we hit Chicago, and I was in a nightclub up there -- I think my wife had just come to see me. And Joe was up there, and he come in the club -- the Club Panama we was in. He says, "Give my boys anything they want." So I told the waiter, "Give me two quarts of whiskey." And my wife and I had two quarts. I just did that because he said, "Give them anything they want." I said, "if he won't pay me nothin', I'll get it some kind of way." So he put the whiskey on the table, and I sat there and drank as much as I could. I got sick as a dog. I was sick as a dog. Last thing I remembered was, I was outside the club with my arm wrapped around a lamppost -- I'm tryin' to hold myself up.
That was when I was just starting to drink. I didn't go for drinkin'. But every once in a while, I run across an occasion like that, and I'd have to take advantage of it.
Now, what about in the South? Wasn't it hard with accommodations?

Yeah, accommodations were very hard. Most of the time, if there wasn't a flea-bitten hotel you stayed in, you had to stay with private families. You'd go around from door to door, knocking on the door; you know, ask people if they got rooms or something like that. It was very tough, very tough.
What did Louis do?

Well, see, Louis had been all over the territory so many times before, he knew where he was going. See, any time you find a good place, you remember that, you know, and keep in contact with them people a few days before you're comin' into town. Or if you're a good roomer with them, they will remember you, and they see the advertisement that Louis is coming into town, they will save a room for you -- they'll save you a room.
I see.
Yeah.
Now, were most of these places that you played for Blacks, Whites, Mixed?
Most of them in the South were Black. Once in a while we'd get a White occasion. Very seldom mixed. Very seldom. Because after all, you know, this was in the Thirties.
Yeah, but I've heard those stories about the rope down the middle and all that stuff.

Oh yeah. Well, that was for the spectators. See, there would be a Black dance. Now, the Blacks would come in there and dance all over the place, one of them things. But the Whites... We'd have as many White spectators. They couldn't dance, but they could spend their

money, come in there and stand up or sit down, and they could watch the band. But they couldn't go on the floor and dance. They were what's called spectators. And there would be as many of them as there were Blacks on the floor dancing.
What were they, then? Theatres?
No-no.
Nightclubs.
No, these were dance halls.
Dance halls.
Well, that's what they called them down there.
Or ballrooms.

Some of them were tobacco warehouses. Tobacco warehouses. Those are big places where they'd keep the tobacco. And they could accommodate a lot of people. Well, that's what they needed when you had an attraction down there, because the people would come out in droves. Yeah, they came out in droves. You needed a warehouse.
And then Glaser had arranged all this from New York.

Well, no. He just gets the dates, and whoever is promoting the dance... Whoever was promoting the dances arranged that. See, that's just like you, you hire an organization from anywhere and they come here. Well, you
know what they're going to need, this-that-and-the-other. But you see that it's there.
And it was mostly one-nighters.
Yeah, mostly.
So as soon as you finished the job, into the bus and...

Into the bus, and four hundred more miles, or five or six or seven or eight hundred miles. We left Chicago one morning, we thought we was going six hundred miles to the next engagement. And when we got on the road and the road manager looked at the contract, we found out it was eight hundred miles instead of six hundred miles. And we had left Chicago...oh, it was after three o'clock in the morning when we left there, and we were due at this next engagement... This was eight hundred miles. We were due on the bandstand at eight o'clock, or else there would have been a big fine for being late -- stipulated on the contract. So this fellow, boy, he drove that bus, too. Oh. He didn't stop for nothin'. At eight o'clock was on the bandstand. We were damn near dead, though. But we was on the bandstand.
And you had only one driver?
That's all.
He did the whole thing.
He did the whole thing. We didn't even

stop for nothin'. And we went on the bandstand. Of course, everybody was dead tired. Louis got up there and blew like he had been sleepin' in a Pullman berth or something. He blew his head off. I said, "This man is...he's too great. Everybody else is..." I couldn't keep my eyes open, I was so damn tired and sleepy. And just blew and blew. I mean, he played... And I said, "No, this is too hard. This is too hard." He said, "Well, you blow out the bad ones like you blow out the good ones. Blow 'em loud." Oh, he liked you to blow loud.

Yeah, he was a hard worker. He was a hard workin' man. He worked hard. There was nothin'... Now we had traveled eight hundred miles, you know, you'd get out, you can't hardly stand up, and you'd think he would take it easy the first few sets or something like that. No-o. No. He got on there that first number, boy, and pound-pound-pound. Well, the house was full of people. And there was no let-up. He was there to entertain the people, and believe me, that's what he believed in. People pay their money, they don't care what you go through. They paid their admission. They want to be entertained. He was absolutely right. Your feelings meant nothin'.
Yessir, he was a hard worker and a hard-workin' man, and he didn't ask you to do nothin' that he wouldn't do.
He played, and played hard. That's why I say he was a great man, because no other leader I know would have put up with what he had to go through.

They booked us out of New York one night to play Boston. We went to Boston and played, then we left there, in the bus, and our next engagement was in Miami, Florida. Now, we finished the night in Miami; our next engagement was in New York. One night. We played one night in New York, and back down to Miami again!

Now, it takes two days to travel down there in a bus. Well, see, if you were traveling two days that's on you, because when you don't work, you don't get paid. When you're traveling, that's on you. You get paid nothin' for traveling. So the only time we get paid was when we were working, playin' the dances. Well, we played a night in Boston, travel two days and go to Miami, and get paid for one night; travel two days back, get paid for one night; then back to Miami again. Well, I mean, when you stop to figure it out, with the time that you spent traveling, you kind of lost money on the deal. See, Louis wasn't the type of guy to come up and say, 'Well, boys, you did a good and keep this-that-or-the-other,' you know. If anybody did that, it was Joe Glaser. Which...that was him doing the dealing. No, the money was pretty...
Well, what kind of relationship did Louis have with the band? Did he in any way...?

Louis got up there and blew his horn. He had nothin' to say to the band as far as running the band was concerned. He wasn't interested in what the band's business was. Luis Russell was running the band...and Joe Glaser. Joe Glaser run everything. See, all the orders come from Joe Glaser. And Louis, he didn't bother himself with the band. Louis didn't know where he was working the next night. People would come up to the bandstand and ask, "Oh, Louis, where are you playing tomorrow night?" And Louis would have to ask somebody in the band. "Where we at tomorrow night?" He didn't know.

He never knew. He didn't care. You know, when he got through work he would get dressed and get in the bus and go to sleep in the bus -- and he could sleep on the bus, too. It would make me so mad! He would sit across from me, and I could never sleep on a bus... I'd be awake two and three nights at a time. And he'd come in the bus, and right away [SNORE]...and sleep the whole trip. When we'd get there, he's all right, he feels good. I couldn't sleep, and I was very nervous. And when I get out of the bus and get on the bandstand, I'm ready for a bed. And it was all... I'd sit on the bandstand and I couldn't keep my eyes open. But I
get in the bus and I'm wide-awake, I can't sleep.
What about the breakdowns? The buses...?
Oh yeah, we had them, too.
Flat tires...

Everything happened. Yes, we had it all happen. We was in Mississippi, and half the road was paved and the other half was gravel. And boy, we had more blowouts on that road. Oh, brother, did we have some blowouts.

So we got to one town, Monroe, I think it was...Monroe, Louisiana or somewhere down there. We had to hire some cars... We had to hire some cars to get where we were going, you know. So we get in the cars, and the cars got split up. So I don't know, maybe I'm ahead of my story. I know the car I was in went a hundred miles in the wrong direction And when we found out where we were at, went in the wrong direction... I think it was time for the dance to start then. Now, we're a hundred miles in the wrong direction from where we were at. Well, we never made that dance. I don't know how the people carried on. But there was about five or six of us in that car. We didn't make that dance. The rest of the band was there. I guess they did the best they could.
Well, Louis was there.
Yeah. Well, I mean, as long as he's there, that's all they need anyway. They were satisfied as long as he's there. But if he's not there, you'd better get out of town.
Was Joe Garland in the band?
He'd come in just before we'd taken over...he'd come in the band. He wasn't in the band too long.
Didn't he have a lot to do with the arrangements and looking after the band...the so-called straw-boss?

Well, he was the boss when... See, Russell was tired of the way things was run, and he was in the middle. Russell was in the middle between the band and Joe Glaser. Russell was catching hell from the men in the band plus Joe Glaser.

Joe Glaser would listen to everybody out in the street here in New York, the unemployed musicians tryin' to get jobs, and this-that-and-the-other, and they'd go sing a song to Joe, telling him how bad so-and-so sounded in the band, this-that-and-the-other, "Why don't you let me replace him?" and this-that-and-the-other. Somebody was always shooting for your job. Well, they talked to Joe, and Joe didn't know. First thing Joe wanted to know, "Well, who did you play with?" and they'd name some names and things.

Next thing you know, Russell would get a notice from Joe, or he called him up or something, from Joe Glaser, to let so-and-so go. Now, here's Russell... He's got to fire a man for no reason! As far as Russell's concerned, the man is doing his work and doing his job. But the boss said, "Fire so-and-so-and-so." So what's Russell to do? He's got to let him go. So he gives out the notice. Joe Glaser can't fire him. Joe don't even belong to the union. So Russell got to give him his notice. But he makes himself a bad fellow then.

Well, he gave out quite a few notices, which he had to do. And consequently, the people that he fired, they never liked him. They hated him. So Russell got tired of people hatin' him. And after all, that was Louis Armstrong's name up there in the lights, and he wasn't doin' anything but getting all the glory. And Joe Glaser wasn't firing anybody. That was Luis Russell they'd say fired me. And Russell got tired of that, catching it from both sides -- the band and Joe Glaser.

So Russell, he threw up his hands. He told me... He would play piano in the band, he would just be a member of the band. He didn't want... So that's when Joe got the whole band together, Joe Glaser, and asked us all, one by one, did we want to run the band, because Russell wanted to
give it up -- and who wanted to take it over. Nobody wanted... Nobody wanted to take over the band. He said, "Okay, we'll leave it."

Well, two days later, he sent for us to come to rehearsal. Joe Garland's going to take over the band. Joe Garland? Man, he was the last one to come in here. And he's gonna take over? Well, I thought that was kind of funny, you know, the last man to come in the band. But I said didn't say nothin'. It's all right with me. I learned my lesson from the Blue Rhythm Band. It didn't make no difference to me what happened.

So anyway, Joe Garland, he was the boss from then on. And he started givin' out his rules and one-thing-and-another, and... Boy, the first thing he did was, he had directions written in the dressing room, like we was playin' theatres. We had two or three different uniforms, and he'd have all different combinations and one-thing-or-another. And he had written up in all the dressing rooms what you wear the next show, this-that-and-the-other, and you change this... And after the first show every day, the' reed section rehearses. We rehearsed in between shows. "Damn," I said, "this is worse than going to work in a damn factory." We come off the stage and we've got to go to rehearsal right away." Then we finish rehearsal, and we've got to look on
the bulletin board and see what we're wearing for the next show.

It was funny. We'd come up, and we had blue suits and white suits. Because we had combinations. We changed the pants and jackets. One time, the reed section came out there with all blue pants and white jackets on, and the brass section was just the opposite. Everything was all mixed up. See, they did that just for the devilment, you know. Boy, it was a grand mixup.

But see, Joe Garland, he was so...he wanted things to be just exactly right. And I must say, from the records that I heard that they made, you know, under him, they were very good records. Very good records. He'd mark your music where you're supposed to breathe at. You'd play so many bars and then you take a breath. All them little things. He has us phrasing together. So it sounded much better. It really did improve the band.

But who wants to go through all that hassle? And we're not making that kind of money. And who is getting the... Louis Armstrong is getting all the credit and the money. And he didn't even... It didn't make no difference to him one way or the other. He'd go out and blow his horn. He don't know what's goin' on! He didn't care. As long as his chops was all right, he didn't care about nothin' else. All
he cared about was his chops. Practice all the time, blowin' his horn. And that's all he cared about. The band, they had a hard time. But...
Now, when you first went in a band in those days, you got fitted for uniforms right away. How did that work? You went to a tailor or something?

Yeah. Well, the tailor would make the uniforms, you know. He made all the uniforms. He was a... In fact, the tailor practically made his living off of Louis Armstrong's band and Joe Glaser...because there was a lot of bands. Joe had a lot of irons in the fire, you know. And this tailor practically made his living off it.
Because some bands had like three and four changes.
Oh, we had a lot of uniforms. We had a lot of uniforms. But they was all suits; they was suits we could wear.
Oh, I see.
But we had to pay for them.
That was my next question.
Yeah, we had to pay for them.
So that was deducted from your salary?
Yeah.
So that they made sure they got the money.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, we used to pay for

them. They weren't buying them. They should have been paying for them. One time, Joe Glaser and I, we had a little argument about the uniforms, you know. We weren't supposed to wear the uniforms in the street, naturally enough...but it wasn't nothin' but a suit.

So here we are, we're down in one of them Southern towns one Sunday morning and gettin' ready to leave. So I come to the bus all dressed up in my uniform. And Joe Glaser saw me about a block away, and he hollered at me. Joe hollered anyway; he got excited, you know, he would holler anyway. He says, "Charlie, you know you're not supposed to wear that uniform out in the street!" I said, "Well, Mr. Glaser, if you don't want me to wear a uniform in the street, you pay for it." I said, "I paid for this one. I wear this anywhere I please. You don't tell me where to wear this. This is mine." Case closed. He said no more. I was perfectly right. You can't tell me where to wear my clothes. If he wants me not to wear his uniform in the street, let him pay for it, and I'll wear it wherever he says.

But see, I used to talk back to Joe. And you know, it was only about two people in that band that didn't get fired. And I was one of them, and Louis Bacon was another. He was another one would...he would bass right back at Joe

Glaser. Joe would say anything to him, he'd bass right back at him -- he had a heavy bass voice anyway. Heh. Joe didn't bother us. Well, he would jump on me every now and then, you know, and I... I think he liked... He liked people to fuss with him, talk back to him, you know -- which most of the people in the band didn't. But I'd straighten him. Didn't make no difference to me. I could take it or leave it.

I wasn't that crazy about workin' in the band. I mean, it wasn't no kicks to me to be workin' in there. I was just workin'. And believe me, it was work. And when I'm dissatisfied in something, nobody tells me what to do or what not to do. Not if I'm dissatisfied. If I'm happy there, okay, that's a different thing. But don't let me be dissatisfied, and then I'm gonna take that too? No, it don't go like that. If I'm gonna be unhappy, I'm gonna be... I'm not gonna be there. If I'm gonna be unhappy, I'm not takin' nothin' from nobody.

As small as I am, you know, I've been very lucky to reach this age that I am...small as I am! But I've had a lot of friends tell me, say, "You know, Charlie, you're pretty tough to get along with." I says, "Well, no, I don't think so." They say, "Oh, yeah, you're hard to get along with. You don't take no stuff." I say, "What do you mean I
don't take nothin'? I've been takin' it all my life. At some points you get tired of taking."

But I mean, it makes you hard. That kind of life makes you very hard. Especially when you're working and you're not pleased with what you're doing. You know, if you're not happy, it's best not to be there. Because if you make yourself miserable, you make everybody else around you miserable. And if you get that way, that's not good.
[PAUSE]
You must have had other problems, like with with laundry. If you're going from one place to the next...

Yes, I had a problem like that once. I remember I put my clothes in to a woman in Baltimore. We had just finished playing Washington. I got a week's worth of dirty clothes. We get into Baltimore, I give it to a woman to wash. Well, we're in Baltimore a whole week! So she don't come by the theatre with the laundry. We're getting ready to leave. And I go by her house to find out if I can get my laundry. This is the last day. So I go upstairs, and I go in the kitchen, and she had 'them in a tub of water -- and you should have seen that water. I said, "Oh, that's all right I just come after my laundry, but I see you're not ready yet." She said, "No, I'm not ready yet." I said, "You can forget it. You should have seen
that water. It looked like she was washin' rubber tires or something in the water. Oh, it was black and greasy...!

Holmes (10/31) - 9
