Oh, sure. Sure, everybody come in there on a recommendation. Nobody just didn't walk in and say, "I'm a trumpet player. I want a job." No, they'd come in under the recommendation. I don't remember who recommended Otis, but he was well known around... You know, he was well-known around the musicians before he joined the band. He was a good trumpet player.
All right. Let me put on "Doctor Blues."
[MUSIC PLAYS]
That was a number that was in the book.
Oh yeah, it was in the book, sure. It had a Doctor title to it. Oh, that was something big. "Doctor Blues."
What do you think occasioned the title?
They had nothin' else to call it. They just called it "Doctor Blues."
When Henry Allen came into the band, did you feel that was a step forward?

No. Henry Allen came in there as another trumpet player, just like Louis Armstrong comes there as another trumpet player. There was nothin' great about them when they come there. You didn't get no feelin' of exaltation, "Oh, I'm working with this, that and the other."
No, it wasn't like that at all. They were just other musicians. Could have been anybody.
But you stuck together. You must have had a feeling...

We stuck together because we didn't have nowhere else to go! That's why they stuck together. They had a job. You had a job, somebody was working -- sure, they stuck together. Duke Ellington's band stuck together for sixty-some years, fifty years. They didn't have nowhere else to go.
Now, what can you tell me about the Alhambra Ballroom? Didn't you play there with Russell?
Yeah, I worked there. It was a ballroom, just like it said. It used to be a taxi dance hall.
I see.
It used to be a taxi dance hall, and then they changed it into a ballroom. Jelly Roll Morton's band worked there a while. Not long.
Here in one of the liner notes it says that "Luis Russell's orchestra was one of those featured at the Alhambra Ballroom in Harlem on the night of Friday the Thirteenth of September, 1929."
Mmm, could be. Sure. Well, that's one of them nights when they had three or four or five or six different bands, you know. We happened to be one of them.
Do you remember where it was?
Yeah. 126th Street and 7th Avenue. Right on the corner, upstairs.
I've seen it.

Yeah. Nothin' to see, really. You had to take an elevator to get up there. Lord help it, if a fire had ever happened or anything. They had to ...(?)... the people, and they had to wait for the elevator to come out of there. It would take you longer to get out the place than you'd stand in there at night! It was terrible. They didn't have big fires in them days, I guess. Luckily, nothing ever happened. It was a beautiful-looking place, too. Nice ballroom. Beautiful.
Of course, with the opening they would make it more festive by having several bands. But was there usually one band or two bands at the Alhambra?

Well, let me see. As a rule, I think they used two when they started off. I mean, as a general rule every night I think they had two bands. Maybe when the business fell off, they used one band. But I'm sure that they used two bands. After the opening night. You know, they had all the big things opening night. Then they went into the regular routine with two bands. And then as business fell off and got worse, then they used one band.
Now, the Savoy was already going.
Oh yeah.
So they were copying the Savoy in a sense.

I don't know if the Savoy wasn't running that place, strictly speaking. They could have been backers. I'm not sure. I'm not sure that they weren't. I never got mixed up in the business of the places. As long as the place was open and hired me, that's all I was interested in.
How about the Harlem Opera House?
That was a theatre.
Oh, I see.
That was a theatre, you know. That's like the Apollo Theatre, or the Lafayette Theatre at that time. That theatre had been there for quite a few years.
So there the band would be related to a show.
Well, yeah. I mean, they had shows in there. They had regular shows with chorus girls and so forth, comedians, dancers, bands.
And the Renaissance Ballroom.
That was a dance hall. Strictly a dance hall. And they used to have basketball games in there sometimes, but mostly it was a dance hall.
With one band or two?

Well, they had one band, and two bands on special occasions. But they would have one band as a general rule. I can't think of the fellow's name who used to be the bandleader there. He stayed there for years.
Well, Vernon Andrade was the...
Andrade. Vernon Andrade. He was the leader of the band. He stayed there for years. Yeah, Vernon Andrade, that's right.
It seems like if you hung around Harlem long enough, you'd eventually work for him.

Yeah, eventually you'd wind up working for him. That's right. Because I mean, they were coming and going in his band all the time. I mean, his band, he had no aspirations for going any place or doing anything. But he had a job. And that was the name of the game in them days -- a job. So different fellows, they'd be working or rehearsing in the big-time bands. Like Chick Webb's band, you'd be rehearsing with Chick Webb, but Chick wasn't doing anything, so they'd go to work with Vernon Andrade until the other band found something to do. And they were always in and out of Andrade's band. It didn't seem to faze him none. As long as you could play the music, that was the main thing with him.
What did he play himself? Or did he?
He had a guitar.
But he fronted the bands mostly?
Well, it was his band. It was nothing elaborate about it or spectacular. He sat down and played his guitar, and the rest of the band just played the music.
Did he arrange?
No.
Or compose?
No.
What did he do? Stocks then mostly?
That's right. Stocks, or somebody had something they wanted to play, then...
I think he came from the Islands? The West Indies? [PANAMA]

Mmm-hmm. And he had some good musicians who worked for him down through the years. Some of the best in the business worked for him. They were glad to get the jobs. Yeah, some terrific saxophone players worked for him. Howard Johnson worked for him for years. Another fellow named Fats Green. He could play all of the reeds, and I mean he could play it. He was terrific.
Do you remember where Fats Green was from?
No. He was from around here somewhere. Fats Green had a band of his own. Later on he got plenty of
work around Harlem.
What was his main instrument? Alto?

Alto... Saxophones. He played all the saxophones. Clarinet. A very good clarinetist. Yeah, Fats was very good. He had a lot of good musicians in Andrade's band. In fact, some of the best musicians. I even think Buster Bailey was with him at one time. You name 'em, they had worked for Andrade. Sure.
And he never toured or anything.
No.
He just stayed at the Renny.
He just stayed right there. He wasn't thinking about going no place. He was just one of them kind of guys he had a job, and that was good enough for him. He wasn't trying to elaborate on anything.
Now, what about things like Harlem rent parties? Did you get involved in any of those?
Harlem rent parties?
Yeah.
What is a Harlem rent party?
Well, it's supposed to be where someone can't afford to pay his rent, and then has a party, and the piano player... I guess it was mostly the piano players...
A Harlem rent party is just another house

rent party. That's all it is. It's a house rent party. Somebody... Well, at that time, I mean, things were tough. And the funny thing, there was more night life going on in Harlem then than there is now, and there was more money in circulation in Harlem... Well, I wouldn't put it like that, because there's an awful lot of money in circulation now. But I mean, they were talking about conditions being hard and bad, but there was a lot of money in circulation in Harlem. And this was back in the Depression days. A lot of money was in circulation. And people were jumping out of windows downtown in the financial section; they were getting wiped out by the stock market and jumping out of windows. It wasn't safe to walk the streets downtown. And up here in Harlem, they were ballin' morning, noon and night! Wasn't nothin' else could happen. Good times was the thing of the day.

And you could walk anywhere you wanted at any hour of the night. Nobody would bother you. People would be out in the street. There would be just as many out on the street at three or four or five o'clock in the morning as there would be in the afternoon. You'd always find people in the street. Always! Nobody was rippin' off anybody. Nobody was getting ripped off. People would go out and leave their doors unlocked, and go away, and go out for dancing or any
place else they wanted to go, and come back, and the place would still be there, with doors unlocked and everything. Nobody would bother you. But that's a long time ago. Not like it is now.
Well, they said people could come Uptown from Downtown with their furs and everything...
Oh yeah, they did!
...and leave them in the car, and they'd still be there.

Oh yeah. The Cotton Club at that time, they entertained nothing but Hollywood celebrities. Sunday night was their Celebrity Night at the Cotton Club, and anybody who was ever a star in Hollywood, as soon as they'd come to New York, they would be at the Cotton Club that Sunday night.
To be seen.

To get their introduction. And I forget the fellow's name that used to be the MC there, but he knew ever star in Hollywood, and he would introduce them and this-that-and-the-other thing. It was just a meeting place for the stars. And they would come up here in Rolls-Royces and everything else. Nobody bothered them. No, they weren't ripped off at all.
Now, the Cotton Club was primarily for the Whit...
There was a White clientele, right?

It was definitely White, sure. But the place wasn't... The show and everything else was Negro. The band was Negro. But the club itself... Colored could go in there, Colored could go, but they... What the hell, they couldn't stand that tab. You know? You spend a lot of money.
So nobody would have been refused entrance.
Well, they might tell you the place is filled up or something like that, one of them things. But if you insisted on it, you could get in there. If you could prove that you had, you know...
The bread.
Sure. Yeah, Bill Robinson used it for one of his hangouts, the Cotton Club.
And I imagine if Joe Louis wanted to go...
Well, he had no trouble going anywhere. You couldn't stop Joe Louis. He would have punched you in the nose! Heh-heh.

Yeah, Harlem used to be a beautiful place. You could go, and there were a lot of places to go and there was a lot of things you could see and do. It wasn't half-bad at all. Because it was a beautiful place. But things change. Everything changes. Well, it's deteriorated. It's not too
good now. It's not bad compared to a whole lot of places. But I mean, it's not the same. The feeling is not the same.
Well, what was the mood of Harlem in those days? Everybody pulling together? Everybody having a good time? Everybody trying to...?

Well, people were having a good time, because... First thing, it's composed of a lot of poor people -- poor young people. But you see, they had some place to go. I'm not speaking of the (?). You'd hear the talking.. The young people had some place to go for entertainment.

They had the Savoy Ballroom to go to. And I think at that time the admission was around a dollar, maybe a little bit under that. Now, they could go to the Savoy Ballroom, which could hold six thousand people, and it was a beautiful ballroom, and they always had two bands playing, continuous music, a beautiful place, you could and meet people or you could just go there and sit and enjoy the music, or you could go and sit over there in a booth and you could get food served to you -- anything. I mean, the atmosphere was so conducive to keep you on a down(?) (?). You know what I mean? I mean, you were so contented. So you could sit up there and imagine you were this-that-or-the-other, because the place was a beautiful place.

And these people would spend a dollar or less to come in there, and they could come in there and sometimes stay in there five and six hours at a time. Well, that will take you off the street a whole lot of hours. And that's where all the youngsters would go. They'd go up there and learn how to dance, and they'd have different games and things for them. It was beautiful. It was really beautiful.

Now they don't have any place like that, the youngsters who come along. And I'm glad they don't have a place like that now, with all this corruption and one thing and another that they have, because...
They'd wreck the place.

Oh, conditions are terrible now. I mean, life doesn't mean anything no more. Not only wreck the place, they'd kill off a whole lot of people. The Savoy, nothing ever happened there. You never had no big... I don't remember any altercations happening there that even made the newspapers. I never heard of anybody getting killed there or beat up so bad that it even made the newspapers. Very little things happened there. Everybody went there to have a good time. They enjoyed themselves. Just like people going to the Roseland. You've heard of the Roseland.
Sure.

Well, the Savoy looked better than most of the Roseland did. I think it was a little larger than the Roseland. I'm not sure of the capacity of the Roseland, but they were built on the same order. And the Roseland went for years and years and years. You'd never read nothin' in the newspaper about the Roseland unless it was some affair or something that was coming off. You'd never hear nothin' detrimental against it. You'd never hear of nobody gettin' killed in the Roseland or gettin' beat up or this-that-and-the-other. Same thing with the Savoy.
Well, people seemed to want to dance to the music.
That's right. Well, that's what they were doing at the Savoy. They was dancin'. They was up there dancin'. Yeah, they was dancin'.
What about the Saratoga Club and the Nest?

Well, that was a.... Well, the Nest was a little cabaret; a little small cabaret. It didn't hold too many people. But the Saratoga was... Well, that was a small cabaret, too. They didn't draw people like the Savoy did.
But there was dancing.

Well, you could dance, yeah. Anything your pocketbook could stand. You needed a little more cash to go in them places. At the Savoy, you could go in there for less than a dollar. But you didn't go in the Saratoga with
a dollar in your pocket. You would come out with your head beat in.
What did it cost to go to the Saratoga?
I don't know what it would cost to get out of there. It's just like any other club you go to. You go down to the Stork Club. How much it gonna cost to go to the Stork Club?
I see what you're saying.
Your drinks are high. Everything is high. Everything's high.
Was there an admission as well?
No, you just paid for...
You went and got a table.
That's right.
But there was a dance floor.
Oh yeah, there was a dance floor.
So generally, you ordered a bottle of something, I guess.
No, you ordered by the drink.
Oh, you ordered by the drink.
And that was higher. But that didn't go too good. They had a show down there, too.
So the clientele, then, at the Saratoga Club was also White?

Anyone who wanted could come in. They didn't do a good business, like the Cotton Club. Of course, they was almost directly across the street from the Cotton Club. But see, the Cotton Club catered to stars and things -- movie stars. That's what they catered to. I can't think of... I can see his name there. He knew everybody who was to be known. And they did a big business all through the...every night in the week. And they were also doing a lot of benefits and things. They were playing a lot of benefits.

Yeah, it was a well-run place. I mean, they knew what they were doing. It cost you plenty to go in there, or to come out -- one way or the other. You were going to spend a lot of money in the Cotton Club. At the Saratoga you wouldn't spend as much, but you would still spend more than if you was goin' to a place like the Savoy. You'd put that dollar down, and that's it -- and you could be in there for five or six hours or more, and be well entertained. The bands and the hostesses and one-thing-or-another in there... They had beautiful hostesses in there.

But see, they don't have all of that now to entertain the youth, take them off the streets, or this-that-and-the-other. And this city needs... They need a Savoy in every borough that they got here. Something for... I mean, a big

place to hold all these kids. Some place where they can go and be taught the right way to do things. It's a big deal, and... What can you say? It takes a lot of money? Everything takes a lot of money now. Youth, I think, is worth a lot of money. That's the future. They are your future senior citizens.
From the Russell band, you ended up joining the Mills Blue Rhythm Band.

Yeah, whatever... In between there, I was... I had worked with Willie Lynch's band. Willie Lynch, I think, had the first Blue Rhythm Band. And I worked with that band a short while, not too long. We worked in the Cotton Club as a substitute for Cab Calloway's band. Cab Calloway went on the road, and the Blue Rhythm band went to work in the Cotton Club as a substitute for Cab.
So here you are now playing for a Cotton Club show or Cotton Club revue, so to speak.
Mmm-hmm.
Now, you must have had to rehearse that with dancers and so on.
Well, of course we rehearsed.
So what did you do? Did you rehearse all afternoon?
No, we rehearsed practically all night after we finished work.
I see.

I mean, rehearsals wasn't bad. The only thing bad about the rehearsals at that time, they didn't have to pay the musicians to rehearse. So any time a chorus girl would get out there during a show at night and she didn't kick her leg high enough, or she missed a step or something, the producer of the show would call a rehearsal after the night's work was over. I think we got through around three o'clock at the Cotton Club, two or three o'clock in the morning. And they'd keep us, the show and the band, keep us rehearsing until whenever they felt like letting us go home. Sometimes it would be broad daylight when we would come out of there. And we would never get a nickel for that, not five cents, and if you complained too much you'd get fired -- which was not exactly right.

Now, when the union stepped in years later and made these places pay off for these rehearsals and things, it was very strange how quickly the musicians knew all of the music, according to the producers. They actually knew it. There were no more rehearsals called, you know, extemporaneously. When you had a rehearsal, it had to be a rehearsal, and then they had to pay you for the time.
But up until then, your time wasn't worth nothin', and they'd have you rehearsing every night, six or seven o'clock

in the morning, which didn't make sense. You used to go to work in there at seven o'clock in the evening. The show went on... I think we went to work around six o'clock, and played dance music up until the time of the show, and they put on the show at seven o'clock in the evening. And the show would run over an hour. It was a big production. And we would put on three shows a night, three shows a night. I mean, it was a grind. Now, after you put on three shows a night, and then the producer comes around and tells you "Rehearsal"... Rehearsal, after you've worked all those hours, and here comes the producer -- "Rehearsal." Now you rehearse until six and seven o'clock in the morning, there's no telling what time you'll get home, because you're gonna stop before you go home to get something to eat. Oh, it was just rough. And by the time you'd get home and get a little bit of sleep, it's time to go back down there to go to work again!

When we was workin' down there with Louis... It wasn't exactly the Cotton Club then. It was the Cotton Club later, but it opened up as Connie's Inn downtown. It was called Connie's Inn. You worked the same hours. At this time, Louis was doing a radio show for Fleischman Yeast, the Fleischman Yeast program. Now, we had to squeeze time in there in the daytime to rehearse the Fleischman Yeast show.

We had to rehearse that to be broadcast. And you talk about somebody not having enough time, we did not have enough time to rehearse one thing and then another. We was blowin'- blowin'-blowin' all of the time.

It was really a tough thing. You're going to work at six o'clock, you're playing three shows until two or three o'clock in the morning, then you're rehearsing after the show until seven o'clock in the morning. Then during the day, you've got to rehearse the radio program. It just wasn't worth it. It was rough. It was really rough.
Louis never complained about anything, and he blew his head off. I mean, he had more stamina than anybody I ever seen in my life. He had it.

And we worked down there, Connie's Inn... Oh, we were there six months the first time. Then the second time we were there, we went out on the road after being there three weeks, and we started doing the broadcasts from different cities, like Chicago, the big cities we'd run into all the way out to California.

But we survived it. It was pretty nice. I mean, that made the pocketbook kind of heavy there, when you're collecting from all these different things. Like, we were getting paid for rehearsals, which we didn't get before, and we were getting paid for the broadcasts, which was extra.
That was good. That was very good. Plus, the regular show, I mean the regular job, which was hard... That was hard. That was a hard job. But when you put it all together, I guess it was good.

My wife and I, we had a little hard time in between there, because she could not believe anybody was blowin' their horn as often and as much as I said I was at Connie's Inn, rehearsing and this-that-and-the-other. She couldn't believe anybody was rehearsing that much. And I guess the other fellows had the same trouble, too. It was tough on a wife. Real tough on a wife. But, that's the business. What are you gonna do? It wasn't the only band. There was other bands working under different strenuous conditions, too. And that was life. That was the way it was.
I guess Small's Paradise was no different.
Well, Small's Paradise, they didn't go through all that rigmarole. They had a show. They put on a show twice a night.
[END OF SIDE 1]
You mentioned that you were in and out of Russell's band, and at one point you went into the Savoy with Willie Lynch.
That's right.
Who was Willie Lynch?

Well, Willie Lynch was a drummer that Irving Mills knew, and Irving Mills was trying to get a substitute band for Cab Calloway in the Cotton Club -- to put in the Cotton Club. So Willie Lynch got a band together and was trying it out at the Savoy Ballroom. Well, we worked the Savoy for about three months, and then Mills put the band into the Cotton Club behind Cab Calloway. He was taking Cab out, he sent him on the road... And this band goes into the Cotton Club.
Well, in the meantime, I wasn't with the band when they went in the Cotton Club. But I had been back with Russell's band again, and consequently, I left them one more time -- Russell's band.
Well, can you mention that at this point Lynch's band had gone to the Lafayette Theatre and had a big success there.

Well, that was Willie's band. Well, they was... They didn't have a name then. It was just Willie Lynch and the band. So they were playing the number 'Stardust,' and they were featuring the pianist, Edgar Hayes -- he did the solos on the number 'Stardust.' And it was really a wonderful thing he did. He did wonderful solos on
it. And he was a big attraction. He was a big attraction on... What's his name?
Edgar Hayes.
Edgar Hayes.
You said they had a big production number.

A big attraction, and they had a big display where the stars were falling, and one thing and another. It was a beautiful thing to see. And they really made a big name then. So consequently, that helped Willie to get in the Cotton Club with the band quicker than if he had just been out there on his own -- one of them things.

So Mills put him in, and put Cab out on the road, and consequently, he started to change his men in the band. And Willie wanted me back in the band. Willie and I, I was just like one of his boys. It didn't make sense for me to be walking the street, and he had a job, and he could use me. So he put me back in his band. That was all right with me.
And you replaced who?
I replaced Jobetus, who was Cass McCord's brother..
Ted McCord...
Cass McCord.
Yes, but Jobetus was Ted McCord.
I don't know what Jobetus' name was.
That's all I know, if Jobetus. How they become twin brothers I don't know, because one was named Cass McCord and the other was named Jobetus.
Well, as I understand it, Jobetus' real name was Ted McCord... [THEODORE JOBETUS MCCORD]
I don't know what his real name.
...and he was a fraternal twin of Cass McCord. Isn't that correct.
I don't know. All I know, they're supposed to be twins, but they looked like twins just like me and you look like and twins.
Well, fraternal twins don't have to look alike.

They didn't look alike. They didn't talk alike. They didn't anything alike. In fact, I had my doubts that they was brothers. I mean, there was nothing to resemble them -- except that they were brothers. And I liked both of them. Both of them were good musicians. But I didn't see no twins, where they were twins.
But that's beside the point. Anyway, I had taken Ted...
Jobetus.
Jobetus' place. And shortly after I went in the band, then Cass, he quit the band, too, and Joe Garland taken Cass McCord's place. Then they started
calling themselves the Blue Rhythm Band.
Now, you mentioned everybody wanted to be a leader in that band, and they had many different people fronting the band.

Yeah, they had a lot of different leaders in front of the band. They started off with Carroll Dickerson from Chicago. He was the first leader, I think, in front of the band. Then they come up with another fellow named Sonny something-or-other, but he didn't last either... Q: Sonny Adams? You mentioned Sonny Adams. Was that the name?

No. Sonny Adams was a tenor player. But this leader's name was Sonny something. Well, anyway, then they had Baron Lee; he was the third leader that I know of. And after that, I don't know, because I was out of the band this time -- I was gone again. Then I think Lucky Millinder was about the last one that was in front of the band. It was still the Blue Rhythm Band when Lucky Millinder taken it over.
Now, you mentioned that everybody wanted to be a leader.
Yeah. There was a lot of dissension in the band between different ones. I'd rather not call their names, but it was about three or four of them that really

wanted to be the leader. And everything that happened, Downtown knew about it before it even happened. And it didn't not make for a good band, because there was too much dissension. Always something, this-that-and-the-other, a lot of jealousy and so forth and so on.
Now, when Cab or Duke came back, then what happened?
Then they was out of work. That's when I'd go back to Russell or anybody else I could find to go to.
In other words, the Mills Blue Rhythm Band really didn't tour.
Well, they toured... They made a tour with me one time. I made a tour with them.
I see.
Yeah, we made a tour. And one was enough. I got fired and didn't come back!
Well, would you care to relate that little experience of how you became spokesman for the...?

Well...it's not a nice thing to repeat. There are things you don't brag about. But while we was on the road we was drawin' big crowds and one thing and another, and everybody thought we should get more money. Everybody but me. It didn't make no difference to me. As long as I was getting paid, I was satisfied. But everybody wanted more money.

So they cut the trip short, and Mills brought the band into New York. And we all got together, and he wanted to know what was the trouble. So it looked like nobody wanted to speak up about the money, so I opened my mouth -- and I was about one of the least interested parties in getting anything; I had never spoken up for no money or anything. I spoke up, I opened my mouth, thinking somebody else would back me up. And I told him, I said, 'Well, the men don't think we're getting paid enough.'

So Mr. Mills looked at me. 'Anybody else got anything to say?' Nobody said a word. So Mr. Mills said, 'Well, we'll replace Holmes, and the rest of the schedule will go down.' And there I am sittin' like a fool. And that was it. What was there to do after that? I come out the band; that was it. That's the reason I got out of it.
Well, you made a few recordings with the band.
Yeah, nothing to speak of.

Maybe you could mention a little bit about how it was when you were out with Louis Armstrong, and whenever you got to somebody's... When there was a member of the band and you got to their home town, Louis would mention...
Well, he would always introduce... In anybody's home town we went to, he would always introduce this person to the audience, and let them know that one of

their own boys was in the orchestra. So we happened to play my home town, which happened to be Boston, Massachusetts. And we were playing in one of the most dedicated spots in Boston, which was the Symphony Hall, where the Boston Symphony Orchestra plays all the time. So we were playing there. We're the special... We're not playing symphonic music; we're playing dance music.

So okay, we set up there, and we're playing, and I see a lot of my friends come in, they're waving their hand at me and running up and shaking my hands, and this-that-and-the-other. So I'm sitting back, waiting for the big moment when Louis is going to introduce me. So the night goes on and on and on. And it looked like he wasn't going to introduce me! So I looked over to Russell, and I says... One of those things, you know.

So Luis Russell calls Louis Armstrong over to him, and he told him, "This is Charlie's home town." He said, "Oh, I'm sorry..." -- he called Pickles. Louis would call me Pickles. He says, "I'm sorry Pickles. Yeah. Man, folks, we have one of your home boys here, Charlie 'Pickles' Holmes" -- and made me take a bow. I mean, they give me a big hand, and one thing and another. It made me feel good. But I don't know, it could have been better.
Well, it had just slipped his mind, because...
Yeah, it had slipped his mind.
Yes, because of the time Louis was very generous about trying to bring other people to the fore.
Very much so. It really had slipped his mind. I mean, he hadn't given it a thought, really. Because he didn't do it maliciously or anything like that.
Because Henry Allen was in that band, and you mentioned earlier how he didn't hold Henry Allen back at all.
No... [COUGHS] Turn it off.
[PAUSE]

Yeah, Louis was not the type to hold anybody back. If you could do anything, he'd let you do it, and he'd be glad to promote you. In fact, he wanted that very much. Do something, do it, and do it good. Just like with Red Allen... Red Allen was a great trumpet player in the band, and a lot of people actually thought Red was better than Louis was -- Red had his following, too. But Louis gave Red an hour's time on his own, to play his own numbers; and anything he wanted to do, he would give Red an hour to do it. And Louis would get off the scene. He wouldn't even be seen on the stage. So Red could do anything he wanted to play, and he did it, too.
Red had his own book of numbers.
Red had his own library, books and numbers

and everything else. He played nothing but Red Allen's numbers. And he did all right. But now, when it's time for Louis to come back, Louis would come walking on across the stage, and he'd take his horn and play one note on the horn -- and brother, it sounded like the roof fell in or somethin'. They'd be whoopin' and hollerin', and poor Red, he was forgotten about right away. He was forgotten about right away.

But I mean, Louis was that type of person. He didn't stop nobody. He'd give them a whole hour. And that's very unusual for somebody working with a man like Louis or anybody else, and somebody else playing the same instrument, too -- you wouldn't give them no hour. He'd give him the whole hour, and let him prove himself. Well, then, all Louis would do was come back and hit one note. And it was all the difference in the world! All the difference in the world
Well, the same thing happened at another time when Luis Russell wanted to bring in somebody to replace...

Well, he was bringing in a fellow named Lee Collins from New Orleans, a trumpet player. He wanted to replace Red Allen in the band. And this fellow, he was supposed to be the best trumpet player from New Orleans. There was a big build-up about him. And of course, Red knew
him, and they all knew one another...
Yeah, Red and Russell...

Red didn't say anything, you know. So anyway, this fellow come in from New Orleans and joined Russell's band. And Russell's band at that time was real tight. I mean, Lee... Everybody knew one another and knew what was going to happen. If one of the fellows was going to make a curve(?) this way, everybody could feel it -- this-that-and-the-other, you know? And here comes Lee Collins with a big build-up from New Orleans, a young fellow, nice young man... And anyway, he started playing. He was going to take Red's place. But boy... He just wasn't capable. He just wasn't capable. He couldn't do it. And Red knew it. Red was very nice about it. He let the man play and all that. He didn't ridicule him or anything like that.

But I mean, the fella, he was over his head, for one thing; comin' to New York was another thing; and then bein' set in a band like Russell's band... I mean, we knew everything we were doing! It wasn't a band where you just come up and they stick some music in front of you. We knew everything we were playing. And the numbers we were playing were not the type that you heard other bands playing! And this fellow, he was just... He was just lost completely.
You know, he'd never heard nothin' like that before. And it was hard for him to even try to get adjusted. So he couldn't make it.

And I've got to give Red a lot of credit, too, because Red did nothing to ridicule him, and tried to help him out as much as possible, and everything else... He tried to make him feel at home. It was just that the man was scared to death, and he was just out of his class, that's all. Yeah, Red was... I was surprised to see Red was so gracious at first. But...
Well, Red was a big needler in that band, wasn't he?

Oh, he was a big needler, believe me. And he could needle, too. He could needle you. He had some of them up there crying sometimes! He would actually make them men cry. But lucky me...lucky me... He never said anything to me. We didn't kid. Red and I didn't kid. I was his boy. I don't know why he liked me. But he liked me; he said he did anyway -- I had no reason not to believe him. And we never kidded. We never played, you know. He kidded and played with everybody else, but he didn't play with me. But he'd take me with him to different places, and here, there or the other. I was his buddy. We went around bars together, and so forth, and this-that-and-the-other. But he never played with me. I mean, we never kidded.

Because I didn't believe in kiddin'. You see, when I kid with somebody, I actually like them. I have to like them to kid them. If I didn't like them... If there was anything about them I didn't like, I would not kid them, because kiddin' brings on violence. And I've always been too small to fight. Heh-heh. But I mean, if I didn't like somebody, I would never kid them. For me to kid with somebody, I have to like them extremely well. But Red and I, we never kidded.

You know, Red was a fine guy. Man, he was kiddin' everybody else -- and I was enjoying it at the expense of somebody else! Yeah, we went through some experiences together. Red was fine, believe me. Everybody liked Red. Everybody liked him. Most people, when they're loud and... you know what I mean?...got a big mouth and loud, and this-that-and-other -- people don't like them. But everywhere we went, everybody goes, "Red Allen! Red Allen!" They'd be shoutin' for Red. And he liked it, too. He liked that. Well, I wasn't so much for that. He liked it.
What about J.C. Higgenbotham? What can you tell me about him?
It's nothin' much I can tell you about him...except that he was a helluva trombone player. And he did his work, and he could play. He loved to blow his horn,

and he loved to take a little taste. And he didn't bother nobody. He was not the violent type or anything like that. He didn't care what anybody did, as long as he could sit up there and play his horn. And you couldn't find too much for him to play. He loved to blow. And he could blow...and now and then he'd take a little taste. Sometimes he'd take a little taste too much. But I guess that happens to you.
But Higgy was great to work with. He was great. Yeah, him and Red worked together for years, after they got out of Russell's band. Yeah, they worked together for years.
Well, would you rate Higgy as one of the best trombonists around at the time?
One of the best I ever heard in my life.
Yeah.

He was one of the best I ever heard. I mean, just for a plain, every-day trombone player, yes, he was one of the best I ever heard in my life. He was fine. And I don't think... Higgy I know didn't have no whole lot of musical education. He was no Juilliard man or anything like that. He was a plain, ordinary musician. But he could play. Hell of an instinct. Yeah, a good man. One of the best I ever played with. Very creative. And easy to get along with. Very easy to get along with. A very nice person.
Boy, you're taking me way back a whole lot of years. You make me...
But that Russell band must have been something special, though, because you stuck together, you knew each other, and as you've mentioned, the music...
We enjoyed working with one another. You know what I mean? There was nobody in the organization that was mad with somebody else, you know, in the organization. We all enjoyed working together.

And Pops Foster was... Let me see. Pops Foster was supposed... He was the bass player. He came to New York in 1929. I was 19 years old when he come here. Pops Foster was supposed to be 65 years old when he joined the band. Well, I don't know how old Pops was. He looked to be 65. But whatever his age was, he had more life in him than I ever had in me, and I wasn't but 19 years old. And Pops and I used to run around together! And everybody liked Pops Foster. Everybody! He was just one of them old men... He wasn't all that old either, but he looked old.
He was 38. Because he was born in 1892.
He don't know when he was born. How would he know? But anyway, he was one of them old-looking men... I say, old-looking...
Yeah, it's true.

Because we'd go different places, and "Pops Foster, Pops..." -- everybody wants Pops, Pops... They think he was an old man too. He looked old. He was supposed to be 65 years old. And that's what I thought, too. Well, you could be right with that 38, because ain't no way in the world an old man 65 years old had the get up and go like he had. I mean, he had an old look on him, but he had a devilish head. His head had devilish ideas in it -- a younger man, you know?
I see.

Yeah, Pops was somethin' great. And him and I, because I was the baby in the band and he was the old man... And him and I, we were seat-mates on the bus. And boy, he was something else. Pops was a great old man.
A funny thing. I seen Pops almost fifty years later, maybe not that many years but it seemed like it to me, and he was telling me... He passed by my house one day when I was looking out the window, I stopped him, and we got to talking. And he was telling me, he said, "You know..." At that time, he was living in California, but he happened to be in New York working. He said, "You know something, Charlie?" He said, "I'm playing down there on Eighth Avenue (or in the Bronx, someplace) with some of my people, and I've got a whole lot of grandchildren around me. All my

grandchildren." I got to thinking, "What kind of children is he talkin' about?" I never heard of him havin' no children, period! And he was telling me he had so many grandchildren around, and then this-that-and-the-other... I said, "Yeah, Pops, it's all in the mind. All in the mind." [LAUGHS]
But Pops, he was great. He was a fine person. He finally passed away [1969], but his wife, I think she's still living.
Yes, she is.
I've got to send her a Christmas card this year. We got to sending one another Christmas cards, oh, I'd say about eight or ten years ago.
Isn't her name Alma?
Alma.

And of course, last year I didn't send her a card, because Liscotte(?) passed away during the year, and I didn't send out any Christmas cards at all. So as far as I'm concerned, she don't know that Liscotte(?) has passed away. I don't know if she knows or not. I guess so. But I'll send her a card this year, if she's still around to receive it. Nice person, Alma. Very nice.
Now, a member of the Russell band that's received perhaps the least amount of mention or fleshing out, so to
speak, is the guitar player...
Bill Johnson.
Bill Johnson. [1905-1955]

Yeah. Well, Bill was a nice guy. Nothing extemporaneous about him. I mean, he was just a quiet person. And he played guitar and did his job. Very well-schooled person. He was a college man or a college graduate. And he was very well-liked. There was nothin'... You know, he...
Was he there when you joined the bad the first...? I think he was, wasn't he? He was kind of already...

I think so. I think so. [CHILTON SAYS HE JOINED RUSSELL IN 1927] I think he was at the Nest Club when I first went down there. Yeah, the Nest Club, where Russell was the piano player. Yeah, Bill Johnson. He used to sing...
Where was he from? Do you know?

He was from Kentucky. Louisville or Lexington, one of those places -- Kentucky. [b. LEXINGTON, KENTUCKY, 1905] But he was brought up around Washington D.C. In fact, I think he was a graduate of Howard University. He was very well educated. And a nice person. Very quiet. I have to say nice... Never bothered nobody.
He used to sing with the band?
Yeah. He sang that number, 'You Might Get Better, But You Never Get Well.' He sang that. He sang a lot of numbers.

But he liked a little taste, too... Well, I guess everybody in the band did at that time. We were all young. Nobody was married at the time. Yeah, we all indulged a little bit. We weren't what you would call... We weren't lushes or anything like that. But we would always take a little drink, get a little spirit.

Well, now, that rhythm section has been mentioned as maybe one of the greatest rhythm sections in Jazz. How did you feel about the Russell rhythm section? Wasn't that a powerhouse behind you, that made you feel like...?
Oh, it was a very good rhythm section. Very good. Paul Barbarin, you mean?
Mmm-hmm. Well, I mean the whole thing, with Pops, Barbarin, Johnson...

Yeah, and Luis Russell, too. Very good. They had that real Dixie...that real New Orleans beat -- because they were from down there. So Paul and Pops Foster, they knew what they was doin'. And Russell was brought up around there, New Orleans. Yeah, they had that beat all right.
But the kick I used to get out of the band is when
Russell would have them up there as a small band out of a big band, and he'd have all these fellas from New Orleans playing.
What would that be?
Well, there was Red, there would be Higgenbotham in it, and there would be Pops Foster, and there would be Albert Nicholas, and there would be Russell, and I don't know who the other ones...
Barbarin.
Paul Barbarin.
Oh, they used to do things.
They used to play, and they played the New Orleans numbers. That's the first time I used to hear some of them New Orleans numbers. Man, they could lay it on you, too. Oh! Terrific, terrific.
So this is something that would happen while you were performing? In other words, it would be like...

Russell would tell us, 'Man, lay out' -- you know, get off the stand. And they would take over. They would take over. And it would be something worth listening to. They had the place... They had the Saratoga Club packed at night, like that, with musicians from downtown. What's the name of... Everybody says Benny Goodman was first, I don't know why... But Benny was there

also; he used to come in there. Of course, he wasn't Benny Goodman then. He was just another clarinetist. But Jimmy Dorsey, Tommy Dorsey, Dick McDonough, you name 'em, they were all up there. And they were diggin' that beat; you know, that New Orleans beat that they were puttin' down. Because nobody else was playing it. And they were diggin' it.
Of course, to Russell it didn't mean a thing. Well, that sounded good to me. That's all I wanted to do, was listen at it. I'd get off the stand. That's my paranoia(?). But they would be wailin'.

And then one night, Benny Goodman came in with his clarinet. And Sidney Bechet had just come back from Europe, and naturally, Sidney, being from down in New Orleans, they were featuring him. Russell just announced him, and this-that-and-the-other. And Bechet was up there blowin'... And I was gettin' a big kick out of Bechet. You know, he was... At the time, his hair was white, he looked like older than what he really was. And he was blowin' the soprano. He was creating a lot of attention.

So Benny Goodman runs up on the stand and takes out his clarinet. He wants to know... He asked somebody, 'Who's that old man playing the soprano saxophone?' Benny takes his clarinet and they start to battling one another. And

that's all Sidney wanted to hear. And they just battled backward and forward, backward and forward, backward and forward. That was a great night in the Saratoga Club, because all the musicians were around and just the two of them, backwards and forwards.

It did me good because I didn't have to play it! Because Jimmy Dorsey was sitting up on the bandstand, you know, and I had just gotten up. Jimmy and I had just... Because at that time, Jimmy had recorded a number, a saxophone solo on a number "Sensation," and I knew the number -- I knew the solo, you know. And we was on the stand playing "Sensation," and just before Jimmy's solo, I played -- and I played his solo on the number. Which was very unprofessional, you know. And Jimmy was so surprised, he turned around and shook my hand!

Well, we had a good time, though. But right after that, then Bechet was introduced, and that's when him and Benny Goodman got to battlin' up there. But it was all in fun. Nobody got killed or anything in that battle.
No, no.
Yes, it was... Both of them were battlin', though. They was wailin', too.
Did Bechet play his clarinet as well as...
No, no, he played soprano.
Just the soprano, yeah.

He just played soprano, and then he played clarinet. But at that time, Benny... Benny was a good clarinet player. But he wasn't no... He's not like he is now, you know. Benny wasn't always great. He had to start, too. Yeah, he wasn't that great. He was good, but he wasn't always so great.
But of course, Sidney was a mature musician at that time.
Well, Sidney was...
A genius.

...an experienced musician. Benny was young. You know what I mean? Benny was a youngster. Sidney, he had been to Europe and back and one thing or another, and he had a lot of experience. Good musician. He had his ideas. He really had ideas, too. Yeah, good man.
You were probably as impressed with Bechet as Johnny Hodges was.
Not quite the same way.
Not quite the same way.

Sidney did not impress me... I mean, he was a good saxophone player, and I was thrilled when I heard him. You know, naturally I would be thrilled. But to me, see, I was always Johnny Hodges. He didn't sound as good to

me as Johnny Hodges did. He never did -- to me. But I mean, that's the way I thought about it. That's my own personal opinion. Now, Johnny, he was wrapped up in Bechet. And I don't know why, because to me Johnny sounded immediate(?) to me. But that's an opinion. That's just... Well, that's what makes (?). Well, he was pretty good, I think.
That's an exciting evening at the Saratoga Club.
Oh yeah.
About what year do you think that must have been?
Oh, it's hard for me to say. I don't know. It could have been in... In the Thirties maybe. In the Thirties. The early Thirties.
Well, now, you wrote some numbers yourself which were recorded.
Yeah, yeah. We don't normally write any of my music. I might leave a symphony or something out there, you know. After all, I did play with a symphony band, you know. I started at the top.
[PAUSE]
I thought we could flesh out a few of the musicians who you used to know -- or still know. For instance, Joe Steele.
Joe Steele. Great man of the piano. One

of his sisters was my Sunday School teacher when I was a little boy. And Joe was a great pianist, at that time playing Classical Music and dance music, as it was called in those days -- just the beginning of Jazz. The name "Jazz" wasn't used in all families. So he was a great dance pianist.
Do you know where he came from?
I'm sure he was some part of Georgia. I think it was Atlanta. But on that I'm not too sure.
Because apparently he was a graduate of the New England Conservatory.
That's true.
Now, you said about some of his idiosyncracies...

Well, he had little weird ideas. Well, not weird, but a little strange. He was so wrapped up with his music and his hands and his fingers, he wouldn't shake hands with a stranger or anything like that because he was always protecting his fingers. And sometimes he would have his hands folded, like the Chinese used to hold their hands years ago, keep them close to his side and covered over, just to keep his fingers from getting hurt. And next time you'd see him, he'd be in the street there playing hard ball. He was a great pianist, but he loved baseball, too, and he loved to play.
So he didn't worry about his hands then, but...
But anything else, he worried about his fingers.
...anything else he worried about his fingers.
Yeah, he loved baseball.
Now, you said at one time that he played "Rhapsody in Blue" for Gershwin.

Well, they were putting on a show. "Rhapsody In Black" was the name of the show. An all-Negro show. And Gershwin provided the music. So they were using Gershwin's "Rhapsody In Blue" in the show. Now, this goes way back to the early Twenties, and "Rhapsody In Blue" at that time was not so popular -- it was just beginning to get known.

So they sent for Joe Steele to make an audition to play the Rhapsody to be used in the show, and Gershwin was there, amongst other nobility of the music world. So Joe comes in and he sits at the piano, and the conductor gives him the go-ahead signal. So the band started off, and Joe sits at the piano -- and he went all through the Rhapsody, beginning to end. And when they got through, Joe got a big hand from all the commentators standing around, musicians and one thing or another.
So Lew Leslie, the head of the show, this show, he was
the leader of the show, he told Joe, Joe Steele, to stand aside and...
Let Gershwin...?
Yeah... I'm trying to think of his first name.
George.

That's right. That's a weird name. He told Joe to sit down, and George Gershwin would explain to him just what was what and how it was really supposed to go. So Gershwin heard Lew Leslie make that remark, and he said to Lew Leslie and everybody else standing around there...he said, "Well, there's nothing I can tell this man about playing 'Rhapsody.' He played it perfectly. There's nothing to tell him." Well, I mean, that was the big feather in the cap of Joe Steele, I mean, to have somebody like Gershwin make a remark like that about him the first time he sat down to play the music... "Rhapsody In Blue" was nothing easy to sit right down and play. And he played it right off, just like it's supposed to be done, and Gershwin was right there, and said there was nothing he could tell him.
Now, was this just the piano, or was it with an orchestra?
The whole orchestra
Do you remember who took the clarinet parts?
Oh, no. I don't know... I wasn't even there!
I see. You just heard about it.
I heard about it. Because you know, things like that, they have a way of getting out to the musicians.
Because you played with Joe Steele at the Savoy Ballroom.
I worked with him. Yes, I did.
Because he was in Willie Lynch's band, right?
That's true.
And that later on became the Mills Blue Rhythm Band.
Yes.
Now, you mentioned that Willie Lynch was a good friend of Irving Mills'.
Yes.
So therefore, when...

When they wanted to... See, Irving Mills put Duke Ellington's band in the Cotton Club. Then when Duke come out to go on the road, he put Cab Calloway's band there. And both of them were so successful in the Cotton Club, when both of them come and was on the road, then Irving Mills got an idea that he would put another band in the Cotton Club in Cab Calloway's place, and that's where

Willie Lynch got the band together for Irving Mills -- and they called it the Blue Rhythm Band, Irving Mills' Blue Rhythm Band. And Willie Lynch was the leader, but they called him...his name was automatically changed to Earl Jackson, to keep the royal names up -- Count Basie, Duke Ellington, Earl Jackson. They were all royal names. Earl Hines and so forth, you know?
You had also King Carter.
That's right, King Carter...
Which was nothing but the Mills Blue Rhythm Band when they recorded. You were on that session.
Well, Mills Blue Rhythm Band, let me see. When I was there, we didn't have no royal leader. The leader was either...
Carroll Dickerson?
Either Carroll Dickerson... I'm trying to think of some of the leaders that used to be there... Carroll Dickerson. Sonny... Sonny something. And there was...
Charlie Holmes (11/29/82):

Well, I was telling you about the time I went with Chick's band, Chick Webb. He had an eight-piece band at the Savoy Ballroom, and he was enlarging the band to ten pieces. And he added myself and Cootie Williams on trumpet to the band, which enlarged it to ten pieces.

Cootie was a trumpet player that came here with Alonzo Ross's band from Florida. And they fell into hard times, and the band broke up -- and they had some pretty good musicians in the band. They had a trumpet player named Melvin Herbert, who was a very good trumpet player, and then Cootie Williams. Then they had a well-known guitar player, Casper Cowie(?) was his name, and he later shortened it to Cass Carr. Cass became a leader himself, and did quite a bit of booking his own orchestra, and had quite a few of the musicians from New York working for him. Then there was a piano...
Tell me more about Cass Carr. He played all kinds of instruments, I think.
Well, he played... He had a banjo or a guitar, and he played bass and musical saw -- bass violin and a musical saw. And he used to take his choruses on the musical saw.
I see!
[LAUGHS] You know, it was a novelty. But
Holmes (11/29) - 2

he was quite a bandleader. He would get a lot of work. Just gig work. He didn't work anywhere steady or anything like that. He was just giggin'. And he had a nucleus to his band, which I don't remember... But he would always have openings for anybody that was giggin'. And that way, he used, oh, numerous musicians that was in the street giggin', lookin' for gigs and one-thing-or-another. They could always get a gig with Cass Carr. That's that they called him. He shortened his name from Casper Cowie(?) to Cass Carr.
Oh, it was Cowie(?), not Towey(?).

Well, I don't know what it was. But they called him Cass Carr. And he survived for years in the business. And he was a very good photographer. He went in for photography more than he was music. He was interested in taking pictures, and one-thing-or-another. And now, he's in the line of... He sells photographic instruments. He sells photographic instruments to professionals. He's got a place downtown somewhere. He's out of the music business altogether.
But you gigged with him, though.
Oh, plenty of times. Numerous times, yes.
What type of groups were they? Five or six pieces?
No. He had ten pieces, up... What the
Holmes (11/29) - 3
occasion called for. But he would always have three saxophones at least, three brass at least -- and more sometimes.
What kind of work, then? Society work? What kind of gigs did he get?

Well, I wouldn't call them Society. It was dances. He played for different groups in clubs and things. Dance music. But he had some good musicians in the band. You know Bob Williams. He worked with him many a time.
I see.
Oh yeah. In fact, anybody you name, they have worked with Cass Carr. Any of the musicians that you know, they have worked with Cass Carr.
When he had his bands together, did he primarily then play his guitar?
Well, no. He primarily played bass violin. He played bass violin. And then he would draw his saw out in the middle of the night...! Which was nice. He had a number that he did on the saw, you know.
Do you remember the number?
No. Who would want to remember it? But I mean, it was his band. He'd play what he'd want to play! And I mean, if you didn't react to the way he thought you should... No, strike that out.
Holmes (11/29) - 4
You were out of his band!
You were out of the band.
Well, who were some of the other saxophonists that you...?
Well, at different times, I mean, he had... He's had them all. Howard Johnson and... You name them, he's had them. It's a funny thing.
And he paid off all right, right after the gig, or did you have to wait...?

Oh yeah, you got paid. Yeah. He didn't mess with your money. He might be a little light on it. I mean, he might not pay as much as everybody else, or one of them things. But he didn't mess with your money. You didn't have to worry about it.
So in other words, if he called you for a gig, you'd take it.
Yeah, you'd get your money.
Now, other members of that Ross De Luxe Syncopator Band that came here, one who was at the time playing bass in the band was Richard Fulbright.
Fulbright, yeah.
What can you tell me about Fulbright?
Well, Fulbright was a bass player, and a damn good one, too. I mean, he was one of the best. He
Holmes (11/29) - 5
really was. But it's one of them things. Some get the breaks, some don't. You know what I mean?
Right. Now, he was the kind of bass player that could play both tuba and the string bass?

Yeah, he played everything. He was very good. Uncle Dick, yeah. There's nothing more I can say about him. Just a good bass player, and some of them get breaks... He worked with quite a few bands. I can't remember whose bands he worked with...
Bingie Madison, I think.
It could have been.
Edmond Hall came in with that Ross De Luxe Syncopated Band, too.

Well, see, Hall, he... I don't know what happened to him when they first got here, because I didn't meet him until later. I think he was kind of implanted with the Dixieland boys downtown. You know, I think. Of course, I mean, he was giggin' around up there, too. You'd take a gig wherever you could get 'em. They were hard times. But I think he hung around with the Dixieland boys more than uptown.
Then there was another trumpet player, Robert "Cookie" Mason.
Well, there's nothing I could say too much
Holmes (11/29) - 6

about Cookie, because I didn't know until years later that Cookie was even in a... I didn't know Cookie was a musician. I had been knowin' him for years and didn't know he was a musician. But at the time I met Cookie, I think he was a chauffeur for some big man downtown. He had a chauffeur's job. Every time I saw Cookie, he was all dressed up like he was a rich man or something. I didn't know he was even a musician.

Yeah, he would always be around the club... Oh, I actually thought he was a big-time gambler. Because he was around the Rhythm Club, where they gambled. Most of the time they had a big game goin' in there. And he would always be around, and I figured he was just another gambler hangin' around. Because he was dressed up all the time. He was very neat, you know.
But he was a good trumpet player, too. I've worked a few gigs with him. A very good trumpet player.
Yeah, they had good trumpet players in that band.
Yeah, you mentioned that when these bands would come into town, that they would...
At the jam sessions.
And cutting contests.
And cutting contests, yeah. And those that could show some promise, they could stay, and the ones that
Holmes (11/29) - 7
couldn't, they had to get out of town. They didn't hang around.
Speaking of odd instruments, like the musical saw, there was a musician that you got hooked up with (for a recording date anyway) by the name of Wilton Crawley.
Yeah, but that was not no weird instrument he had. He was a clarinet player. A clarinet is a legitimate instrument.
But maybe it was perhaps the way he...
Oh, the way he was playing it.
Maybe you could tell us about Crawley and about his successful act and so on.

Wilton Crawley, let me see. I couldn't put him down as a clarinet player. I couldn't call him a clarinet player, because the man had more to offer than clarinet players have to offer. Because the man was an acrobat, he was a contortionist, he sang, and he wrote music... Well, he did just about it all. He had his own style of playing, and I wouldn't say that it was bad. But I wouldn't say it was good either. But he had his own style of playing.
And he was a very big act on the B.F. Keith Circuit. That was the top vaudeville circuit at that time. And he was a big act on the B.F. Keith Circuit. He could come out
Holmes (11/29) - 8

with that clarinet, and play it, and start taking it apart from the lowest joint, take that off, and then he'd take the middle joint off and be playing half the clarinet, and then he would take that joint off, and it would leave him playing nothing but the mouthpiece -- and he would still be playing. And then he would go to the end of the stage, and look into the wings, and he would come back with a lamp on his head, a kerosene lamp -- and it would be lit. He'd come in with this lamp on his head, he's still playing this mouthpiece...
So it was a live flame.

Yeah. And he'd still be playing his clarinet, you know. So he's putting the clarinet back together again now. Because he'd got down to the mouthpiece. Now he's putting it back together again, and he's playing it, and he's balancing this kerosene lamp on his head, and he's going into all kind of contortions, acts and things. So it ends up where the clarinet is...he gets the clarinet back together, he's playing it, gets the clarinet back together, the lamp is on his head, and I don't know how he does it, but he ended up being on his head, too, playing the clarinet and balancing the lamp. I mean, it was a wonderful act! You wouldn't believe it. I don't know how he did it. But it made a lot of big money.
And he was on stage just by himself.
Holmes (11/29) - 9
He was by himself, yeah. He was a single.
And he wrote his own music?
Yeah, he wrote his own music.
And then the pit band would play it.

Well, I don't say... I mean, he would write his numbers. But I don't say he arranged the music for the orchestra. I don't think he was an arranger. But I mean, he could scratch out a melody, you know. Oh, he was very entertaining to look at, but I could do without listening to him. Strike that out.
What do you remember of the recordings?
Well...
Because some of them had Jelly Roll Morton on them.

I don't know that the recording... They was his recordings. But something happened. He had Russell's group to come in, to record with him. And while we were there, Jelly Roll Morton walks in with a group, and he's supposed to record with him.. I don't know how they got mixed up. The two of them... Jelly had his group there to record with Wilton Crawley, and so did Russell.

So anyway, he was (?) out there (?) with so-and-so, and we split up the band or something like that. We both do the recording. So Jelly would play a little piano on some of the numbers and Russell would play the piano on some of the
numbers. I would play the saxophone on some of the numbers, and then somebody else would play. It was agreeable. And nothing was nerve-wracking or anything.
Did Russell and Jelly ever play together on the recording?
No.
So that you had four hands?
Not that I know of, no. Could have, but I don't know. Because I wasn't paying that much attention to them. Because when I wasn't on, I was doing something else around the studio.
But you remember that there were separate sessions. Some of them were months apart.

Oh yeah. Well, they were different, yeah. Well, that happened... Well, I mean, all of them wasn't like that. I mean, Russell would go in with his group, the next group. Well, I don't know if Jelly was making the records for him, too, any more. But I was just telling you about that particular time when the two bands got together there.
I remember you said they were like two prima donnas squaring off.
Oh yeah. Well, see, that sort of caused some dissension, you know. Because Jelly thought he was going to be the star, and Wilton Crawley knew he was the

star. He knew it was his show. And Jelly thought Mister Jelly Lord was gonna take over, and he'd come in and: "Hi, Wilton. Caught your show last week at the Lafayette Theatre." So Wilton said, "Yeah?" He said, "Well, next week, I'm at the Paramount." The Paramount is downtown. The Lafayette Theatre is a little colored theatre up inn Harlem. See, Jelly Roll was very sarcastic about it. But Wilton, he come right back at him: "Next week I'm at the Paramount."
Of course, at the time Jelly was not...

At the time Jelly wasn't doing good. Jelly would have been glad to be anywhere. At that time he would have been glad to be in the Lafayette. He wasn't doing good. Jelly did not do good. See, Jelly didn't take New York by storm. I didn't know Jelly was a big man in the music business until years later. I had to read it in a book, Jelly Roll Morton was the big man from New Orleans. I said, "That must be a different Jelly Roll than the one I know." Because Jelly Roll, he was going through some hard times around here in New York, just like King Oliver was. But King Oliver had an excuse. His gums was bad. You know, he had pyorrhea; he couldn't blow.
But Jelly could talk. Oh, and he could talk and he would talk. He'd talk the leg off an iron pot. And he was

very educational! I mean, to listen to. He said some mighty witty things, you know. He was the type of guy, you'd hate him if you first hear him. But then, the more you listen to him, the better you would like him, you know. You'd stop paying attention to some of the things that he was saying, and you had to like him for it.

That session... They turned out all right. All of them sessions turned out all right. There was just so many musicians around there, it was hard to tell who was playing on what. But everything turned out nice. Yup, a lot of musicians in the studio that day. I mean, you wouldn't overwork yourself. You know, you'd be playing on this number, and when you finished that number, somebody else would take you up and they'd play another number. So you didn't work too hard. Very good.
Can you remember who was in the studio? Or anybody that... Because there have been so many names suggested.
Yeah. Now, who was there? Well, Freddy Jenkins was on one of the numbers. I mean, he was in the studio -- Freddy Jenkins, the trumpet player.
Did he come in with Morton. Because he certainly wouldn't...
Well, I don't know who he come in with. But he was there.
Because he wouldn't have been there with Russell.

No. Well, he could have been with Morton. I guess all the rest of the fellows that were there that wasn't with Russell was with Jelly Roll. But there was a gang of them in there. I can't remember all of them. In fact, there's very few of them I can remember. Right now I can't think of nobody's name.
But you recognized your own playing on one of the records.
Oh yeah, yeah.
So you're definitely there.
I can't always tell my playing, but I know that was my playing. Usually the ones that I mistake for me sometimes, they're much better players than I am. But they sound bad, then I know it's me.
Well, I think it's a great solo, and it's on "Keep Your Business To Yourself." Now, Crawley brought in music.
Yes, he brought his music in. All we had to do was just play it. He passed out the music, and we'd play it. It was written out, yeah. Now, what else?
Some of the trumpet playing you thought might have been Lincoln Mills.
Well, yeah, one number I heard, it sounds similar to Freddy Jenkins, but I would say it's not Freddy

Jenkins -- definitely not. Freddy was too clean in his playing. He was very precise, but he was very clean. This playing was fast, the notation was fast, but it was not clean -- it was sloppy. Freddy was not a sloppy trumpet player. He was very precise, and anything he hit at, he hit it. The notes were clear.
You said when he executed triplets, they came out like triplets.
That's right. This particular record I heard just wasn't clear or precise. That's why I said that wasn't Freddy.
You also mentioned Freddy being a very sharp and fastidious dresser and...

Oh yeah, a dresser...! Oh yeah, he was neat as a pin. Oh yeah. He was something else. And that's why he was such a big man in Duke Ellington's band, he was so classy and he was a real showboat. Oh man, he was something else, sitting up on the bandstand with his left-handed trumpet. He played trumpet with the left hand, you know. And then playing... Oh, he was something. He was class personified. More people would come and ask for Freddy Jenkins than they did for Duke Ellington. Freddy was a big attraction in that band.
At the Cotton Club.

No, I'm talking about in theatres, when they played theatres. Oh, he was something. Yes, indeed, Freddy was the big attraction. And always had... He was a little-bitty guy, you know, and he was... Freddy was about the size I am right now, and I'm only 5 feet 3... But he was small like I am now. And always had a big cigar in his mouth. Great big cigar. Big fat El Producto cigar. He always had that big cigar. And he loved to talk. He was a real showboat.
Did you ever play with him at any other time?
Oh, I gigged with him a lot of times, sure. Different gigs and things, sure.
Well, Freddy Jenkins was from New York City.

Yeah, he was born here. That's how he got his hands on that stuff. He was hopping on the back of a truck, so they tell me. And I think the tailbone or something... He snapped all the fingers on the right hand. That's what I heard.
Yeah, because according to Chilton he switched to playing left-handed early in his teens.
Yeah.
He was briefly with Edgar Hayes in the Twenties, but you weren't involved in that.
I have never been involved with Edgar Hayes
except with the Blue Rhythm Band.
And then according to this, Jenkins had a brief spell conducting the Luis Russell band at Connie's Inn around 1936.
Yeah. You weren't with Russell then.
Oh, but that might have been one of Russell's bands. In '36, Russell was with Louis. In '35 to '36 Luis was with Louis. That might have been one of Russell's bands that he got together with somebody.
Yeah, in between Louis Armstrong's featured numbers it said that Jenkins did some direction of the band.

I was talking about how I was at the Rhythm Club one day, my favorite hangout spot where the musicians gathered to get the gigs and one thing and another, and Leonard Feather walked up to me and asked me would I be interested in working in a small combination with Bobby Burnet, a trumpet player. I told him, 'Well, why not? I'll work with anybody.' So I was introduced to Bobby, and we talked, and he explained what he had. He didn't have much work, but he thought with him and Leonard Feather, they could get something going.
But anyway, they had a week or two engagement at Nick's

in the Village, and we got the band together and rehearsed. I don't remember all of the members of the band, but there was Bobby, he was the trumpet player... Bobby Burnet was the trumpet player, Leonard Feather was the pianist, and Manzie Johnson was the drummer, and I was the saxophonist. Now, there's two that I don't remember, one or two. I don't know if it was a five-piece combination or a six-piece combination.
But you probably had a string bass.
Most likely. But I can't think of who it was.
And this was February to March 1941.
Yes.
So this would be after you had left Russell for another time...
Yeah. No, that was Louis' band I had left. Louis' band. I left him in '40. And this was '41.

Well, Bobby Burnet was a trumpet player. He was a White trumpet player. He used to work with...what's the tenor saxophone player's name? Charlie...?
Ventura?
No, the one that recorded... Charlie,
Charlie, Charlie, Charlie... All these great names; I don't remember the great ones.
A White tenor player?
