Well, we can come back to it.

Yeah, we can come back to it. We will come back to it. Because you know who I'm talking about. I mean, he was very popular. He was one of the big ones, do you know what I mean? Like Benny Goodman and them. Charlie... It wasn't Charlie Spivak, because he wasn't a tenor player. [CHARLIE BARNET IS THE TENOR PLAYER]
Bobby Burnet apparently was very wealthy.

Well, for them days he was very wealthy. He inherited between seven and eight million dollars in his own right, and he was a young man then. So he was pretty well-to-do. But you would never know it, because he had an old, broken-down, second-hand car and a reversible raincoat that he wore all the time. To me he looked like Pete the Tramp. But he was supposed to be a millionaire, so I guess maybe he was starting off to be eccentric.
And you had a job... Where did you play with Burnet?

Well, he had a job at Nick's in the Village. Nick's was a nightclub in the Village. he sold very good steaks. The best steaks in New York City. Nick had them. And he tried the band out a couple of weeks. But we were no big attraction. We didn't attract nobody in there. You know, people didn't... We weren't turnin' nobody away at the doors. We'd go in there and play. We had Leonard Feather's music. He was the musical director, and he had his arrangements, which I mean, it was all right. Nothin' too jazzy about 'em. I mean, they were nice arrangements. They were written correctly, but they wouldn't cause you to turn your head and applaud or anything like that. They were just nice. Nice arrangements.
You had no problems from the fact that it was a mixed band racially?
No, no, no. They had mixed bands in them days. Sure.
You weren't pioneering anything in that sense.

No, no. We weren't pioneering. Benny Goodman had Cootie Williams, one-thing-and-another. I mean, there was mixed bands at that time. No, we weren't pioneering. We just wasn't drawin' any people. And the Village at that time was kind of rough down there. I mean,
business was bad in the Village at that time. It was very bad. And you know, it was wartime now, 1941... I mean, that's when they were talking about war.
Well, the War in Europe was already on.
The War in Europe was on, but we didn't get in the War until Pearl Harbor. That was in December. We hadn't exactly got into it yet, I don't think.
No, we hadn't.

But War was in the air, you know what I mean? Everything... And the Village wasn't doing good at that time. So we weren't doing any worse down there than anybody else, but the business just wasn't there. You could see for yourself there wasn't no business. Well, I think we stayed about two weeks.
Bobby was a nice guy. But nothin' happened, you know? So I left there, and the next thing I heard was Cootie Williams getting a band together...
Well, in the meantime, you returned to Boston for a few....
No, no. I'm back from Boston now. Yeah, I'm back. I'm through with the machine shop.
I see. You went up to the machine shop, then, before joining Bobby Burnet.
Yeah, yeah. When I had come back, I

joined Bobby, because I was hanging around the clubs, you know, just to pick up gigs or anything I could get. And Leonard Feather walks in and asks me would I care to work with Bobby Burnet, and I told him it didn't make no difference to me. So I worked with Bobby for the two weeks.

Then I heard Cootie was getting a band together -- Cootie Williams. So I go in touch with Cootie, because you know, I knew Cootie; Cootie was a friend of mine. And I knew I was going to be in on that band. You know, I went up there. So I got in touch with Cootie, and he told me, "Yeah, sure." So I told Cootie, I said, "Well, look, I don't want any solos." He said, ""That's all right. That's fine." He said, "I got somebody to play solos." He said, "You don't have to worry about no solos. I said, "That's beautiful." He said, "I got a man to play my first parts and solos." I said, "That's beautiful. That's just how I like it. I'll play third parts, and just lay dead and take it easy."

Because in Louis' band, boy... Mmm, that was hard working in that band. I mean, they had worked me to death, you know. And I didn't like it in Louis' band. They made a whole lot of noise. So when Cootie told me that, that was beautiful.
So I asked him, "Who is going to play first saxophone?"

He says, "I've got a man, I've got a man. He's coming here from Texas." I said, "From Texas?" Well, I had never known no great first saxophone men from Texas! They have a whole lot of good saxophone players from Texas, but they weren't what they would call a lead man, you know? They were all what you'd call get-off men. They could solo and everything else. But not no lead. So I said, "Okay, all right. Third part's good for me."

So Cootie started rehearsing the band. He sent out a notice for different musicians and one-thing-or-another. And he started rehearsing. Well, the lead saxophone player wasn't there at the first rehearsal. So Cootie said to him, "Well, Charlie, you play the first chair until my man gets here." You know, to see(?) (?). And in the meantime, he was trying out other men that was standing around with their horns. Everybody was trying out. And Cootie was very generous. He had plenty of whiskey there. And it was just like they was having a party or something.

So we would rehearse a number, and then we'd stop and take a break, have a little taste and so forth. Well, they would take up the afternoon, you know, take up the time, and come back the next day. Well, we kept on rehearsing. So I say to Cootie, I said, "Well, Cootie, when is your lead saxophone player coming?" He said, "Well, he'll be here
tomorrow." I said, "Really? Fine."

Well, the next day I got to rehearsal. We're all sitting around there, and Cootie walks in with this saxophone player. He's pulling him by the arm. So he said, "Fellows, I want you to meet our first saxophone player. Boys, this is Eddie Vinson." So we met Eddie, and Eddie was standing up there with his hat on, you know. So Eddie said, "Well, gentlemen, I'm glad to meet you," this-that-and-the-other and a whole lot of crap. He said, "Let's do it now and get it over with." I don't know. Do what now and get it over with? So he taken off his hat...heh-heh...and he's just as bald as a cue ball! But everybody fell out, because in them days they weren't wearing their hair like that! And boy, we all fell out. We had a big laugh. "Damn, Mister Cleanhead." So we had a big laugh about it, and that was it.

So anyway, Eddie taken his horn out. Naturally, he's scared to death. Anybody just comin' right out of Texas and set in a band up here in New York with a bunch of New Yorkers, you've got to be scared to death, or else you crazy. So he was good, just naturally(?) enough(?), and we (?) go on the road. Take it easy, you know. But he was a very slow reader. He didn't read good at all. He could read, but very slow. But I told him, "Take your time, take
your time, it's all right; and I'll help you out as much as I can."

Well, we got along fine. Eddie and I got along fine, and everything was great, because I did not want to play first saxophone, and I would go to any length to teach him the parts or anything, because I did not want them parts. So Cootie had him to play first part. That's mainly why Cootie put him on the first part. But he had him on the first part, and playing all the solos... Now, you talk about somebody working, he had him playing all the solos, and he's doing his act, I mean himself, he's singin' -- and he's really the star of the whole band. And Cootie had him workin'. And I'm sittin' there, and I ain't doin' nothin' -- playin' the third part and takin' it easy. And Eddie was working. Boy he was working like mad.

And he could sing. You know, he could sing the Blues. He's a showman. He's a real showman. He's real funny. But he looked funny anyway. But he used to tear up the house. He used to really tear up the house. And it ended up to find out he had (what you call those?) one of them complexes. He had a complex about himself.
An inferiority complex?
Yeah, it was inferior... But when he'd get drunk, when he gets high... I wouldn't say drunk. When he

would get high, he figured people were picking on him. Now, Lee Polk came in the band. When Lee Polk came in the band, he and Lee Polk... Lee Polk was a tenor player, and him and Eddie became very good friends. They were real buddies, you know.

Well, when we were sitting all next one another... Let me see, Lee Polk was on one side of me, Eddie was on the other side of me, and I'm in the middle between them two, and then there's two more saxophones -- we had five saxophones.
I've got here Bob Dorsey and Greely Walton.
Yeah, that's it. That's right. They was the other two.
And John Williams was on baritone.
Well, that's when it started. That's when we started out. But I'm talking about later than that, when...
I see.

Now, I was saying that this showed a little example of Eddie. When I was talking about Lee Polk... Lee Polk had come in a little bit later, and Eddie and him became very good friends. But when they'd get to drinking... Now, one night we were playing at the Golden Gate Ballroom, New Year's Eve night, and Lee was on one side

of me and Eddie was on the other. So Eddie, he's half-high -- everybody's drinking New Year's Eve. And Lee is on this side of me. So Lee said something to me, so I bent down and I said, 'What did you say?' -- because I couldn't hear him, because of all the noise. And Eddie Vinson at that time, he saw Lee and I with our heads together, and he reached over and WHOMP, and he hit Lee Polk and jumped back... He hit Lee Polk, and Lee Polk got up there and WHAP! And Eddie sprawled out on the bandstand. And Cootie, he backed up and let him fall, and Cootie was laughin', and people were all up there standing in front of the band, and there's Eddie Vinson, he's sprawled out where Lee had knocked him down. So Eddie's wife jumped up on the bandstand...his girlfriend, I mean. She jumped up on the bandstand and picked Eddie up. Talkin' about nobody would help him, nobody in the house help him. He was out.

But Lee Polk hit him. You know, before the night was over they were standing at the bar drinkin'! Drinkin' some more. Well, see, now his complex told him that Lee Polk was talkin' about him. Lee Polk wasn't even thinking about him!
It's like a persecution complex.
Yeah. That's the kind of complex he had, you know. And that's the way he was. Oh, Greely flattened him one time, too. I don't know if he ever told you about
it...
Well, we'll get to that in a minute.
No, we ain't gonna get to that. I can't talk to somebody else.

Norman Kenon on string bass, yeah. He later went with Basie's band.

George Ballard. He was a drummer from Philadelphia, a young boy -- and he went with Duke's band.

Robert Horton. Yeah, he was a real veteran. He was older than me. And I was a few years younger than (?).
But that was the nucleus of the band. And they played good music, but everything was a jump. I mean, Cootie wanted to swing, and that's what he had, a Swing band.
Well, it must have been successful if you stayed there so long.
How long?
I mean, because I've got...
You mean at this place.
Yeah, at the Grand Terrace.
How long was I at the Grand Terrace.
Well, I don't know. I just know that in April of '42, you made some recordings in Chicago with that band.
Yeah.
Now, was it the winter of '41 or the winter of '42?

Oh, no. We hadn't been there... We weren't there all that time. No, we only played there a few weeks, I don't know how many weeks, and then we came out of there and we came back to the Savoy. See, we had come back to New York to the Savoy -- in New York here. And I think that's when Ken Kersey left the band... But see, they was always getting changes in the band. And I think Jonas Walker left the band. And of course, Bud Powell taken Ken Kersey's place. I don't know if he taken Ken Kersey's place or not, but... Because they was always changing piano players. We had a lot of different piano players. Good ones, too. Piano players I'd never heard of before.

But Bud was the greatest of them all, Bud Powell -- and he was a genius. He was really a genius. He was about 17 years old when he come into Cootie's band. And he was a kid, and we was sittin' up there rehearsing. So Cootie's rehearsing this theme song for Bud; you know, so Bud can see how it goes.
What was the name of the theme song?
I don't know the name of it. No matter. And especially theme songs...
It was "Fly Right".
Oh, no. It's some funny name he had on it. It was a funny name and it was a funny tune. Anyway, we had

to rehearse it for Bud, you know. So we would start off, and pretty soon Cootie would stop the band and said, "Wait a minute." He said, "Bud, don't improvise on this number. Just play what's on the music, just like it is." Okay, Cootie starts again. Here we go. [SINGS THEME] And Cootie stops the band again. "Bud, I asked you not to improvise. Just play what's on the music." "Okay, all right." So we got off again. Here we go. [SINGS] Cootie stopped the band. He said, "Bud, how many times do I have to tell you, don't improvise. Play what's on the music." Bud looked at Cootie and said, "If you think I'm gonna play that sad stuff, you're crazy." He said, "I ain't playin' nothin' that sad." I couldn't believe it! I had to look around. I said, "Well, who is this kid talkin' to the leader like that?" Bud ain't but about seventeen years old, and he's up there talkin' to the leader... He's lucky to be in a band. And he told him, "I'm not gonna play that sad stuff."

Well, I come to find out Bud was right! Bud was really right. Because Bud, he was a genius playin' the piano. He could play. He was a genius. And like all geniuses at that time, I mean, they was no something... You know what I mean? And down through the years... He made some wonderful records, though, Bud did. Beautiful records. And down through the years, just like Charlie Parker, you
know what I mean. And it shortened his life. He went over to Europe, and this-that-and-the-other, back here... Well, he didn't last long. He just killed himself, you know.

But he was a fine kid. He used to call me "Dad", like I'm his Daddy or something. Bud would want to borrow some money or something, because he was always broke. He'd get paid just now, and in fifteen minutes he wants to borrow something on next week's pay. I don't know what he'd do with his money. They told me one time he went in a bar, and just set all his money on a bar and told the bartender to pour the whiskey til the money run out. That's the type of guy he was, you know.

And one time... Well, he would come to me, he said, "Dad, I want to borrow some money." I said, "Well, Bud..." This was after the first show on the last day in a theatre. We'd always get paid between the first and second show. Now, all he had to do was wait for the man to come and pay him. We had played the first show already. He said, "Dad, I'll give you seven dollars if you loan me five." I says, "Seven for five? All you got to do is wait ten or fifteen minutes, and you'll get your whole salary." He said, "No, I want the money now." I said, "Okay, here's five dollars." So I give him the five dollars, and he went and did whatever he had to do -- I don't know what he did. But I know when

he got paid, before we went on the second show, he come up to me and handed me seven dollars -- which was about twenty minutes later. I said, "Bud I don't want your two dollars. Just give me the five, that's all." I wouldn't take his two dollars. But he just... That's the way he was. If he promised you something, he'd give it to you. He wouldn't haggle about it. If he said he wanted five dollars, give him the five. He'd give you any kind of interest for it. And he was gonna pay you back, and no more argument, no anything. Just a nice, easy, what you call a low-key guy.
Now, he came into the band in New York?
Yeah, yeah, the Savoy Ballroom. Boy, he was a sensation, though.
In the Ballroom.

Anywhere. Everywhere. And we were traveling on the road, we run across... One time we run across some show people on the train (we was travelin' by train), and they was on a train from one of them small towns, and they were going to the same town we were going. So naturally, we all got acquainted. So they weren't working that night. They come to see us, you know, at the dance, one-thing-or-another. And naturally, Bud was playing, everybody was playing.
And the next day, the leader of the band, a White

orchestra, he comes backstage... Not backstage, what am I talking about. We meet down at the station, because we're doing one-nighters, and we were going from station to station, from town to town. And we all meet at the station. And he's sitting up there in the car with Cootie, and they are talking about... This fellow, the leader, wanted to know where Cootie found this piano player. He said, "Do you know, that man is a genius! The way he plays and what he's playing?" Do you know what I mean? And this leader, he was astounded. But I knew Bud was a good piano player, but I didn't know he was a genius. But he proved that he was. He really was.

And boy, he could play, and be just as high... I don't know. But a schoolkid, I mean... What you say? Success come to him too quick. And just like Charlie Parker, I mean, one of them things, you know... He made a lot of records with Charlie Parker. He could really play.

But that's the type of band Cootie had, and he had a lot of good piano players come in that band. In fact, all the piano he ever had was outstanding. Good piano players. Of course, he had good musicians all through the band at some time or other. But they were comin' in and goin' out, changing the piano. And Cootie was just as nice as he could be to them. And boy, they were carryin' on. Cootie said
one time, "Boy, if I had good sense, this would drive me crazy."

And another time we get to Chicago for a dance, and we're supposed to leave Chicago, we had a whole list of one-nighters to do, and we set up there in the ballroom in Chicago. And Cootie said, "Men, this is it." "This is what it?" He said, "We finish this dance tonight, and we're going back to the city. I can't stand this." He said, "I can't stand it." Oh, the men, boy, you talk about a no-discipline band... Them youngsters were something else. He couldn't handle them.
So he brought the band back into New York.
So he canceled all those engagements?
All those engagements he canceled. And he tried to reshape the band, one of them things, you know. I don't know. Them youngsters, they just think differently.

And Eddie Vinson was no help to him. I mean, Eddie was getting applause and everything else, but Eddie... I mean, I don't know. He just couldn't handle it. When a man gets in a cab in... Now, Los Angeles is about 450 miles away from San Francisco. And when a man gets in a cab in Los Angeles and tells the driver to take him...[LAUGHS]...to San Francisco, and the driver did, and he gets out of the cab, and tells the driver, "The manager will take care of it,"

his manager will take care of it... So he goes in the theatre and sees the stage manager, and tells the stage manager, "I got a cab out there I want you to catch. Catch that cab for me. I've got a little bill. Pay it for me." That's what Eddie Vinson tells the show manager, you know, to catch the cab. He rode 450 miles. Well, boy, when that manager heard what that bill was... [LAUGHS]

What are you gonna do with a bunch of nuts? Eddie didn't think he did anything wrong. Boy, he didn't think he a thing wrong. But that's the way the band was. And I mean, there was always something going on. It was a joy to work with him, because... We played a battle of music against Duke Ellington at the Savoy Ballroom, and naturally, they billed "Cootie Williams, formerly of Duke Ellington's band [Cootie had a bit name in the Savoy] and Duke Ellington." So boy, here's the night of this battle of music.

Well, Duke didn't show up on time or something. Anyway, the band had to hit without Duke. And naturally, they were just messin' around with some numbers, you know, just playing, and they didn't sound good. Duke's band didn't sound up to par anyway, you know. So anyway, Cootie got on the stand and played his numbers, to get that first whack in. So man, the house was comin' down, boy. They
applauded and applauded. And next time we went up there he put Eddie Vinson on, singing his best numbers and so forth. While you got 'em down you keep 'em down, you know. So man, he was carryin' on.

So Duke did come in, but it was one of them things, if you don't start off right, you just don't get together. That was not Duke's night. And everybody in the place that night, they was applauding Cootie's band, and even the wives of the Ellington members were saying, "Yes, that's right. Duke got cut tonight." Well, they was as much for Cootie as anybody else, because all the wives knew Cootie from Duke's band. And they were saying, "Yes, Duke got cut tonight." Well, Duke wasn't in form that night, and the band wasn't in form -- believe me.

But Cootie did... Well, he outshouted them. They made more noise than Duke. We had a loud band. Of course, all the notes wasn't always right, but they could play loud. And they had a good beat. They had a hell of a beat. So I'll give Cootie that much. Yeah, I'll give him that much. It wasn't often that Duke lost a battle of music. Because Duke had so much stuff he could dig down there and bring out on you, you know, the average musician, you can't compete with him. But he didn't dig out nothing that night. Yeah, Cootie taken it away from him.
Well, the band eventually broke up.
Cootie's band?
Yeah.

I don't know. We came into the Savoy, and... No, we had been out with the Ink Spots. We had worked, oh, six months or more with the Ink Spots, and Ella Fitzgerald... We had a big show. Had a big show. It was quite a show. We played 27 theatres from New York to California. We played 27 theatres, and broke records at 26 theatres.. Broke records. I mean, in Chicago... There was a blizzard in Chicago, and there was a line around the corner of the Regal Theatre in Chicago, and that's a big theatre... And there was a line four deep all around the corner and way down the block, all you could see, people coming into the show. And that's a theatre that seated over five thousand people. And it stayed like that all day long.

The Ink Spots was the big draw. But everything on the show was good. Ella. You know Ella's a show-stopper herself. And there was a dancer named Ralph Brown. We had a comedy act. Who was the comedy act? I can't think of their name right now. But the whole show was good. There were no weak spots in the show. And then, when it come down to the band, then you had the band with Cootie plus Eddie Vinson. And Eddie could stop anybody's show. Because he
was... You know, he was a real clown then. And he could sing the blues. He could really sing the blues and... I don't know, the whole show was.... 26 weeks they broke records.

One week, you could throw a baseball out there and it wouldn't hit nobody. You know where that was? Omaha, Nebraska. Fifteen below zero. It was cold out there. And all week long there was nobody in the theatre. You could throw a baseball out there, and not hit nobody in the theatre all week long. Yet, other places we went, the place was packed and jammed every time we appeared.
Who had arranged that package? Who was the management? Who was back of that?
I don't know. I really don't know who. I knew at the time, but now I can't think of it.
Was it one of those big agencies like William Morris?

Oh yeah, it was a big agency. Sure. Who else could handle it? That was big-time they had. Ella Fitzgerald. She was a big star. You know where she...in the dressing rooms where she was at? On the top floor. In a theatre with no elevator, and she's on the top floor. That's how big she was. The Ink Spots each had a separate room on the stage floor. Well, then, all of them should been in one together; each one of them had a separate room.
She had to go up on the top floor, and big as she is. Well, she wasn't so big then. Well, she was big then, but she wasn't that big.

The Ink Spots were the big attraction. And they were big, too. Boy, them were happy days working with them. Happy days, believe me. The happiest days of my life, working with them. They liked a good time, and they liked plenty of money, and they liked to see the money get around. They liked to see the money get around. And it got around, too. Boy, everybody in the band was just as happy as they could be, you know. And boy, the money was floatin'. But we had a good time.

Well, the show come back... Oh, they come back into the Savoy for the summer, because Cootie had gone in the Savoy with the band, you know. So at that time, I was goin' with a little girl, I can say it now, that was a waitress...not a waitress, an usher in the theatre. She had never heard me play any time that I'd been in the theatre with Cootie's band -- he used to play in there quite often. And she had never me play anything. Yet she's an usher in 'there, she hears all the shows. She never heard me play any solo or anything. So every time we'd get to talking, she said, "Well, Charlie, when am I going to hear you play something?" I'd tell her, "Oh, well, you know, this show is just for the
theatre," one of them things, "everything is arranged that way." I wasn't thinking about playing. She said...

So when we come into the Savoy, now we're playing up there for dancers. We were up there four and five hours a night. Now we're playing dance music, one number right after another for about a half-hour, and then the other band plays. I still hadn't played no solos. So she caught me when I come off the stand one time, she said, "Look, I've heard this band play two or three sets, and I haven't heard you play anything yet." She said, "When are you goin' to play something?" She said, "Can't you play anything?"

Well, when she said, "Can't you play anything?" that struck me kind of funny, you know. I said, "Now, this is funny. Now, here's the girl I'm supposed to be going with, and she has never even heard me play, if I can play or not. I said, "If she thinks I can't play nothin', what do the other people think?" So I said, "Well, I'll talk to Cootie."

I spoke to Cootie and I said, "Hey, Cootie. What's the chance of you having a couple of arrangements made so I can play something. Not that I want to be featured or anything. Just a couple of numbers so I have something to play."
Cootie said, "Nobody wants to hear you play. My name is in the lights downstairs, not your name. Nobody wants to hear

you. The people come in here to hear me." So when he said that, I looked at him, and said "Okay." I reached down, I got my case, put it up on my chair, taken the horn off the rack, folded up my horn, put it in the case. I said, "You stay here and blow all you know." I said, "I'm gone. Goodbye." And I walked out.

I walked out, just like that. No hard feelings, no nothin'. I just walked out. Yeah, he said, "Nobody want to hear you play." Which I didn't want to be featured or anything. You know, the girl kind of embarrassed me.
So she never did get to hear you play.
She never did hear me play. No, she didn't.
Now, you probably have got some stories about... You can't have been on the road as much as you have been on the road without having been stranded at some point.
Well...
Maybe you've got some stories about being stranded.

That stranded stuff, I can... That can go way back to when I first started out in the business. I got stranded the first night, before I even got started! I got stranded... I was sixteen years old, and a bunch of kids around home had a little band.
[PAUSE]
Carry on with your little Boston stranding.

Well, talking about getting stranded. I was stranded the first job offer I ever had in my life. I was a child, and these people come to Boston and they wanted a saxophone, an alto saxophone. And I was just sixteen, and I was anxious to go someplace. So they had this little show, with chorus girls and things, and they had a date booked up in a small town close to Boston, about fifty or sixty miles from Boston, called Limister, Massachusetts.

So, my mother, she let me go. So we had a small band, about five or six pieces... And it had a chorus and a little show, a couple of comedians. So we get to Limister, Mass., and then we find out that the theatre don't know anything about a show that's supposed to be there that night. So there we are, we're in the theatre; no place else to go. So we were hangin' around, can't get back home, nobody has money. And we decided to play some cards. So we're in the dressing room in the theatre...
[PAUSE]
Now, you were saying you were sitting around playing cards after you were stranded in the little theatre.
Yeah. Well, I mean, we were stranded, we couldn't get back home. That was about my first engagement, and there was no engagement. The management of the theatre

didn't know anything about any show supposed to be there. So there was nothin' for us to do, but we were just stuck there. Nobody had money to get back home. So we're stuck. So we stayed there overnight. And the next morning, one of the boys called for his mother, and his daddy drove the car down and picked him up, and about four or five of the rest of us. That's how I got back to Boston. I was glad to get back, too.

That was my first time being stranded. And it's not a nice feeling. Of course, that wasn't bad. I was right at home, but I didn't realize it. Of course, sixty miles is a long way, too, if you have to walk. But that was the first time I was stranded.

I've been stranded a couple of other times. You get so... When you're with a big bunch, it don't make too much difference. You have a lot of fun. As long as everybody's healthy and you eat now and then, you get some food now and then, I mean, it's good... You don't eat as regularly as you would if your pockets were full of money. But if you can get something to eat now and then, it's not bad!

And we were... Let me see, later, when I was with Louis Armstrong's band, we was down in Greenville, Mississippi, and we were stranded there. We went in to play a one-night engagement in Greenville, and come to find out the rest of

our dance engagements were canceled, and our next playing engagement was two weeks later right back in Greenville, where we were already at. So there was no need for them to take us out of town. The left us right there stranded. We don't see the managers or the road managers or anybody else, or the star, who was Louis Armstrong -- we don't see none of them. For two weeks, we were just around there doing the best we could. And every time we come out the house... We had played our first engagement, and the whole town turned out to see us. But every time we come out the house now, people would see us and they'd say, "Oh, you haven't left town yet? You still here? You must be stranded." We were stranded. They're telling me I'm stranded. I know I was stranded.

Yeah, we were stranded. And boy, that was a tough two weeks. And there's nothin' to do but try to get money the best way you could. It was rough. The managers, you didn't know where to find them -- you couldn't find them any place. Then they come up just before the engagement, the last engagement, which was in the same place, then they'd appear on the scene and want to know if everybody got their rent paid and one-thing-or-another, if they'd be ready to leave right after the dance. Got the rent paid?! With what? We was scufflin' around tryin' to get money to buy food to eat,
and they're talkin' about is everybody's rent paid and are they ready to leave. So we had to bail everybody out, you know, straighten up the bills and one-thing-or-another.
But that was good. Most times you'd get stranded, you know, you had to get out of town the best way you can. I mean, that's on you. But I mean, he did pay up the bills and...
This was Joe Glaser, now, under Joe's management.
Yeah. We left with a clean record. We could go back. One of them things.
What about in Los Angeles? Didn't you get stranded there?
Let me see, Los Angeles... Did I get stranded in Los Angeles? I don't know if I...
Or somewhere in California, you said you were three thousand miles from home.
Well, let me see. I wasn't exactly stranded. I was broke, which was nobody's fault but mine. And I was stranded. The rest of the band wasn't stranded.
See, we went to Los Angeles with Louis, and he was making moving pictures at the time, Heebie-Jeebies or what's that "Big eyes..."
Oh, Jeepers-Creepers...
I mean "Jeepers, Creepers, Where did you

get those peepers." And he was making moving pictures, but we weren't in the pictures. We had nothing to... No, we did have something to do. We were working in a ballroom. The band was working in a ballroom...
Going Places was the name of the movie.
Yeah, I don't know what it was. I don't even know if I've even seen it. I didn't want to see it. I didn't even see the inside of a studio.

Anyway, we were working a nightclub...not a nightclub, it was a ballroom. And when Louis would finish at the studio in the daytime, he would come out to the ballroom at night and blow at the ballroom. So we worked there about three or four weeks, while he was making this moving picture, and then he was still coming and doubling with us.

Well, they had a bunch of girls out at this ballroom, a chorus line or something -- they put on a little show at night. Anyway, the girls, they invited the band to a party out in Watts -- at that time, Watts. Well, we was supposed to leave the next day and go upstate through California, all the way up the coast to Washington. So they're giving the band a party, a going-away party.
So we're in the ballroom just before finishing up, and Joe Glaser walks in and said we would not be leaving the next day, because everything is snowed in all up the West
Coast. They had a terrific storm up there, and everything was snowed in and nothing could move. So there we are now. I said, 'What?' Well, okay, we'll stay around Los Angeles. Suit 'em up.

So we go to the party that night, and at the party... I mean, it was a nice party the girls give us. Drinkin', one-thing-and-another, and some fellows go in the back and start a little nickel-and-dime crap game. Well, you know how them little crap games, they grow... It soon got to be dollars, and five dollars and ten dollars, whatever you could afford to bet. I got clean so quick... I'm always in them games, and I start all the games, and I'm always the first one to get broke -- and I got broke. Which didn't mean nothin' to me to get broke. I'd just borrow some more money, and keep on til you...you pitch til you win!

Well, I got broke, and the different fellows, they start to cuttin' out, goin' home, this-that-and-the-other. And the first thing I know, the party was over and I almost didn't get back to Los Angeles, to where I lived there. And it just happened Wilbur DeParis, the trombone player, he saw me out in the street trying to get a cab or something... I wasn't trying to get a cab because I didn't have any money. But I was trying to get in to where I lived. And he had transportation, so he picked me up and brought me back to
the hotel. So that was beautiful.

The next day was Christmas, Christmas Day, and I'm sitting in the hotel, and I felt terrible, because outside in the street I could look out the windows, and it's pretty and green, the trees are green, the grass is green, people are walking around in their shirt sleeves, Christmas Day -- it's warm out there. It happens sometimes in wintertime. And I'm thinking about my family in New England, in Boston, where there's a lot of snow and cold weather. That's how Christmas is supposed to be. Snow on the ground... And I really got blue. I felt very bad. And here I'm sitting in a big, empty hotel room, and don't have a dime nowhere -- I can't call nobody, and none of my family... I'm always with my family at Christmas, but not this Christmas; I'm three thousand miles away.

And I thought, "Jesus, the next big city to here is Chicago, and that's two thousand miles away from here, and I'm another thousand miles east of Chicago" -- three thousand miles. Boy, I just sat there and I cried like a baby. I didn't have no money, I didn't have no food, I didn't have anything.
I'm sitting there with my door open in the hotel room, and a girl passed by, one of the waitresses from the restaurant downstairs in the hotel, she passed by and she

asked me what am I looking so blue about. "It's Christmas Day. Cheer up." So I said, "Well, things are a little rough. I have nothing to be happy about. All our work is canceled and I'm broke. I went to the party last night and got broke, and I don't have any food to eat. So what have I got to be cheerful about?" She said, "Come and have breakfast." Well, I hadn't had anything. I said, "I don't know when I'm going to get anything." I can't find anybody around the hotel that I know. I don't know what happened to the men in the band. They had all disappeared. I said, "No, things are not good. They don't look good."

So she said, "Well, I'll tell you what you do." She said, "When you come downstairs... I'm going on duty now. When you come downstairs, you come to my part of the counter..." Her section. "Sit up at the counter, and don't say anything. Just sit there." She said, "You'll be taken care of." I said, "Okay."

So sure enough, I went down and sat up at the counter, and pretty soon she came by with a plate of food and put it in front of me. Well, if it hadn't been for that girl, I would have starved to death then in Los Angeles. But she looked out for that meal and many more meals. She was very good to me. She was really nice. I mean, she didn't have to give me anything. And believe me, I... It made a
difference in me inwardly. She sure was wonderful to me, because she didn't have to do it. Nobody has to give you anything.

My mother always said, "Be good to people." Because my mother would buy anything from anybody coming to her house, selling any kind of thing, any kind of junk or anything -- my Mama would buy it. She would always say, "I never know when somebody might have to help out one of my children." That's how my mother thought. So them words come right back to me. I said, "Yeah, Mama sure was right. Who would have ever thought that I would have been this far away from home, and can't even make a call home... I can't call nobody." I had nothing, not a nickel in my pocket, and here's this girl come out of the blue, the clear blue sky for no reason whatsoever, and gave me some food and take care of me. I appreciated that. And I mean, we were nothing to one another or anything.

And the thing about it, I didn't see her when I got ready to leave. When I got some money, I didn't see her. And that time, you know, I said, "Well, I guess that's experience; I'll put that down to experience." And I never did see her any more. Because when I went back out there, which was years later, she wasn't around then.
But you never know who can do you a little good in

life, and you never know when you're going to need it. Especially when you're traveling. Because you never know what's going to happen when you're traveling. You can have your pockets full of money and walk into a town, and when you come out the next morning, you don't have to have a nickel. And nowadays, the way people are stealing and carrying on now, I don't know whether it's safer to walk with money on your or not to have any. Because I mean, it can be taken away from you so easy, and you never know who is going to do you some good.
Did you ever get into any movies? Any soundies or anything?

I made one with Cootie's band, and I made a feature picture... Well, we was only in one ...(?)... in John Kirby's band, Sepia Cinderella. It was an all-Black picture, you know. A good show. Billy... Well anyway, it had a nice bunch of characters in it...
[END OF TAPE V-A, SIDE 2]
The movies that you made in... You made that Sepia Cinderella?
Well, that was with Kirby. That was with Kirby's band. That was around... When was that? '47? It
had to be '47 or '48, somewhere around there. I don't remember what year. When I went with Kirby's band. Is it in the book?
Yeah, you went with Kirby early in '47.
I should know that, because that's when I started doing new stuff, when I came here... Yeah, John Kirby was something else.
And you said you did one short.
Yeah, we did a short. Is that on there?
Yes.
Oh, you taped it.
Yes.

Oh, I didn't know. Yeah, I went with Kirby's band in 1947, and we did a short up in the Bronx. I mean, that wasn't a short. That was a feature picture. But we were just in a cabaret spot. In the band there was Buster Bailey, Charlie Shavers and myself in the front line, and there was John Kirby, there was Fuller, the drummer...no, Big Sid was the drummer... John Kirby, Big Sid and...
Billy Kyle?
Billy Kyle, that's right. That was the band. Six pieces. And it was a nice picture. It wasn't a bad picture. But it wasn't no house-breaker or anything

like that. It wouldn't tear the house down. We just did a couple of numbers, maybe a little short number or (?). And we were out in the middle of the stage, then back of us was a big band, a cabaret band it was supposed to be, and all the people sitting around in a nightclub. They had more musicians sitting up in that band that weren't musicians, but they looked the part -- they looked good. Old Budd Johnson was back there, had his saxophone, and... They had some nice-looking girls in that picture. I know that. Boy, they had some nice-looking girls. The only thing about us, we was only up there one day, and we were through.
But you had to look quick, though, to catch us in the picture, because it was such a short... You know, just two short numbers. That was about it.

But Kirby, he had some nice jobs to work on. He really did... He could get high-class work. The only thing about it, Kirby himself wasn't high class. Now, when I joined the band, he had a whole new band, because this was war times, the war was just over, and the war had broke up his band, his original band, with Procope and Billy Kyle and them... Well, Billy had come out of the Army; Billy was back with him. Buster Bailey wasn't with him. I think Bill Beason was drumming with him at the time.
Anyway, Kirby come to me. He says, "Charlie..."

Because he had tried to get me when I was with Cootie's band; two or three times he'd tried to get me. So he comes to me this time, he says, "Charlie, are you busy?" Well, at the time I wasn't busy doing nothing...or anything... I wasn't busy doing anything. And I said, "What's up? What's...?" He said, "Well, do you want to go down to Washington?" I said, "Well, I don't know. What is it?" He said, "A little nightclub down there. We'll be there a couple of weeks." I said, "Two weeks?" -- because two weeks sounded great to me. At the time, I think it was summertime or during that time, there wasn't a whole lot of work -- there wasn't a whole of gigs. So I says, "Okay." He gave me the name of the place.

But anybody that heard Kirby's band play, knows they played a different kind of music than any other kind of band. His is very precise. They were what they called "the biggest little band in the land," and believe me, when they put them three horns together, they sounded big too. It wasn't nothin' but a clarinet, a trumpet, a muted trumpet, and an alto saxophone. But when they got them arrangements, which Charlie made most of the arrangements...Charlie and Billy Kyle did most of the arranging. When they played the arrangements, boy, it sounded like a great big band. And they were playing all the light classics and one-thing-or-
another... Oh, I don't know, I can't name them. They had so many of them. They had a big, thick book.

So anyway, it was just a different type of music, dance music. So anyway, I said, 'Well, yeah...' You know, he told to be at the hotel, a certain hotel at 4 o'clock in the afternoon for rehearsal. And we're going to stay in this hotel; it's not the hotel we're working at. So okay, 4 o'clock. He says, 'Do you need any money to get there?' I said, 'No, I've got transportation. I can make it.' See, I didn't know nothin' about Kirby. I didn't know him. I had never worked for him. 'I got the transportation. I'll be there at 4 o'clock.'
So at 4 o'clock I was in the hotel in Washington, and everybody was there. Everybody was in the room. We're sitting around. Everybody had a glass in their hand...
Now, who was everybody? Was there O'Neil Spencer now on drums?

No. I'll tell you who was on drums. What's his name, Wallace Bishop was on drums. There was Billy Kyle on piano. There was Jerry Blake on clarinet. There was Kirby on bass. And a fellow we used to call 'Minnow,' Clarence Brewington, on trumpet. A nice group.
And you on alto.
Me on alto.
You didn't double at this point.

No, no, just alto. So here I am. I've come in. Well, being the new man, I just know they're going to get the books open and show me this-that-and-the-other. So Kirby said, "The book's over there." So I went over and I picked up the alto book. And boy, the music was all torn and dirty, filthy, like somebody had been wiping their feet on it and turning the pages with the feet. And I see there wasn't nobody else getting any books. They all had glasses. So somebody asked me would I have a drink. And I said, "Oh sure," and I got me a little taste. After one bottle would get empty, another would appear.

So I'm still waiting for somebody to call a rehearsal there. So while I'm waiting, I have another drink. Well, after the second drink, boy... When they poured a drink they'd almost fill up a water glass. And after the second drink, I felt so happy, I said, "I don't care if they don't rehearse; it's all right with me."
So here we are. Kirby, he's rumblin' about this-that-and-the-other, "blah-blah-blah, and you shouldn't do this, and this," one-thing-and-another. Nobody's paying him any attention whatsoever.
So all right. The day goes, and it's getting close to time to eat.
[PAUSE]
So it's getting close to...

It was getting close to time to hit, you know, in the place. So we all got out there. We got in a cab and went to the club. And boy, it was a little place. It wasn't a big place. A small club. And very dark in there. And on the bandstand, boy, they didn't have no music racks. They had to put the books on the floor. And you couldn't see; you couldn't see the floor, it was so dark in there. And I'm looking, I said, "Man, if this was on a rack I wouldn't be able to see it." So Kirby must have felt, you know, that it wouldn't be too good to be trying to read any music, because you could see that. And he had three new men in the band, too.

So anyway, Kirby started off, he called "Sunny Side Of The Street." So we opened up with "Sunny Side Of The Street," and he told me to take a chorus. Well, I played my chorus, boy, and he hollered. Oh, he screamed! He was so tickled. "Play another one, Charlie. Play another one." So I played another chorus. Boy, he was grinning from ear to ear, and the people were applauding. I said, "All right..." So anyway, Clarence Brewington, he played, and everybody, they got their little applause and one-thing-or-another, you know.

So when we finished the first set, Kirby was so tickled, boy, he come and grabbed me around the shoulder... Because you know, Procope was his man. Nobody could do no wrong as long as Procope was there. And he was so tickled with me, because when Bill Beason had been in the band, he had tried to get me in the band for years, but I never would go with the band. So Kirby, he was tickled to death. He just put his arm around my shoulder, and he said, 'How much did I promise to pay you?' So I told him. Well, he'd promised me a hundred and forty dollars, which I mean, wasn't bad in them days, because I was out in the street gettin' nothin'!

I said, 'You promised me a hundred and forty dollars.' He said, 'You got a raise.' I said, 'Okay.' First time I ever got a raise that quick in my life. So he says, 'Come on, let's have a drink.' So he goes... Now, all you got to do is walk out the door of the place, and right next door is a whiskey store, and whiskey is cheaper in Washington than any place you know in the country. Just walk out the door, and halfway...not even halfway, right next door to the place is a whiskey store. Do you know he wouldn't walk out the door and go in the whiskey store? Do you know where he got the whiskey? He got the whiskey from in the place. At that time, fifteen dollars a fifth, and I think we was drinkin'
Seagram's Seven -- which is cheap whiskey. He was paying fifteen dollars a fifth for it, and he could have got it next door for around seven dollars.

But he didn't go to the store. Oh, no. "Send my boys...put the whiskey in the back." So he sent the whiskey back in to the musicians' room back there, and they're sitting around there just like that's the way it's supposed to be. And Billy Kyle is pourin' out whiskey in water glasses. Boy, he could drink some whiskey. Billy could drink some whiskey, and never show no signs of anything. And Bishop could drink a lot of whiskey, too. Jerry Blake didn't touch anything, because he had been sick. And Minnow, the trumpet player...

Poor little Minnow. He was drinkin' with them, and so was I drinkin' with them. But see, I was kind of cautious, you know. But we got halfway through the night, and Minnow went to stand up to play a solo. And he was so drunk he almost fell off the stand. Somebody grabbed him and pulled him back right quick and sat him down! I had to laugh. I said, "Damn, this man is drunk!"

So anyway, the night went on, we finished the night, and Kirby... Oh, every time we'd come off the stand, Kirby would have another bottle of whiskey there, and they'd drink it up before they'd go back on. We'd only be off a half-

hour. And that bottle was empty, and every time we'd come off he had another bottle of whiskey, and he's paying that kind of price for whiskey for his band. He wouldn't go next door to get it at the whiskey store. I mean, he was that type of person. And he just liked to drink whiskey himself, and he wanted his boys happy.

His band to him was the greatest thing in the world. The band wasn't that good, now. I'm not saying it it was good because I was in it. It wasn't that good. It was nothing like his original band. His original band was great. But this was just a little pick-up band he had. Damn, they was all drunk! How good could it be? But he was tickled, he was tickled to death, and he taken me home where I lived, he taken me home in a cab...
Didn't he give you a second raise that same night?
I don't know. He was... Any time I wanted any money, he had it!
Didn't you mention once that you got...

No, what it was... This was a few days later, a couple of days later. He asked me did I want to draw any money. So I told him, 'Well, no.' I liked to get my salary intact, all at once. Unless there's something wrong or something suspicious; then I draw-draw-draw, as much as I can. But if I think everything is going to be all
right, I'll just get my salary all at once. So I told him, "No, I don't want to draw nothin'."

So he says, "Oh yeah, you got to draw. You got to draw something." And I said, "All right, give me ten dollars." He said, "Ten dollars? You can't do anything with ten dollars. Here. Take a hundred." A hundred dollars. A hundred dollars to draw? I never heard of such a draw like that, you know. So I taken it and I held on to it.

But I mean, he was just that generous. He didn't care. He'd give you his money until it just run out. So he wouldn't care if he didn't have nothin' for himself. He was just that generous. And a lot of people that have worked for him really taken advantage of him, because he was a good heart. And he was so in love with his band. You and him together, boy, that would be something! He was crazy about his band, and you're crazy about music, one-thing-and-another...

Oh, I mean, he was unbelievable. He was just unbelievable. A nice guy... Boy, I mean, with money... But one thing about him, when he gets paid... You'd get better be there when he gets paid. Don't let him hold your money. Because when you see him, he ain't gonna have none, your money or anybody else's. Give it all away! Give it all away. Big-hearted, he'd buy anybody whiskey. Whiskey was
the main thing. Got to drink the whiskey. Whiskey was the main thing. Yes, indeed. He wouldn't give you a dime to get nothin' to eat, but he'd give you twenty dollars to get a bottle of whiskey.

He did that to me three mornings straight. He come in my room, he said, "Charlie, give me a drink of whiskey." We were in Chicago now. I said to Kirby, "Where am I gonna get any money to buy any whiskey?" We're here in Chicago, we're laying off; now, where do I get the money to buy whiskey?" I said, "I don't have money to buy food." I says, "I need about five dollars to get something to eat." He says, "You don't have no food, huh?" I said, "No." "That's too bad." He said, "Here's twenty dollars. Get a bottle of whiskey. Oh yeah, and here's five dollars; get something to eat." Twenty dollars for whiskey, five dollars for food. Three days straight he come in my room, and that's what he handed me. He handed me twenty-five dollars three days straight, twenty dollars for whiskey and five dollars for food.

And then at the end of the week, you know, when you're paying off, he says, "Do you owe me any money?" I said, "Well, I owe you what you come in my room and gave me. You gave me seventy-five dollars for whiskey and food." He said, "No! I don't mean that. You've got to have whiskey." He said, "Did you draw any other money from me?" I said,
"No." He said, "You don't owe me anything." Boy, he was a nut, but he was a beautiful nut, believe me.
Who got the engagement? Did he handle all that?

No, Joe Glaser. No, he had agents. He was working here in New York, and he was getting their commissions and spending that up and giving it away and one-thing-and-another. Oh, he was all messed up at the offices. I tell you, don't let him go to sleep with your money because you wouldn't get none -- your or anybody. Yeah, he got in bad with all the offices. He owed all of them. And he was around here looking like a bum, and just giving the money away and buying whiskey. But he was a big-hearted guy.
And it was a pleasure to work in his band. It was a pleasure to work with him.

Billy Kyle, boy, he was the man behind the band, you know what I mean? What little was straight, he was the one to keep it straight. Kirby, he... When they did have a rehearsal.. They'd always call rehearsals, but nothing ever happened. And when they did have a rehearsal, they had to put Kirby out, put him out of the rehearsal so they could have a rehearsal.
Well, later on you went with Billy Kyle, with his sextet.

Yeah. We come back here when Kirby had got so bad... He was all in bad with the officers and things downtown, and he couldn't get any work. We had worked up at the 845 Club in the Bronx, and we finished our engagement up there -- and I think Kirby owed a big whiskey bill up there. Anyway, we finished there, and the man hired Billy Kyle to come in with the band without Kirby. So Billy made a couple of changes, and taken the band up there.
Who did you get on bass?

The fellow with the long hair who does all the work nowadays, one of your top bass players, he lives up here and his mother lives in Queens. I'll think of his name after a while. Good bass player, one of the best.
Aaron Bell?

No, no, it wasn't him. He's been around. Good bass player. He still works around. Let me see. Bill Coleman was on trumpet. Bill Coleman was with us once. I'm trying to think, was he with... I don't know if Bill Coleman was with Kirby or Billy Kyle. Because Bill Coleman worked in one of the bands, and Wallace Jones worked in one of the bands. I forget which was which.
See, because Kirby had been in the place, and then he come out, I think he was out about two weeks, and then Billy taken the band in there. It was practically the same men,

the same deal, but I mean, I can't remember which band who was in... But Billy was nice. I liked him as a leader, you know. Billy had a lot of personality, and Billy could drink a lot of whiskey and never change anything. You'd never know he'd had a drink.
So Minnow was out and Coleman was in as far as you know?
Yeah.
What about Jerry Blake?
Jerry was out, too, and he brought in Pete Clark. You know, Jerry was a sick man anyway. He brought in Pete Clark. Minnow was sick, too. That's why they got Coleman.
What about the drummer?
Well, at the 845, I'm thinking... Bishop was still with the band at the 845, I think. I'm quite sure he was. But I think he stayed with the band until he went to Europe.

Then they brought in a fellow named Nelson, Kirby's man. Oh, Nelson. I forgot all about Nelson. He was in Kirby's band; he was a trumpet player. And we had a return engagement to Milwaukee -- a return engagement. We had been to Milwaukee, and put Milwaukee on the map, and did terrific business in a place that never had but three or four beer

drinkers a night... A great, big long bar, and they had about three customers a night in there drinking beer. And the man turned the place over to his two sons who had just come out of the Army. So the sons wanted to put music in the place, make it like a cabaret, put tables in there, it had this long bar and had the band behind the bar.

So they contacted Kirby, and Kirby had taken the band out to Milwaukee, and we opened up. Well, they had the band that I named before... No, it had Pete Clark, Wallace Bishop, Billy Kyle, Kirby, and who else....
You need a trumpet.

Trumpet was Rostelle Reese. So anyway, they are trying something out with this band. Well, they had billed Kirby like a circus around there, on the air with his records and this-that-and-the-other, and consequently, the place was packed and jammed with people. Packed! Well, ...(?)... two kids in the country, man. I mean, one of them was 23 years old, the other was 25 -- nothing but kids. Because the old man had run the bar and never had over three customers in it, but he was a wealthy man. He was retiring, you know. And he was satisfied with the three customers.
But here's the kids up there, the place is packed full of people. They don't know what to do. They've got this big bar, and they've got a big tray on the end of the bar,
and it's all filled up with whiskey where the waitresses could come up and just take their glasses off, you know, for the orders and things. Big tray.

Well, when the band come off the bandstand, there was a place for us to sit down there if we wanted to sit. We don't know nothin' about Milwaukee. So we come off the stand and we're sittin' down there, and the guys are sittin' there talking, always BS'ing and one thing and another. And here's this big tray of whiskey sittin' up there on the edge of the bar. Oh, them cats wanted a drink so bad, and they see this whiskey lookin' them in the face, you can't help but smell it every time you walk by it. So we keep looking at it, looking for about two sets. So nothing happened.

Pretty soon, the third set, we're sittin' down there, and Bishop said, "I'm gonna get me one of them glasses of whiskey. I ain't gonna look at that whiskey no longer." He went up there and picked up a glass, picked this glass up and lifted it up, and looked around -- and there's the boss lookin' him right in the face, the old man. Bishop said, "This is on you." So the boss says, "Sure, sure, help yourself. Help yourself. After all, we're off the nut." He's made his money already. He said, "We're off the nut. Help yourself. Anything you see you want, help yourself."
He just shouldn't have said that. That's the worst

thing he could have said. All them cats scrambled for that tray. And then, when you go back on the stand, you had to pass through the bar. Well, there the bartenders all up there, everybody knew the bartenders, and the bartenders are right at your feet. So Pete is sitting next to me, and we had two bartenders sitting there -- our boys. And they would fix drinks, drinks, drinks, and they wasn't charging us... Nobody was charging anything. We could drink-drink-drink 'til it run out your ears. And we didn't have to pay a nickel for anything.

And Kirby even called a rehearsal. Now, to show you how square they were in this town, when the bar closed, the bartenders didn't even take the whiskey off the bar. Just leave it, you know, on the bar, right in the bottles and everything. And we come in to rehearse, and the bar was all set up! Heh-heh. So it's nobody there but us. And we're supposed to be rehearsing, and everybody got a bottle in his hand -- and in walks the boss. So he looked up there and seen everybody with a bottle... And he was so nice, you know what he did? He turned his back and went out the door. He didn't say a word. They was nice people. They was nice.
And I mean, Kirby, he was just lucky enough, you know, to get them kind of jobs. Oh, he was puttin' down some whiskey. And he could drink. He could drink, but he'd get

drunk. Billy could drink, but he didn't show it. Of course, the whole band could drink. If I had stayed in that band about two more weeks, I'd have been an alcoholic. I was glad when the band broke up. I was actually glad, because boy...
And then Kyle more or less took it over.
No... Well, Billy had his own group, but he didn't keep it long. He went back with a... Well, we was all with Kirby until Kirby just didn't do anything, he couldn't do anything. He kind of got...
[PAUSE]

Kirby, he got so that he was undependable, and he... I don't know, he wouldn't pay his bills and one-thing-and-another. He got so that he was just goin' down, goin' down-down-down. So he left around here, and he went out to California by himself, and while he was out there... He died somewhere between here and California.
I think right after that, soon after that, Billy went with Louis. I think. I'm not sure who he worked with in between that time.
So after you'd finished with Billy Kyle, you more or less left music as a steady thing.
When I left Billy?
Yeah. Because I think you left...
What year is this? Does it have the name and...?
Well, it says that you were briefly with John Kirby early in 1947...
That's right. That's when I came here, I met Liscotte(?)...
"Later that year worked with Billy Kyle Sextet."

That's right. And '47... Well, I was here with Liscotte(?) until '52. I don't mean I was here. I mean I was with her in '52, and then I went to work for the insurance company. Now, what I did between '47 and '52...
What about the Wall Street insurance brokerage firm?

No, no. I was working for the Great American Insurance Company. See, I went to work there in '52, and I stayed there until they moved the company to California in 1970. I stayed with them eighteen years. But that's when I started doing gigs with Joe.
Joe Garland.
I was still giggin' with anybody, you know, because on that job I could still gig and make the time, because when I went on the job we didn't have to start until 11:30 or 12 o'clock.
But you stopped being a member of a permanent band that traveled.
I wasn't going to travel no more. I was through traveling. I didn't like to travel anyway. But I had so much fun traveling. I never liked to travel! I hated traveling.
Oh, I did forget... I forgot to tell you about our trip overseas, didn't I. Yeah, that's right.
What trip was that?
USO.
Oh, yeah. I figured we could come back to that...
Yeah. Well, we'll come back to that. But that was a great trip, too.
Well, this was before Kirby that you were with the USO.
Let me see. The USO was... When did the stop the War? 1945?
Yeah.
In '45 they stopped the War?
In '45, the War was over in Europe...
No, the War stopped in '45 here. Wasn't it? Japan?
Yeah, '45. That's right.
Yeah, in '45. That's when I signed up to go on the USO. When they said peace, then I signed up!
And that was with Jesse Stone.
That's right. He was the leader of the

band, but Sylvester Lewis was the manager of the show. He's the one that had the say. He run everything, Sylvester. When the show left New York, Jesse Stone had no more to say whatsoever. He had no more to say than me or anybody else. But it was supposed to be his band.
But he put the group together.

Well, I mean, he was supposed to... We all put the group together. Not the group, the band, you know. It was his band. You know, there's always got to be a leader. Then they'd bring in a manager to manage your group.
And that was Sylvester?
That was Sylvester.
Did Sylvester play?

No, he didn't have to play. He was the manager. The manager didn't have to know anything about music anyway. You see, Sylvester had managed other USO shows, and he was such a good manager... He was a great manager.
But he was also a trumpet player, wasn't he?
He was a trumpet player. He used to be with Claude Hopkins. He used to be with a lot of bands. And he was my buddy. He was a great manager, he really was. I was amazed at him, you being a manager.
Now, who was in this band?
Jesse's band?
Yes.

Dave McRae. He was an alto player. The tenor player was from Chicago, a ...(?)... He's still going, I guess; plays clarinet and tenor. I can't think of his name right offhand. The drummer, I don't know what his name is. He's from Brooklyn. He was not what you would call a real legitimate drummer. He was one of the boys I never even seen him or heard of him before. And Louis Bacon; Louis Bacon was in the band. And the same fellow, Nelson, the trumpet player...
It wasn't Dave Nelson.
No.
Some other one.
Ah, Nelson, Nelson, Nelson...
Was his first name Nelson or last name?
I don't know. But he was with Duke's band. He went with Duke. He left and went with Duke. And they went to Europe, and I never heard no more about him.
Oh, I know. He ended up staying in Europe.
He was a good trumpet player. A helluva trumpet player. I don't know where they dug him up from. He had been in the Army, because he told... When Roosevelt

was making that speech about "none of our boys shall die on foreign soil," he was talkin' about he was up in Iwo Jima or some place then... No, down on one of them islands. He was there when Roosevelt was making that speech, "tellin' that damn lie," he says.
Anyway, you set out for the Orient.
Yeah, but that was a long story. I can't tell you that tonight. We'll save that for a later date.
All right.
That is a long one.
Okay.

A lot of things happened on that, and that's the greatest trip I ever had. They told me it would be, and it was a great trip -- for me anyway. Because I hadn't done much traveling before that. I had only been around the country about forty times. Yeah, that was the greatest... They told me that... Not only me, they told all of us, "This is the greatest trip you'll ever make." And they said, "You will eat Spam until it runs out your ears."
See, the trip was only six months long, the trip itself. But like I say, I was going from place to place and day to day, and wondering when we were going to eat all the Spam they talkin' about we gonna eat until it runs out our ears. Well, we did four months in the Philippines. No

Spam. And six months we were supposed to be in Japan. The fifth month, when we left the Philippines, we was in Okinawa. We were there for about thirty days. That's where the Spam was. For me, I mean, it was there every day. Every day that Spam was there. And I said, "Oh, this is what they mean." They were short getting supplies, you know. And one time, I even had to eat them rations; they gave us K-rations and C-rations. Yeah, their supplies were very short.
Nelson Williams, I think you mean.
Nelson Williams, that's right. That's his name, yeah.
He stayed in Europe.
You remember that. Nelson.
Yeah, Nelson Williams.
Because he was a funny guy, man. He was funny.
He's dead now.
He's dead?
Mmm-hmm.
When did he die?
About a year ago.
What happened to him?
He died in Europe.
In Europe, huh?
Yeah.
Yeah, Nelson. I didn't know he was dead. I never heard no more from him, one way or the other. Nelson Williams, that's right. Boy, he could blow, though. He sure could blow.
He was a big guy..

Well, he was tall. You know, he had been in the Army, so he was muscular. He was kind of forward, you know, kind of pushy, but he wasn't smart. Do you understand what I mean? He was pushy but he wasn't smart, like I tell you. You're recording now?
Yes.

Well, I'll save this and tell you about it later. No, I mean... See, we had been to... I'm talking about when he was with Kirby's band. We had come back, he was with Kirby's band... And I believe the band had been to Milwaukee. See, that's where Kirby's band opened up, in Milwaukee, you know. And Nelson wasn't with the band then. That's when Rostelle Reese was with the band. We had a good reception, a very good reception, you know. They liked the hell out of Kirby's band out there. And we were just like a bunch of movie stars or something -- celebrities. So anyway, we leave, and we come back to New York, one of

them things... So we get a return engagement in Milwaukee. So this time, Nelson is with the band. He replaced Rostelle Reese. Nelson is playing in the band now. So we go back there, and naturally they give us a big ovation when we played... Oh, they were applauding and one thing and another. And you know how people will say, "Gee, the band sounds better than ever." One of them things, you know. Well, I mean, the people meant it. The band sounded good.

So I'm standing down there, and Nelson walks up to me and he says, "Hey, Charlie." I said, "Yeah?" He said, "Were you with the band the last time they played here?" I said, "Yeah." So he named everybody in the band, and wanted to know if they had been there the last time. I said, "Yeah, it was practically the same band. Sure." I said, "Why? What's wrong?" He said, "Well, why is everybody talking about the band sounds better than it did before?" He says, "And since I'm the only new member in the band, it must be because of me." I says, "Yeah, I guess so." He said, "I'm going to ask Kirby for a raise." I said, "That's what you're supposed to do."

Well, see, him and Kirby was just like that. Kirby was praising him and this-that-and-the-other, because Kirby liked good musicians. Well, he went and asked Kirby for a raise because he was making the band sound better than it

did before. Well, that turned Kirby on him just like that. Boy, Kirby could have shot him! I mean, a guy to be that stupid, to make a remark like that, you know? "Well, I want a raise because everybody tells me the band sounds better than it did before, and all of you were here before, I'm the only new one, so I must be the one reason why it's better."

Well, he didn't last long with the band when we come back to New York. I mean, that was the end of him. But he went with Duke, and he went to Europe, and I didn't never hear no more from him. You're the only one who ever told me anything about him, and you tell me he's dead. That's the end.
He stayed in Europe.

Yeah. I know he didn't come back. He didn't come back with Duke. And the funny thing, I never thought to ask Harry Carney or anybody what happened to him. I never thought that. When I was talking with them, I wasn't thinking about him. Yeah, you're the only one who ever told me anything about him.
But that's a long story, that overseas thing. But it's a good one. But it's long.
All right, we'll save that for the next session.
In the meantime, I'll try to think of some of them names that was in the band. Like the drummer. I

don't remember what his name was. Some of them, I can't... Let's see, I can't say how many pieces was in the band. I remember Dave McRae. He was like the straw boss. I think it was about... I don't know how many pieces was in the band. Just about eight, I guess. I think it was eight pieces. Because Herbie Collins had a band over there, and I think he had about six pieces, five or six. We had more than he did.
Okay. Well, we shall call it quits for now, and continue with your Oriental adventures on our next session.
Yeah, that will be good, because it will give me a little time to think about some of their names and things. Yeah, that was a great one. It's a funny thing, I hadn't thought about overseas at all.
Well, you never went to Europe. Or did you?

I've never been to Europe. It's the only place I ever wanted to go and never been there. The one place I didn't go, two places I didn't go where I wanted to go... Montreal, Canada; I've never been there. That don't sound right, does it? I've been all over in the Pacific, to Asia and one thing or another; never been to Montreal. All over this country many times. And I've never been to South America...
Well, did you ever have a chance to go to Europe with
Armstrong or anybody?

No. I had a chance to go to Europe with a USO show, with Noble Sissle. He had a big show over there. And I had a chance to go with him. But at the time I was working at one of these summer places up in...
Charlie Holmes (12/5/82):
And I'm through with Cootie.... Now, I'm walking down the street on Seventh Avenue....
This is after you left Cootie Williams.

This is, oh, around September 1945. I meet Herbie Cowens, a drummer, who I had worked with many a time, who had been doing a lot of USO work. So Herbie asked me would I like to make a trip to Europe? Not in Europe, I'm sorry. He asked me if I'd like to make a trip to Japan. And I told him, "Sure!" Because I thought he was kidding about Japan. Who goes to Japan? We was just fightin' a war with them, you know. I thought he was kidding about the trip. So I told him, "Sure, I'll go. Gladly."

Well, to make a long story short, I didn't see Herbie no more that day, and before the day had ended, and I'm still in the Rhythm Club, another fellow, Dave McRae, a saxophone player and leader, he asked me would I care to go to Japan. And I thought it was the same proposition that Herbie was telling me about, Herbie Cowens, and I said, "Sure! I'll gladly go." So he said to me, "All right, come around Jesse Stone's house." Jesse Stone was a bandleader and a music writer...
He's the one who wrote "Idaho".
"Idaho." And he had quite a few hits. And one of them that wasn't wanted(?) was "WPA"; he wrote that,
Holmes (12/5) - 2

too, but he had to take that off the market. And Jesse was to be the leader of the band. Well, now I'm getting confused. He tells me to meet at Jesse Stone's house, and I wondered, how could Jesse be the leader, and Herbie Cowens was always the leader.

So anyway, I appeared at Jesse's house. And there were other fellows; they were getting the band together. They were there. And he had me... He had the fellows to appear downtown at the office and sign the contracts.

Well, I go down and I sign the contracts, and I don't see Herbie Cowens nowhere around. I'm still lookin' for him, because he's the first one asked me did I want to go. I'm still thinking that I'm going under Herbie Cowens' group. Well, when I did see Herbie Cowens, he said, "I thought you said you were going with me." I says, "I thought I was going with you." He said, "But you signed up with Jesse Stone." I said, "Well, I don't know. I didn't know nothin' about Jesse Stone." I said, "I thought it was all the same thing. How often does somebody walk up to you and ask you if you want to go to Japan? We just got through fightin' a war with them!" Nobody goes to Japan just like that. I said, "I thought it was for you. Now, who else was goin'?"
He said, "Oh, I don't know. They're sending over a
Holmes (12/5) - 3

whole flock of shows, USO camp shows" -- you know, to entertain the troops. I said, "Well, I didn't know. I thought this was one big deal to go to Japan. I didn't know it would be a whole lot of shows." He said, "Yeah, they'll have shows from one person to fifty people in the personnel" - so from one to fifty. I said, "But I didn't know a thing about that." Anyway, I was already signed up. Nothin' I could do. I had signed with Jesse Stone.
Well, Herbie didn't like it very much, but there was nothing you could do about it, except find him somebody else to play saxophone with his group.

So anyway, the deal was, we'd rehearse the show and get everything down letter-perfect. We'd rehearse every day. We would get paid while we are rehearsing. And we would leave in about... Well, they didn't exactly tell you when you were going to leave, but they'd give you... You know, you'd be around town a while. If you were working or you had a night job playing anywhere or anything, you could still continue your business, and you had two or three months before you would leave.

So that sounded all right. So I was still playing my gigs and one-thing-or-another at night, and at that time I happened to be working at Small's Paradise, a nightclub, and rehearsing for the USO in the daytime.
Holmes (12/5) - 4
Who were you with at Small's?
Gus Aiken, a trumpet player. He used to be with Louis' band, Luis Russell and Louis Armstrong. And a whole lot of other bands. Gus had been around for years.
Tell me more about the Small's Paradise job.

Well, that was a nightclub. Small's Paradise was a nightclub on Seventh Avenue and 135th Street. And they had shows in there, but at the time we were working in there they was just renting it out to clubs that were having dances -- club dances. And we were working there... There was no special number of nights that you would work. Some nights during the week... You might work five nights a week, or you might work one night a week. But we were pretty busy in there at the time I was there with Gus. Gus was working every night.
What size band?
He just had a small band. About six pieces. I don't remember any of the personnel of the band at all, by name. I can't think of them right now.
Now, was Ed Small around at that time?
Well, he was alive. It was his place. He was still running the club. Oh yes, he was alive.
Did you get to see him at the time?
See him for what? [LAUGHS]
Holmes (12/5) - 5
I mean, was he around to...
He was nothin' great to see, you know.
Well, he owned one of the most famous nightclubs in Harlem.
Well, he owned it. He was there every night! Yeah, I seen him. [LAUGHS] I'd see him every night.
What kind of a person was he?
Well, he's short and dumpy, just like me. Well, I mean, he was a good nightclub, what you call 'em, impresario or something like that -- I don't know.
Did he have the nose for the talent, do you think, or did someone else help him get...?

Well, I don't know. He had so many people, stooges and things working for him... As far as what he knew, I actually don't know. I don't know what the secret was to his success. Because he had, oh, a lot of people working for him. Everything that was done was done by somebody else, and he was... Actually, he was smaller than I am! But not now! I mean, at the time. I was a little heavier than I am now.

But we had a good time at the club, too. I enjoyed working down there, you know. But I mean, I worked there so often, that was another home to, me, just like working in the Savoy was a home to Russell's band. Well, I could go in
Holmes (12/5) - 6
