Small's and work in there any time I wanted to. I worked in there with a lot of different groups, you know. We had nothing to do, so we're game(?). So we're in Small's, in and out, in and out. At that time, they were doing wall-to-wall business. Wartime, so they were doing very good business.
Now, getting back...
To the USO...

To the USO. So I'm rehearsing with Jesse Stone every day. And there would be different units in the billing where we was rehearsing that. We was rehearsing at Noll Studios downtown on 52nd Street, I think...51st and Broadway. We rehearsed there. And there was a lot of bands rehearsing in there for different things. Well, that was takin' up my day. I mean, it was nice. I'd go down there. But after you get the show down letter-perfect, which the show only...it only run an hour... And after you get the show down letter-perfect, you still had to rehearse, you know....
Now, this was what kind of show? This had what kind of acts?
Let me see. We had an MC, a Master of Ceremonies. There was only 13 people in the show, which consisted of three girls... There was three girls in the
Holmes (12/5) - 7
show, two of them danced together. One of them was Jesse Stone's wife, one of the girl dancers. The other girl, Gwen Tines(?), she was a vocalist. She was from Canada. She was a very good vocalist.
The MC, three girls, four... I think the band had seven or eight pieces in it. And we had a manager. Sylvester Lewis was the manager. He was an ex-trumpet player at the time.
He had been with Claude Hopkins.

Claude Hopkins. He'd been with a lot of different bands around. And he was the manager of the show, and he turned out to be a very good manager, too. I mean, I was actually surprised. Well, he had did it before. He managed a big show, a big USO show over in Europe. That was before he come with us. And he was very successful with it. They thought the world of Mr. Lewis.
So anyway, all together, intact, we had thirteen people, including the three women.
[PAUSE]
Now, the USO show personnel.
Yeah. Now, I'll give you the reed section first. There was myself first -- I get to be at the top of the list.
Did you take along a clarinet, or just the alto?
Holmes (12/5) - 8
No, just the alto. And there was Franz Jackson on tenor saxophone. And Dave McRae, who played alto and baritone saxophone. In fact, he could play them all. He played clarinet.
Didn't Jackson double?
He could play clarinet, but he didn't do any clarinet playing. Dave McRae played the clarinet.
Any doubling that was done by the reeds, he did.

Yeah, McRae did it. Then in the brass section was Louis Bacon, trumpet, Nelson Williams, trumpet - - and I think that was all. I don't think there was a trombone. Then there was Jesse Stone on piano...
Did Stone do any arranging?
Not after the show had started. He didn't change anything. When the show opened up, that was the way it went for the entire engagement. And Teddy was the drummer's name, a fellow from Brooklyn.
And then you had a bass player.
Elwood Reynolds was the bass player. And then we had three girls. Two of them danced together, and the other girl was a vocalist, Gwen Tines(?).
Gwendolyn...?
Tines. She was from some place up in Canada. She was Canadian, but she made the trip with us.
Holmes (12/5) - 9
Sylvester Lewis was the manager.
Sylvester Lewis was the manager. He didn't play in the band, but he was a former trumpet player.
So now, you're all assembled in New York and rehearsed, got the show together...
We rehearsed for three months during the day, we got the show together, and after we got it together, then not a note was to be changed. We couldn't change any numbers in the show if we wanted to.
So the show was programmed to go off like clockwork.
That's right. That's right.
Did they time it then, and they knew what...

Oh yeah, they knew the time. They knew the time. There was timing. That's why they had to rehearse. Now, we rehearsed... Although the show was complete and everything, we had to rehearse until it was time for us to leave. We didn't know when we were going to leave. So consequently, we... We're getting paid every week, so we were getting paid for rehearsals. So anyway, word come through when we were going to leave; it was the '30th of November, 1945.
So we packed up and went over to Jersey, and got on a train. I forget what line it was, the B&O maybe, but I don't know -- I don't think it was. They had some other,
Holmes (12/5) - 10

the Lackawanna or something Road in Jersey, and taking us out to California, to Frisco. So we get out there, and hang around there about three or four days, maybe a week. Then the orders come through for us to catch a plane, and...
Now, had you been fitted for uniforms at this point, so that you would...?

Oh, no, we had been in uniforms when we left. Because the uniforms were distributed right from New York. When we left, and we left (?) gigs. And boy, were we somethin' to look at, all in brand-new suits and Eisenhower jackets. They were nice-looking uniforms. We had a big patch on the side of our hat, a square patch. It had something on it, "USO" or something. Well, at that time you'd see a lot of different signs and emblems and one-thing-or-another. Anyway, it was a nice looking uniform.

So we stayed around Frisco for about four or five days or a week, then we got our orders to fly out. So we left one night at nine o'clock. And I never will forget what Louis Bacon, the trumpet player, said. We got in the plane. It was a bucket job, what they call a bucket job in the plane, which is a plane that has seats along the sides -- you sit facing one another along the side of the plane. There were no chairs for you to sit in. These were made out of steel, and you sit on that. And when it comes time you
Holmes (12/5) - 11

want to lay down and go to sleep, because this trip would take us about twelve or thirteen hours... We had to fly from Frisco to Honolulu. And at that time it taken from twelve to thirteen hours. So if you wanted to sleep in the meantime, you'd just pick up some blankets and spread them on the floor of the plane, and lay down there and sleep -- if you could.

Well, between hitting the air pockets and one-thing-or-another, and being shook up like you're in a tin can, we finally made it to Honolulu. Well, when we left here it was the 30th of November, and it was pretty cold in the States. And when you got into Honolulu, it was hot. And here we are all dressed in winter garbs and overcoats and sweaters and one-thing-or-another, and it was hot down there... First thing we did was come out of them overcoats or raincoats, and taken off some of them sweaters and things. And we're going to be around Honolulu...well, we don't know how long we're going to be there. We're just there until we get our next moving orders.

So we're lookin' the place the place over and one-thing-or-another. The hotel is nice. The next day, Sylvester says, "Charlie, let's go out to Waikiki Beach," and I said, "Okay." So he got four or five of us together, and we got a jeep, and we made our way to Waikiki Beach. I
Holmes (12/5) - 12

don't know who found it. None of us had ever been there before. But we found our way around. So we're standing on the beach, Waikiki beach, and it didn't look like anything to me -- it looked terrible. I mean, it was just nothin'. I don't mean it was bombed-up or anything like that; there was nothing like that happened there. But the beach itself didn't look like anything to me. I've seen much better beaches right here in the States. Jones Beach, for instance, looked better than that did. I mean, that was a big disappointment, too, because I had always heard so much about it. So that was my first big disappointment in Honolulu.

Well, this is the second day we're there, and when we come back to the hotel, our orders were to leave immediately. So there was only about five or six of us, half of the show had come back. So Sylvester is trying to tell this Special Service Officer, "Well, we can't leave right now; half of my company is out in the street somewhere." We don't know where they are. So the Special Services Officer said, "Well, we'll put you all on a plane, and we'll send the rest of them when they come in. So, well, we had to settle for that.
Anyway, we were shipped out, and they shipped us to Guam. The next stop was Guam. We were just stopping over.
Holmes (12/5) - 13

And we're on our way to Manila, but we stopped over in Guam. And that's where the rest of the show caught up with us the next day. They caught up with us. Well, Guam wasn't no big deal. The only thing about it, one of the outfits was there that I... Well, we all knew quite a few of the fellows in the band, because there was a band on there from New York here that had a bunch of musicians that we all knew. So my brother, he had been stationed on Guam, too, but he had just went home... I guess the same time we were leaving New York, he left out there to come back to the States. So I missed him. And Howard Johnson, he was stationed out there, too, and I guess the same thing happened to him, because we went out to where his company was located, and most of the fellows that I knew, they had just left, you know, within a few days ago. And Howard wasn't there... A few of them were there.

Well, anyway, we stayed awhile, and then we come on back to our area. And the next day we left there, and then they shipped us off to Manila. Well, when we got into Manila, I guess we was in the back end of Manila someplace...
You didn't perform in Guam.
No-no-no... No, we just went to visit some friends. See, we had no working orders. All we was doin'
Holmes (12/5) - 14

now was traveling to Manila. We were making stopovers. So anyway, we got into Manila, in the back end of it someplace, and it ended up raining like it always does over there, is rain -- nothin' but mud. It was thick with mud. We had on boots and things, but it was still mud to me. I wasn't used to that kind of...you know, that kind of life.

Well, anyway, we stayed out there in the mud that night, with our mosquito bars in our tents. I didn't know what a mosquito bar was. I found out right quick. And we made the night out there. Boy, I didn't know people could live under these conditions. And I thought it was bad. It wasn't bad; these are good conditions -- which I found out later. Well, we made it out there that night, and then the next morning we had to get up and get ready, they put us on a truck, and they taken into Manila, in the city, at our staging area, Parinaki(?). I think that's part of the city; that was the name of the part of the city we were in -- Paranaki(?).

Well, they got set up there, and we are just browsing around, waiting for orders. No orders have come in. And then we come to find the plane with the instruments and things hadn't shown up. We were there, but the plane with the instruments, they hadn't shown up. They don't know where the instruments and things are. So we're just layin'
Holmes (12/5) - 15

around, eatin' and sleepin', and enjoying ourself the best we can. What else is there to do? You can't mope about no instruments, because Uncle Sam had plenty of instruments to furnish us. If they don't show up, they have big warehouses, big as Madison Square Garden, full of nothin' but instruments. We wasn't worried about the instruments. But the point is, ours just didn't show up on the plane.
But everybody had brought his own instrument, really, hadn't they? I mean, these weren't...
They were on the plane.
Yeah, but these weren't instruments that had been issued to you. They were your own.
No, these are our own personal instruments.
Your very own personal instruments, yeah.

So anyway, these instruments... I mean, they held up everything. I think we were around... I know exactly how long we were there. We didn't do anything for about two or three weeks, and just eatin' and sleepin'. And one day, the instruments did show up. They finally got there. Well, we're still waiting for orders. So we're still enjoying life. And there's plenty of life in Manila, too. Oh, Manila was just like New York. Meeting the people there, one-thing-or-another, nightclubs... Everything. Stores. Cities. Bombed-out cities and one-thing-or-
Holmes (12/5) - 16
another. But life was goin' on, moving.
Well, I was not the one to venture forth into anything. I stayed right around the staging area, and there wasn't a whole lot of moving for me. I didn't care for it that much.

So there was about fifty different shows stationed in the staging area, shows of one person, one-man shows, up to shows of fifty personnel, big shows. And we was all around the staging area... It was just like a family. And we'd get together, and we'd talk, this-that-and-the-other, and play different games, and sports and one-thing-or-another. And had a ball, you know. At night, some of the shows, they'd go up, we'd do the shows and things, then come back, and get in the games and one-thing-or-another. We really had a good time! So I said, 'Oh, this is not bad at all.' No, no. We hadn't hit a drop of work yet.

So I'll never forget, they changed from where we were stationed... This is right after Christmas. They moved us from where we were stationed in Manila to another part of town, from ...(?)... Why do they want to change us way over there? You know, we was right at home where we was at. So anyway, we go over there, and we're in a quonset hut with a bunch of White soldiers, Southern soldiers -- which wasn't good. When we walked in, we're all Black, they was all White. So here we moved in, and the cots and things are up
Holmes (12/5) - 17
at the other end of the quonset hut.

It's New Year's Eve, I never will forget it. We are all over in our corner together, just about eight of us, I think -- eight or nine. The rest of the quonset hut is White officers; you know, they were all officers. Anyway, they had been drinking, they're getting an early start on New Year's Eve. And I didn't like the looks of it. Because they were drinking and we were sober, and you know, that's not a good thing. So the fellows, we were all pretty touchy. I mean, we're quiet, this-that-and-the-other, we didn't want no trouble or anything. Well, you know how whiskey is. Whiskey makes you kind of frisky.

So they're drinking and we're thinking. Well, you know, you always think the worst, you know what I mean? So pretty soon, one of them... We got a little card game going in our group, and the rest of them are sitting around looking at it. And here comes one of the White officers. He come over and he says, "How do you boys feel?" -- because you know, everybody's "boy" to them. Well, one of the fellows looked up and said, "Okay, okay; fine, fine." So he says, "Well, I want everybody to have a happy New Year," and he put two quarts of whiskey on the table.
So when he put the whiskey on the table, that changed everything. Right then and there, them frowns turned to
Holmes (12/5) - 18

grins. Oh, they were grinnin' from ear to ear. Well, one of the fellows, Louis Bacon, jumped up and grabbed one of them, and he said, "You know something? There's something I always wanted to do." And the soldier said to him, he said, "Well, what is that?" He says, "I'd like to fire a 45. I've never had a chance to shoot a 45 automatic." He says, "What?" He said, "Well, I've got a foot-locker full of 45's." And he taken and opened up his foot-locker, he told Bacon to pick out which one he wanted to shoot, and Bacon ducked in there and got one. Well, I was turning my back on that. I don't want to see nobody playing with no 45 when they're full of whiskey, and he didn't know what a gun was all about.

So anyway, him and the officer went outside, and I could hear them out there shootin' that 45. Well, after that, everything was fine. Everybody was just as happy as could be, and that whiskey got to working -- and believe me, it was really a wonderful New Year's Eve. And believe me, I was drunk... I guess everybody was feelin' something, feelin' the spirit.

So we go to bed, way late at night we go to bed. And what happens? About three o'clock in the morning, Sylvester woke us all up. Woke up everybody. "Pack your gear. We're moving out right away." Now, boy, if that don't hit you
Holmes (12/5) - 19

like a ton of bricks. Now, you've gone to bed and your head is like that. I had slept about two hours, and here comes Sylvester waking everybody up: "Pack up." So we packed up. We had to meet the plane at about six o'clock. Oh, brother, my head was bustin' open, and I know some of the rest of them felt worse than I did.

So we go and meet the plane at six o'clock in the morning, boy. We had about two hours sleep. So we get in the plane, and we're on our way to Lahti(?), goin' to Lahti(?). And we get into Lahti, and it's rainin' cats and dogs. It is raining. It's pouring. And the plane stops in the middle of a big field. There's nothing in sight. Ain't even a tree in sight. Nothing! The plane comes down. He says, "All right." So Sylvester says, "Is there something here to move us or something?" And he said, "Well, the truck will be around to pick you up."

Okay, we get out of the plane, we get in this field, and there we are, standing up in the field early in the morning, and it's pouring brickbats out there. Oh, that rain is comin' down. So there we stand out there. And everybody, they don't feel good anyway. Pretty soon, here comes the truck. And I forget what the truck is called. It's not a weapons carrier. That's big enough to stand up in if they got a cover on it, you know. But this one you
Holmes (12/5) - 20

could stand up in, but it didn't have no cover on it. There was supposed to be a cover on it, but there was no cover. Now, we got to stand up in this truck and go to our area, our camp where we're designated. And it was quite a ride. Quite a ride. And we had to stand up all the way in the rain, the rain beatin' you in the face if you're looking where you're going. And if you turn the other way, it's beatin' you all in the rear parts of you. But anyway, it's still raining; it's pouring there.

So anyway, we get to the staging area, our little camp. We get in the tents, we divide up the tents between us. Thirteen in the show, divide it up by thirteen people. The women, they've got their own little tents, and the men had the rest. Well, we get all settled there, and then in walks the Special Service Officer. That was in the afternoon when he gets there. So he is... Well, see, we had been so accustomed to not doing anything in Manila for the past month... For most of the month we didn't do a thing! So bad as we felt from the night before, we knew we wasn't gonna do anything that night, too. We knew we were going to work, because it was raining too hard. Oh, it was throwing brickbats!
And the Special Service Officer come and greeted everybody. "Oh, the boys are so happy to hear that you made
Holmes (12/5) - 21

it here to the island." "Oh yeah." He says, "Do you know, they're waiting out there in the theatre for you now." And this was about four o'clock in the afternoon. He said, "They're waiting in the theatre, they're waiting now." Gee, in all that rain, we got to go through all that rain to get to the theatre? I just figured these soldiers are sitting in some big, beautiful theatre, high and dry and waiting for us to show up. No. I said, "It's raining out there. How are we going to make it to the theatre?" He said, "Oh, you'll make it to the theatre all right. We'll get you there." I said, "I don't get it. I don't see why they can't put it off for a day or so."

So anyway, we went to the theatre. Well, the theatre was nothing but a stage which the soldiers had built themselves. It wasn't bad, the stage wasn't bad. The only thing, the theatre part where the soldiers had to sit, that was nothing but out in the field, and they were sitting on tree stumps or boxes or anything, and had the raincoats and the things all over their head, and they been sitting there for hours waiting for our show to come on. So I looked out there, and I seen all these soldiers as far as I could see. Soldiers just sitting out there, covered up from the rain, waiting to see a show, like they're going to see something great.
Holmes (12/5) - 22

So I said to the Special Service Officer, "Do you mean to tell me these soldiers have been sitting out here since four o'clock this afternoon?" He said, "Yes. Waiting to see your show." He said, "They deserve a show. They've been here so long," and this-that-and-the-other. I said, "Well, I was dead against it because of the weather, but if they've got nerve enough to sit out there in that rain, the way it is, and sit there four or five hours waiting to see a show, I'm not going to be the one to say no. I'm going to play part. Now, I don't have nothing to say about the rest of the band, but I'm glad to do my part. But they deserve it. They deserve everything they get."

So we did the show in the rain, and like I said, the stage wasn't bad. We were covered up. But they're the ones sitting out in the rain. Boy, oh boy. So we did the show, and oh boy, you'd have thought it was a big extravaganza we did. It went over like a ton of bricks, like it was really something great. They were applauding anything they seen out there.

Well, we stayed on Lahti(?) sixteen days. And of those sixteen days we stayed there, it stopped raining two days. It stopped raining two days of the sixteen days we were there. The Sun came out. And when the Sun came out, it would be so hot, you would wish for it to rain again. So
Holmes (12/5) - 23

when the Sun did come out, we'd all reach in our bags and things to take our clothes off, because they were getting mildewed in the back... We'd take our clothes off and hang them on the line to dry out. But out of sixteen days, it rained fourteen days -- and it poured. But see, Lahti(?) was a beach, and the water would hit the sand and go right down. It wasn't muddy. Well, that wasn't too bad, because after a while you'd be there and you'd get used to the rain. You'd pay the rain no mind whatsoever. And I enjoyed that, because I thought it was nice. I said, "Ready-made shower. You want a shower, you just walk out in the rain." Nobody there to interfere with you.

But that was the Lahti(?) trip. I don't think nothin' happened on Lahti(?). Except that we met a lot of soldiers and things. We had a nice time. Everybody was very nice. Things went down cool on Lahti(?). Except I had carried three bottles of whiskey with me from the States, and naturally, I'm around giving my whiskey away to anybody who wants it. "Oh, have a drink." Stateside whiskey; stateside, you know. "Help yourself." And theh I come to find out, after I gave away all of the whiskey I had... I come to find out some of the boys were making a little bit of money off of it. Well, I mean, I didn't think that was right. Because the soldiers was treating us all right. I
Holmes (12/5) - 24
didn't think it was right to try to commercialize with them. But some people commercialize on anything, you know. So as I can't tell other people how to live their lives...
From Lahti(?), where did you go then?

Well, we did a lot of gettin' around in the Philippines. I don't know where. We did so many islands and things, I can't even remember the names of them. We went to Sabu(?), this (?) called Sabu. All of them. I can't even think of the names of them.
You didn't run into Herbie Cowens by any chance, did you?
Oh, I ran into Herbie Cowens in Manila.
I see.

No, but I mean, that has to do with resonance in the reed.
Oh yeah, yeah, the resonance, sure.
Yeah, because isn't an oboe a double reed?
Yeah, it's a double reed and very small. Very small and very hard to blow.
And that's where you have to get the vibration.
Yeah. And you're supposed to make your own reeds with the oboe. You're supposed to.
Oh yeah?

Yeah. Most oboe players, they make their own reeds. Which I never got that far with it. No, I would buy a reed and let it get soft after soaking it, and this-that-and-the-other. I never could shave a reed. I was never successful shaving any kind of a reed. Even saxophone. I never know the right place to shave a reed. I tried it for years. I could never shave a reed successfully. And then I got to using a certain brand reed, and they had them numbered, and that was...
What brand and what number?
Well, truthfully speaking...
Devol(?)?
It was a Rico reed.
Holmes (1/14) - 27
A Rico and a #2.

A Number-two, you know. It's funny, I got that name. That name came to me. Rico, yeah. You see, because I haven't been playing lately... Rico. They come in numbers. So #2 satisfied me more than #2-1/2. #2-1/2 is a little bit too stiff for my mouthpiece, and with the #2 I could get the resonance that I wanted, you know.

Well, rather than me bother to shavin' reeds and cuttin' them down, I'd buy reeds by the boxes, and I didn't have no trouble. I had no trouble because the Number-Two fitted me pretty good. And I'd just put the reed on and go ahead and play it. And they lasted me quite a while. I was glad for that, because I was never successful shaving reeds. I mean, some people can do it, and do very good...
Well, they (?) with cigarette lighters and heat them and...
Yeah, yeah. Well, they do everything. You know what I mean? Burn them on the edge. Put them on a quarter and burn the edge, the tip of it, all that kind of stuff.
Well, did you ever try any slap-tonguing or any of that?
I used to slap-tongue years ago.
Yeah?
Holmes (1/14) - 28

Sure. Everybody did. Yeah, that was just going along with the times. If you had to do certain things, you did it. If you had to play clarinet, you had to play clarinet. And soprano saxophone, too. Practically everybody had an alto, a clarinet and a soprano. Everybody had them... Those that could afford them. Those instruments weren't sky-high like they are today. You could get an alto for around a hundred dollars. A good-name alto cost you a few more dollars. You could get a good alto for a hundred dollars. And a clarinet, you could get them dirt-cheap. And sopranos didn't cost too much either. They were cheaper than the altos.
But nowadays, I don't know. I haven't priced any instruments lately, but they tell they're around up there in the thousand-dollar class.
Yeah, they are.
Boy..> That's second-hand.
Well, some of them, yes.

A thousand dollars second-hand. I see it in the book, in the Union Book. You know, they have the instruments for sale, used, this-that-and-the-other, and they've got the prices that they want for them. And then flutes, they're out of reach. I think I saw a flute in there for thirty thousand dollars second-hand. Thirty
Holmes (1/14) - 29
thousand dollars for a flute. What can a flute do for thirty thousand dollars?
Well, they've got violins that are...
Now, there's something... Now, what can a violin do for that much money... One of them Stradivariuses. What can it do for that much money? You drop it and you have nothin'!
But apparently, the violinist perceives a difference in tone and...
It still sounds like a violin to me. Some violins sound good. No, all violins sound bad; some sound worse. No, some violins are... I mean, the Stradivarius... You can tell quality, though.
Yeah.
Yeah, some violins ..(?)..
[PAUSE]
You know, my stories are long because I pause for a long time between words...
Anyway, let's get to the Lenox Club.

The Lenox Club was a nice little nightclub, an intimate spot in Harlem in the Roarin' Twenties. It used to be the home of... Well, I don't know. But it was a nice little place. It was not a big place. It was a small place, a small club.
Holmes (1/14) - 30
Breakfast dances?

Yeah, they used to have breakfast dances there. They would start at twelve o'clock Sunday night, and they'd run all night long, until the last couple go out, which was six-seven o'clock in the morning sometimes.

Anyway, Louis made his appearance at the Savoy, which was one block down the street from this place. And after he finished at the Savoy, everybody went... Not everybody, because everybody couldn't get in that little club. They went to... The musicians went to the Lenox Club, to sit and jam and one-thing-and-another. And Rex Stewart happened to be there, and oh, he was blowin' his head off. I think, I'm not certain...yeah, Jack Teagarden was also there. Yes, he was there that morning, too. He was on the stand playing. Rex Stewart, and Rex was playing with his little trumpet -- and he could blow. Rex could really play.
They all played. All of them that thought they could play. Everybody had their chance.

And then Louis got up there and played... Threw Rex Stewart's horn away. Heh-heh. Rex was laughin'! Threw his horn away. He had never heard nothin' like Louis in his life. Louis was exciting. He was something to hear, you know! But...
Holmes (1/14) - 31
[END OF TAPE VIII, SIDE 1]
He was really exciting.
Do you remember the number?

No. No, who would remember the number? He was just blowin', and in that big pretty tone. See, the thing that Louis had on everybody else... Most trumpet players, the higher they go, the thinner the tone got, and they would end up just squeaking, like a flute. But with Louis, the higher he went, the broader his tone got -- and it was beautiful! I mean, he was really playing with real tone. Big, wide tones. And nobody around here had ever played a trumpet like that, where the tones were so big, and he was hitting them notes right on the head, he wasn't fluffing them, and this-that-and-the-other. So big and true.

He just excited everybody that heard him. The only ones he didn't excite was somebody who didn't know nothin' about music period, and couldn't care less! And we'd run into a lot of them people while we was on the road. With Louis, we made little trips and things down South... Well, we worked different little places, the ...(?)...(?)... And some of them places, they didn't know nothin' about Louis. Well, nobody knew nothin' about him then, except the people
Holmes (1/14) - 32
in the bigger cities -- they had his records and things. But the people down there didn't know nothin' about him.

And that's where he showed his greatness, because he would walk into these places, the people didn't... Well, they would come up to him curious, one of them things. Because we were not packing the halls. The halls were not packed! They were just ordinary dance crowds, you know. And believe me, when Louis got to playing, people would be shoutin', whoopin' and hollerin', applaudin' him. He was sensational. But see, these are people that didn't know nothin' about him whatsoever.

I mean, it was not easy, because he was what you call trailblazin'. He was blazing a trail. And it wasn't easy, believe me. Well, it wasn't easy for him. It was easy for me sitting back there and enjoying it. It wasn't my name up there anyway!

But he worked hard. Louis always worked hard. And boy, the perspiration would just run off of him. Oh brother, he worked awful hard. When he finished playing a dance, he had to strip down and change everything. And I mean, you see, places did not have them fine dressing rooms and showers and things then. You just waited until everybody got out of the place, and then he could change his clothes after everybody had gone, and dry himself with his
Holmes (1/14) - 33
own towels and things. There was no running water, no showers or anything. But he sweated so much. He sweated very easily.

He worked hard. He really worked hard. He deserves every little... What little acclaim he got, he deserved every bit of it. A hard worker. He really worked hard. When he says he worked hard, you can believe him. He did. I mean, I worked with other leaders, too, but I never worked with no leader worked as hard as him. And I never worked for Lionel Hampton, and when I see him work I never did want to work with him, because he works hard and wants everybody else to work hard. I never wanted to work with one of them hard-working leaders. Because they get the money and you get laid up in the hospital some place.
What about some other trumpeters that you remember, going all the way back to, say, Johnny Dunn?
Well, Johnny Dunn was about... He was a sensation. He's the one had the publicity, the big note and the long horn, the long coach horn. And he was the king of the valves.
Did the coach horn have valves or not?
Yeah, I think so..
It had valves.
I think so. I don't know. I wasn't
Holmes (1/14) - 34

interested in how they were built. In fact, do you know something? I just found out a few years ago, and I played in a symphony band, I started out in a symphony orchestra... And I just found out a few years ago that a French horn was fingered with the left hand.
Uh-huh.
You understand what I mean?
Yeah.

A French horn. I just found that out a few years ago. I thought it was fingered with the right hand all the time. So I'm not observant on how instruments are built, unless I'm playing it. The brass instruments, I don't notice them at all. That was funny... It tickles me how stupid I was about the French horn. I was so surprised when I found out that was a left-handed horn. But now, what was I talking about?
We were on Johnny Dunn.
Oh, Johnny Dunn, yeah. Yeah. I don't know if the coach horn had valves or not. I imagine they did. I'm not sure. But that's what he used to play!
Did he sort of have an act? Or was he leading a band?
I don't know. I'd never see him perform. I wouldn't spend no money to hear him. He wasn't that good to me, and I never heard him (you know what I mean?)
Holmes (1/14) - 35
perform. I heard him play...
But he was a big name when you came to New York.

He was a big name. Yeah, he was the big man. But see, no, when I come here, I guess he was kind of out of business. Because see, Louis had been here with Fletcher in '25. I came in '27. So I didn't hear much of Johnny Dunn.
No, he was gone by then.
Yes. He wasn't the King no more.
But now, you liked Bobby Stark.

Oh, Bobby! Yeah, that's my man. He could blow. Nice trumpet player. Good man in a band. Good man in a band. Yeah. Chick had eight pieces, an eight-piece band, you know. There was Bobby Stark... I'm trying to think. He had... There was four in the rhythm, right?
Mmm-hmm.

And there was Johnny, Elmer Williams on tenor, Bobby Stark on... Yeah, two brass. Bobby and Slats on trombone. I was thinking that Chick had another trumpet, but he didn't have another trumpet until I went in the band, and I worked with Chick... Which wasn't long, because he didn't work much. I think we had a ten-day engagement up in New England, ten one-nighters, you know. And I worked them with him. That's when he was enlarging his band. And when
Holmes (1/14) - 36

we came back, he didn't have no more work! But we was rehearsing every day. He loved to rehearse, he loved to hear his band, and stand on the corner and talk about how great a band he has. And he'd tell you about all the men in the band, this-that-and-the-other... He didn't have nothin' but the best men.
Did he have Jimmy Harrison at one time?

He had everybody. He had everybody. He damn near had Duke Ellington! Well, he could have got Duke, too, because Duke wasn't doin' nothin'. Duke wasn't doin' nothin' but standing at a bar waiting for a live one to come in. And Duke, he went to work... Duke went to work for Billy Cain's club on Eighth Avenue, a little joint, you know. Then after that, Duke left town and went up to New England, barnstorming through New England. They stayed up there all summer. When they come back from that, then they went in the Cotton Club. Then from then on, he didn't look back. So he almost had Duke in his band.

But Chick would hire anybody quick. You had to be good. Chick didn't want nothin' but the best. And he would tell everybody that he had the best, too. That's what he would tell you. And he spent his money buying arrangements. He'd get good arrangements, and he'd get good men that could play the arrangements. And he had a good-sounding band. It
Holmes (1/14) - 37
sounded very good. I'm not talking about the time I was with him, because I made them ten days, and we just rehearsed from then on. He didn't get no more engagements.
Now, how about somebody like Frankie Newton?
Well, I don't remember him in Chick's band.
No, no, I don't mean that. I just mean as a trumpeter.
Well, he was a good trumpet player. But there was something Frankie lacked in comparison with Bobby Stark. See, Bobby had that drive, which Frankie didn't have. Frankie was a good trumpet player.
He had interesting ideas, I thought.

Oh, he had wonderful ideas. But he didn't have that drive that Bobby had, you know. Yeah, Frankie played some beautiful things, wonderful. Just like Bill Coleman. I like Bill Coleman, too, as a trumpet player. But I mean, he was no comparison with Bobby Stark. And Bill could blow. Bill could blow.
Well, there was a lot of trumpet players. I can't even think of them now. New York was filled up with trumpet players, just like Metcalf and...
Henry Allen?
No, Red wasn't there then. Red, he didn't get here until '29. I'm talking about back around '27.
Oh, I see. All right, you had Bubber Miley.
Holmes (1/14) - 38
Yeah, Bubber Miley. Yeah, there was quite a few trumpet players around. Scotty that was with Fletcher Henderson...
Oh, Howard Scott.

Howard Scott. He was never what you'd call a hot get-off man, but he was a beautiful-sounding trumpet player. He sounded like Joe Smith to me. Beautiful tone. Well, years go by and it's nice to think back to some of them fellows, you know. Have their names come back up in my mind -- with the help of you.
Cootie could really play, too, you said, when...
Cootie could play when he first come here with Alonzo Ross's band... Oh, I know I wanted to tell you something about...

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Institute of Jazz Studies copyright notice
segments.summary: Rutgers IJS boilerplate and copyright warning preceding the transcript.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Birth in Boston and the Holmes family of siblings
segments.summary: Holmes gives his birth date and place and names his brothers and sisters; the family was large, with up to thirteen children over time.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Boston neighborhoods and boyhood schoolmates Carney, Hodges and Howard Johnson
segments.summary: He corrects the interviewer on streets lived on (Warwick, Marble, Roxbury) and recalls meeting Johnny Hodges, Harry Carney and Howard Johnson around Sherwin Grammar School.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: A mixed neighborhood and integrated schools
segments.summary: The Warwick Street house had White and Black families; the school was integrated, and Black teachers arrived before he finished grammar school.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Hearing Johnny Hodges makes him want a saxophone
segments.summary: His parents were not musical; hearing Hodges at about ten made him want to play saxophone, and he explains why music appealed to Black youth then.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Piano at home and his father's job as head janitor
segments.summary: A piano was in the parlor but nobody used it; he played by ear, took brief lessons, and describes his father's work at South Station and his mother's day work.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Howard Johnson's musical family and Bobby Johnson's saxophone
segments.summary: Howard's mother and brother Walter taught and played piano, brother Bobby played banjo and guitar, and Bobby's discarded saxophone became Howard's.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Hodges versus Howard Johnson at Don Donaldson's rehearsals
segments.summary: Kids listened outside Don Donaldson's house to Hodges and Howard play; Hodges had a different tone and was the Boston favorite.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Meeting Hodges at house rent parties
segments.summary: He got to know Hodges by following him to totes (rent parties); Hodges would not let him play his horn, and his father could not afford a saxophone.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Dr. Holmes's Good Samaritan brass band for children
segments.summary: A wealthy Black benefactor named Holmes outfitted a band, with a director who taught every instrument, giving instruments to those who promised to stay.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Tolliver and Carney get clarinets, Holmes gets an oboe
segments.summary: Buster Tolliver and Harry Carney got clarinets from the band; Holmes was given an oboe with a promise of a saxophone later, and he discusses alto and tenor.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Oboe lessons with Trogliano and long practice hours
segments.summary: His paid oboe teacher kept him on the C scale for six months, so he quit lessons and practiced four or five hours a day in the attic.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Hiding the oboe; Joseph Wagner and the Boston Civic Symphony in 1926
segments.summary: He was ashamed to play oboe in Boston dance circles; school conductor Joseph Wagner gave no private lessons, and he played with the Boston Civic Symphony for about a season.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: The first saxophone, a Pan-American, and slipping grades
segments.summary: His father bought a second-hand Pan-American alto in his third year of high school; he played free everywhere, his marks fell, and word spread that he sounded like Hodges.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Hodges offered a place with a burlesque show
segments.summary: Eddie Haywood's father tried to take Hodges on the road; shy Hodges asked Holmes along, who refused, and Holmes met many big-time musicians through Hodges.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Returning the oboe, and the Lorais oboe he later sold
segments.summary: He gave back Dr. Holmes's oboe, got a brand-new Lorais from the school, later bought one himself in New York, and sold it in the Depression for twenty-five dollars.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's band with Armstrong in Boston, 1925
segments.summary: He heard Henderson's precise band with Armstrong, Hawkins, Redman and Buster Bailey, and names its personnel.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: The Henderson dance: a Colored dance, and Hodges commuting to New York
segments.summary: The Henderson band played a White dance first and the Colored dance after midnight; Holmes explains Hodges's back-and-forth work with Bechet in Harlem clubs.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Henderson's reed section impresses him
segments.summary: Redman, Bailey and Hawkins impressed him, all doubling clarinet, though later bands such as Duke's changed his tastes.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: George Tines and Boston dance bands
segments.summary: The most popular Black Boston band was George Tines's eight-to-ten piece dance group, in which he mixed up leader and drummer as a boy.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Opinion: jazz was not only from New Orleans
segments.summary: Holmes argues that jazz was played by Black people everywhere, recalling his mother humming spirituals.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Saxophonists had to own a clarinet; Buster Bailey's wooden clarinet
segments.summary: Every saxophonist carried a Boehm clarinet because the stock parts called for it; Buster Bailey impressed him most in the 1925 Henderson band.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Harry Carney as a boyhood friend
segments.summary: Holmes describes Carney's birth, family, strict upbringing and gentlemanly character; they shared school and Dr. Holmes's band but did not socialize.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Seeing Sidney Bechet in Jimmy Cooper's show
segments.summary: Going alone as a loner, he heard Bechet's soprano solo in a burlesque show and comments that the saxophone then had no standard sound.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Boston saxophonists Eric Brown, Don Pasquale and Benny Waters
segments.summary: He recalls the conservatory-trained Eric Brown, teacher Don Pasquale, and the showman Benny Waters compared with sedentary Hodges.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Pianist Dan Carey and the black keys
segments.summary: Dan Carey played in the hard keys and Hodges would follow him anywhere.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: First gigs: a five-dollar dance and the stranded Watson show
segments.summary: A first gig had a pianist who knew only two keys; then a singer Watson's show band collapsed in Leominster and left them stranded overnight.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Smitty later in Erskine Hawkins's band and Tippin' In
segments.summary: Smitty later played saxophone with Erskine Hawkins and wrote 'Tippin' In'; the interviewer cannot find him in Rust.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Boston band instrumentation and the union hangout
segments.summary: Boston had good reeds, pianos and drummers but scarce brass; musicians hung out in a small union room to find gigs.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Joe Steele's band and Boston working musicians
segments.summary: He met Joe Steele in church; Hodges and Howard Johnson worked with Steele's band, and Carney worked a road house for nearly a year.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Dan Carey and Wendell Culley, whom he never worked with
segments.summary: He didn't work with Carey (hard keys, no music) and didn't know Culley of Worcester before leaving for New York.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Hodges bringing New York ideas home
segments.summary: Hodges returned from New York playing advanced ideas; they never talked music directly.

segments.chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
segments.title: Deciding to go to New York from an ice cream parlor
segments.summary: Friends proposed a weekend trip to hear Hodges at the Savoy; only Holmes and Carney actually went, lying to their mothers and bringing altos and clarinets.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: First night at the Savoy Ballroom, thrown off the floor
segments.summary: Holmes and Carney arrive in March 1927, are awed by the Savoy, and bouncers push them off the dance floor when they try to greet Hodges.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Hodges introduces them to Chick Webb and the band
segments.summary: Hodges brings Chick Webb over, Webb makes them welcome, and Holmes lists the small band's members.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: The Savoy Bearcats, Willie Lynch and Fess Williams
segments.summary: Discussion of who played the Savoy then: the Savoy Bearcats with drummer Willie Lynch, and a clarinetist who was a great technician.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Artie Shaw wakes him up to the clarinet
segments.summary: Holmes liked Buster Bailey but no other clarinetists until he heard Artie Shaw at the Paramount, whom he preferred to Benny Goodman.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Albert Nicholas, Barney Bigard and Simeon replacing him at the Nest
segments.summary: He admires Nicholas's tone and Bigard, and recalls that Russell sent for Simeon to replace him at the Nest Club.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: The cutting contest at Mexico's: Greely Walton, Hawkins, Hodges, Carney and Holmes
segments.summary: At a small 133rd Street joint he heard Greely Walton and Coleman Hawkins, then reluctantly played and was said to have outswung Hodges, which Chick Webb publicized.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Playing tenor in the Savoy relief band for the first time
segments.summary: Reynolds hired Carney and Holmes for a dinner-hour relief band; Carney took alto, leaving Holmes on Elmer Williams's tenor, which he had never played.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Nelson Clark's band at the Lenox Club
segments.summary: He took a job in a five or six piece band at Happy Rone's declining Lenox Club, where pay came in small nightly amounts.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Joining Billy Fowler's band at the Club Alabam
segments.summary: He auditions for Billy Fowler's band at the lavish Broadway Club Alabam, among experienced players such as Edgar Sampson, Freddy Johnson, Ward Pinkett and Ed Cuffee.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: The Club Alabam show, uniforms and why it closed
segments.summary: The Alabam was a lavish nightclub with floor shows and a good-quality, well-rehearsed band, and closed as summer slowed business.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Making $65 a week at seventeen and reassuring his parents
segments.summary: He earned $65 weekly when working men made $15-18, sent money home and found New York nothing like the warnings.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Rooming with Harry Carney in Freddy Guy's apartment, Duke Ellington downstairs
segments.summary: After a week they moved to Freddy Guy's apartment, paying about four dollars a week, with Ellington always in the apartment below.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Duke asks him for ideas, and 'Mood Indigo' appears
segments.summary: Coming home at dawn, Holmes was asked by Ellington for numbers to record; Carney later told him they had recorded 'Mood Indigo'.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Turning down Duke Ellington's offers
segments.summary: Ellington asked him to join many times and Holmes always refused, though the band was his favorite, because he lacked the desire to join the best.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Benny Carter at Small's Paradise, then the cutting contest with Hodges
segments.summary: Hodges sent them to hear Benny Carter at Small's, which left him cold, but at a 129th Street cutting contest Carter played superbly against Hodges.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Chez Florence and the tip-splitting singers' band
segments.summary: At a gangster-run Chez Florence the six-piece band was incidental to singer Kid Snead and others, and the club closed after the boss broke a patron's nose.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: The Tree of Hope and a Brooklyn gangster nightclub with Hilton Jefferson
segments.summary: Benny James introduced him under the Tree of Hope to Hilton Jefferson, who offered a Brooklyn job in a lazy six-piece band under a Cuban or Puerto Rican trumpeter.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Lou Henry's offer to play the Savoy and Carney's advice
segments.summary: Tired of Brooklyn, he took Carney's advice that the Savoy would put him on view and accepted Lou Henry's three-month job.

segments.chapter: First years in New York, 1927-28
segments.title: Lou Henry's band personnel and the thrill of the Savoy
segments.summary: He names those he remembers in Lou Henry's band and recalls how glamorous working at the Savoy was.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Chick Webb's enlarged band on ten New England dates
segments.summary: Webb enlarged to ten pieces for a New England tour with Hodges, Williams and the Savoy band, but the band rehearsed constantly and found little work.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Getting the Nest Club job and playing for gangsters
segments.summary: A phone call to the Bandbox sent him to the Nest, where drummer-leader George Howe and pianist Luis Russell hired him, and gangsters threw money after 3 a.m.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Hodges fills in for Ellington and Holmes stays with Russell
segments.summary: Ellington's trouble with Otto Hardwick put Hodges in his band while Webb idled, and Holmes preferred the steady work with Russell.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Russell takes over as leader; Simeon and Metcalf come in
segments.summary: After the owner fired drummer George Howe, Russell led the band; Holmes kept leaving and returning while Simeon and Metcalf joined.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Who was in Russell's early Nest band, and the unhealthy club
segments.summary: He recalls early tenor players (one dangerous, one named Adams), local drummers, and Pops Foster and Barbarin coming from Chicago, and the airless club.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Recording with Luis Russell and King Oliver
segments.summary: Russell recorded under everyone's name; Holmes made 'Tight Like That', 'Savoy Shout' and 'Call of the Freaks' without knowing titles, plus Oliver dates with Metcalf.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Teddy Hill, Russell's Chicago recruits and the Nest rhythm section
segments.summary: Teddy Hill joined early; Russell hired Foster, Barbarin and Simeon from Oliver's Chicago band; Will Johnson and Bass Moore were already around the Nest.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Cyrus Sinclair and Bass Edwards
segments.summary: He knew Cyrus Sinclair from Small's but never worked with him or with tuba player Bass Edwards.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: The Saratoga Club audition and number banker Cass Goldstein
segments.summary: Russell assembled a band for the Saratoga Club across from the Savoy, owned by an indifferent number banker who promised pay whether or not customers came.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Louis Metcalf's lyrics and the family feeling in Russell's band
segments.summary: Metcalf and Teddy Hill clowned on the stand and Holmes says the band was like a family.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Red Allen teasing Higgenbotham
segments.summary: When Red Allen joined, he constantly teased Higgenbotham about women; Holmes stayed out of it and Russell let them have fun.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Sunday matinee dances and head arrangements at the Saratoga
segments.summary: The empty club filled for Sunday matinees; the band hardly rehearsed and played mostly head arrangements with Red Allen fitting in.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Who wrote what: 'Poor Little Me', 'Saratoga Shout' and 'Saratoga Drag'
segments.summary: Holmes says 'Poor Little Me' was Barbarin's, he and Greely Walton wrote the Saratoga numbers, and everyone contributed for love of the life.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Why Russell's band was exciting and never lost a battle at the Savoy
segments.summary: Holmes argues Russell's band deserves more recognition, swung hard and won every Savoy band battle, though its records have a monotonous rhythm.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Acoustic recording horns and the day-long 'I Can't Give You Anything But Love' with Armstr
segments.summary: Early recording used horns, and the Louis Armstrong date spent half a day on a single melody-backing number before 'Mahogany Hall Stomp' the next day.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Rehearsal takes and how Russell sessions differed from Armstrong's
segments.summary: Russell's sessions gave three or four takes described as rehearsal, and he never knew about alternate takes; Russell's band knew its numbers unlike the Armstrong sessions.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Hoagy Carmichael, 'Rockin' Chair' and Armstrong's genius
segments.summary: Armstrong accepted any tune brought into the studio, leaving Russell to make arrangements, and Holmes calls him a genius.

segments.chapter: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
segments.title: Closing the first interview session
segments.summary: Holmes says 10 o'clock is his bedtime and the session ends.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Willie Lynch's band at the Savoy and how it was founded
segments.summary: Holmes recalls Willie Lynch of the Savoy Bearcats forming a band for the Savoy manager, with Holmes on alto, earning more than Chick Webb's band.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Wages and what leaders earned
segments.summary: Sidemen made fifty dollars a week and up, while leaders' earnings depended on what the band took in.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Lynch band personnel, Jabbo Smith and Holmes as straw boss
segments.summary: Holmes recalls a six-to-eight piece band with Joe Steele on piano and Jabbo Smith on trumpet, and that he called the numbers.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Lynch band at the Lafayette Theatre and Irving Mills
segments.summary: After the Savoy closed the band scattered, then Lynch's group had a hit playing 'Stardust' at the Lafayette Theatre and Irving Mills put them in the Cotton Club.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Joining the Mills Blue Rhythm Band under Carroll Dickerson
segments.summary: Holmes joined soon after the band went into the Cotton Club, replacing Jobetus McCord; he recalls Dickerson, Hayes Alvis and Crawford Wethington.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Blue Rhythm Band trumpets, trombones and Gus Aikin
segments.summary: Looking at a band picture, Holmes works out the trumpets (Wardell Jones, Anderson, Aikin), trombones and banjo, and recalls how he forgot about working with Gus Aikin.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Taking up the lower-register clarinet on 'Cabin in the Cotton'
segments.summary: On April 28, 1932 Irving Mills rejected the written arrangement until Holmes noodled the melody on low clarinet, which Mills wanted.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: His first record on clarinet, 'Slow and Steady', and how the solo was made
segments.summary: The interviewer reveals Holmes played clarinet on 'Slow and Steady' for King Oliver in 1928; the Cabin solo was a head, over a stock three-clarinet arrangement.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Asking Irving Mills for more money and being fired
segments.summary: On tour the band wanted more pay; at a meeting at Mills's office Holmes alone spoke up and was replaced, teaching him to speak only for himself.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Joining Teddy Hill's band at the Savoy
segments.summary: Teddy Hill hired him after the Blue Rhythm Band; Holmes lists the personnel including Blanchard, Pinkett, Sam Allen and Bill Beason, with Roy Eldridge replacing Pinkett.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Doubling on clarinet and Howard Johnson and Chu Berry replacing him
segments.summary: He carried clarinet and soprano in one case, had given up baritone, and left Hill's band when Johnson and Chu Berry came in.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Blanchard and Bill Dillard working out at the Y
segments.summary: Blanchard, once small and sickly, built himself up at the Y; Dillard and Benny James were strong; Blanchard later moved to Florida.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Luis Russell's later big band personnel
segments.summary: Back with Russell, he names the later band: Henry Jones, Bingie Madison, Rex Stewart, Archey, Pops Foster, Barbarin and the Palmer Brothers.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Bingie Madison's too-difficult arrangements
segments.summary: Madison wrote brilliant but very hard arrangements that left the band scuffling, which Holmes thinks does not make a good band.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: Dancing schools and taxi dance halls: why musicians learned to read
segments.summary: Many players learned reading in ten-cents-a-dance halls, playing stock arrangements chorus by chorus for fifty-five minutes an hour, which gave Holmes no inspiration.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: The Circle Ballroom and Russell's ballroom engagements
segments.summary: He found the Circle Ballroom very boring and lists the Savoy, Roseland, Empire and the classy Arcadia as ballrooms Russell played.

segments.chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
segments.title: How hostesses and tickets worked at big ballrooms
segments.summary: At big ballrooms patrons paid admission and bought tickets for hostesses, and bands alternated half-hour sets.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Three bands at once, and why the Empire Ballroom failed
segments.summary: Holmes played one engagement with three bands, mostly playing cards; Carter opened the Empire and Russell followed, but the new room could not compete with Roseland and Arcadia.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Sonny Woods and the Palmer Brothers
segments.summary: Sonny Woods was a fine but short tenor vocalist; the Palmer Brothers of Providence sang popular songs and recorded with the band but worked separately.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Hearing King Oliver's band at the Savoy, with Red Allen
segments.summary: Oliver fronted his Savoy band without playing while Red Allen did the trumpet work, and the band broke up and mostly returned to Chicago.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Meeting Luis Russell and Russell sending to Chicago for Oliver's men
segments.summary: Playing the Nest Club he met Russell, who enlarged the band by sending for Pops Foster, Red Allen, Simeon and Barbarin and later got the band together at the Saratoga.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Clarinet on 'Slow and Steady' and hating the clarinet
segments.summary: The Brunswick session of November 14, 1928 under Oliver's name was Holmes's first record; he says he hated clarinet but all saxophonists had to play it.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: The January 1929 Okeh sessions and the tuba players
segments.summary: They made 'Savoy Shout', 'Call of the Freaks' and 'Tight Like That' under Russell's name; Holmes recalls Bass Moore and Pops Foster both being on the date.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: King Oliver in the studio, sick and silent
segments.summary: Oliver attended the recording dates but never played; Holmes found it a letdown and says Oliver was at the end of the line with bad gums.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: 'Call of the Freaks' as the band's theme song
segments.summary: Holmes hears the number, calls it the theme song and thinks Russell, not Barbarin, wrote it.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Recording under three minutes and Russell's arranging
segments.summary: Numbers rehearsed on the job had to be cut to under three minutes for records, with Russell arranging and many head numbers.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Metcalf's ideas and the young band's good time
segments.summary: Metcalf was the lively one and the young band enjoyed itself as much as the public did.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Audiences at the Savoy and the Lindy Hop
segments.summary: Audiences of all ages and races came, and the young crowd did the new Lindy Hop named for Lindbergh's flight.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: The Savoy beat and Russell's band winning band battles
segments.summary: Only young people could dance to swing; the right beat won applause and Russell's band, in and out of the Savoy like a house band, beat all rivals.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: House-breakers 'Old Man River' and 'Ease On Down'
segments.summary: The band's first house-breaker was an 'Old Man River' arrangement largely Metcalf's idea; 'Ease On Down' was a chorus-girl number whose title was misprinted.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Other numbers: 'Saratoga Shout' and 'Panama'
segments.summary: Holmes cannot recall titles but claims 'Saratoga Shout' as his own and names 'Panama' as a top number.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Playing soprano or alto freely, and C.B. Conn saxophones
segments.summary: He liked Russell's band best because he could choose soprano or alto; he played a Conn soprano and alto and had little regard for Selmers.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Failing at flute and the stolen soprano
segments.summary: He never could play flute even on Walton's and Howard Johnson's flutes, and his soprano was stolen from a California club, ending his soprano playing.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Never keeping his own records or scrapbooks
segments.summary: He didn't buy or listen to his records or keep scrapbooks and regrets having no photos with the celebrities he worked with.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Photographs from Edward G. Robinson and Bessie Love at the Palace
segments.summary: The only photos he has are autographed ones he asked for from Edward G. Robinson and Bessie Love when he worked the Palace Theatre in the Thirties.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Sylvester Lewis and the tape proving he was a musician
segments.summary: He recalls Sy Oliver and trumpeter Sylvester Lewis, who after a USO tour worked in the subway and borrowed a tape to prove to co-workers he had led a band.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Being a sideman, unknown to the public
segments.summary: Holmes says he was always a sideman, never a leader or star, was hard to get along with, and found the music business life best for the young.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: The 'Tight Like That' vocalist from New Orleans
segments.summary: Hearing the vocalist, he recalls working with him in an act at Chez Florence, a job that lasted two weeks.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Listening to 'Tight Like That' with Red Allen, Barbarin's chimes and Metcalf's vocal
segments.summary: He identifies Red Allen's solos and Metcalf as vocalist, who contributed the lyrics though no longer in the band.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Many good New York trumpeters
segments.summary: Holmes says there was no shortage of trumpeters and none outstanding, naming Bobby Stark and Rex Stewart.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Louis Metcalf's crown and Armstrong's high F at the Savoy
segments.summary: Metcalf wore a crown as king of the band until Armstrong played a high F on a two-night Savoy visit and Teddy Hill threw the crown into the audience.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Armstrong's March 1929 recording visit and the acoustic horns
segments.summary: Armstrong's studio sessions the next days were difficult, with no microphones, no drums and the band scattered around horns.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: 'I Can't Give You Anything But Love' with no arrangement
segments.summary: With no arrangement and a three-minute limit, the technicians held all the say and the whole session produced one side.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: How 'Mahogany Hall Stomp' was made up in the studio
segments.summary: Hoagy Carmichael brought a lead sheet, Armstrong agreed to it unseen, Russell scribbled an arrangement, and the hurried number became the big hit.

segments.chapter: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
segments.title: Recording pay and who handled the business
segments.summary: Record pay came months later via the leader with no bonus; Russell handled the business and musicians simply received what they were promised.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Condon, Mezzrow and Armstrong's hangers-on in the studio
segments.summary: Eddie Condon, Mezz Mezzrow and others followed Armstrong to every record date, so the studio held more bystanders than band members.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Hodges sitting in at the Saratoga Sunday matinee
segments.summary: The Sunday matinee was the only time the Saratoga had a crowd, and Hodges would come in and Holmes would invite him up to play.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Subbing for Hodges on Duke Ellington's Cotton Club broadcast
segments.summary: When Hodges's wife was having a baby Holmes took his chair in Ellington's broadcast, and Hodges later told Kirkpatrick the sound was Charlie's, not his.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Bill Coleman in the band and listening to 'Feelin' the Spirit' and 'Josie Lightning'
segments.summary: Holmes identifies the soloists on two flag-wavers, including himself, and explains that the written parts had been played many times before recording.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Pops Foster's string bass changes New York bands
segments.summary: Only Ellington used string bass, with Wellman Braud, until Pops Foster's style spread; guitars were the last instrument bands hired.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Pops Foster, Barbarin and the Russell rhythm section
segments.summary: Holmes praises Pops Foster and says a rhythm section should be felt rather than heard, comparing it to Sonny Greer in Ellington's band.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Sidemen who never became names, like Doc Cheatham
segments.summary: Many fine musicians, such as trumpeter Doc Cheatham, worked their whole lives as sidemen without becoming known.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: The Bandbox and the Rhythm Club as musicians' hangouts
segments.summary: The Rhythm Club, newer and with a pool table, drew musicians away from the Bandbox one corner over on Seventh Avenue.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton at the Bandbox
segments.summary: Morton played piano at the Bandbox, was loud-mouthed and surrounded by a crowd, but Holmes finds him a good, intelligent man.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: The Wilton Crawley date where Morton and Russell's men clashed
segments.summary: Morton arrived with his own group for a Wilton Crawley record date, and he and Crawley traded barbs until the players split the sides.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Wilton Crawley's clarinet act and the TOBA circuit
segments.summary: Crawley took his clarinet apart on stage and played upside down, toured the TOBA circuit, and Holmes now admires his tone.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Who played on the Morton and Crawley session, and Morton's bands
segments.summary: The studio was full of familiar musicians, Holmes can't separate Russell's men from Morton's, and it was his only recording with Morton.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Coming and going with Russell, then five years with Armstrong
segments.summary: He left and rejoined Russell freely, and from 1935 to 1940 worked with Armstrong, finally unable to take the hard work.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Armstrong did not excite him; only Hodges and Carter did
segments.summary: Holmes says he was only interested in saxophone, naming Hodges and Benny Carter as the two at the top with Willie Smith a rank below.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: The violins on 'Song of the Islands'
segments.summary: Asked about violinists added to an Armstrong record, Holmes sees nothing remarkable in it.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Armstrong's band paid better than Russell's, but Joe Glaser got rich
segments.summary: Armstrong's fixed nightly pay was steadier than Russell's hit-or-miss dates, though Glaser made far more from Armstrong's name.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Touring by bus and Armstrong's red Packard
segments.summary: The band toured everywhere by bus with Armstrong's dogs, wife Alpha and a maid, while Armstrong refused to ride in Glaser's red Packard that Holmes rode in instead.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Joe Glaser on the road and two quarts of whiskey at the Club Panama
segments.summary: Glaser rode the bus the first year and told clubs to give the band anything; in Chicago Holmes took him at his word and got sick.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Finding rooms in the South
segments.summary: Accommodations were rough, and bands stayed in poor hotels or private homes; Armstrong kept contacts who saved him rooms.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Southern dance halls, spectators and tobacco warehouses
segments.summary: Dances were mostly Black, with White spectators watching from the side; some were held in big tobacco warehouses arranged by local promoters.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: An eight-hundred-mile drive and Armstrong playing hard regardless
segments.summary: A Chicago-to-engagement run turned out to be eight hundred miles, and Armstrong still blew everyone off the stand on arrival.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Boston, Miami, New York, Miami: unpaid travel days
segments.summary: A booking run of Boston, two days to Miami, back to New York and Miami again paid only for working nights.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Armstrong never knew where the band was playing and slept on buses
segments.summary: Armstrong left all band business to Russell and Glaser and slept soundly on the bus while Holmes could not.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Breakdowns, blowouts in Mississippi and missing a dance
segments.summary: Bus blowouts on half-gravel roads led to hired cars, and Holmes's car went a hundred miles the wrong way and missed the dance.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Russell caught between the band and Glaser, and giving up leadership
segments.summary: Glaser had Russell fire men on the word of job-seekers; Russell tired of the hatred and resigned, and nobody in the band wanted to take over.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Joe Garland takes over with strict rules and uniform changes
segments.summary: Garland took over, posted uniform changes and made the reed section rehearse between shows; the band improved but the work felt like a factory.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Paying for uniforms and arguing with Glaser
segments.summary: Uniforms were deducted from pay, so Holmes told Glaser he would wear his own paid-for suit wherever he liked.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: Talking back to Glaser and being hard to get along with
segments.summary: Holmes was one of two band members never fired because he talked back, and says he walks away when he is unhappy.

segments.chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
segments.title: The Baltimore laundry
segments.summary: A woman in Baltimore was washing his week of laundry in filthy water, so he took it elsewhere.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: 'Lou and His Ginger Snaps' and why those tunes were recorded
segments.summary: Asked about a September 13, 1929 session, he says the Savoy first billed Russell as the Ginger Snaps and that the tunes were outside material Russell was asked to record.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Daytime sessions with no rehearsal and little interest in records
segments.summary: Sessions were mostly daytime, tunes were often handed out in the studio without arrangements, and records were just a means of survival.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Bill Coleman leaves and Otis Johnson joins
