segments.summary: Russell rarely fired anyone; Coleman probably left for Europe, and Otis Johnson, young and easy to get along with, replaced him beside Red Allen.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Two trumpets and parts marked by player's name
segments.summary: As the band grew to about ten pieces, arrangers marked parts with players' names instead of first or second chair.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Staying out of hiring decisions; everyone came by recommendation
segments.summary: As the band's baby, Holmes kept out of discussions about new members, who always came on a recommendation.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: 'Doctor Blues' and why the band stuck together
segments.summary: Hearing 'Doctor Blues', Holmes says Henry Allen was just another trumpeter on arrival, and bands stuck together because members had nowhere else to go.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: The Alhambra Ballroom on 126th Street
segments.summary: The Alhambra was an upstairs former taxi dance hall with a slow elevator; Russell played its multi-band night of September 13, 1929.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: The Harlem Opera House and the Renaissance Ballroom
segments.summary: The Harlem Opera House was a show theatre like the Apollo, while the Renaissance was a dance hall that sometimes held basketball games.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Vernon Andrade's band at the Renaissance
segments.summary: Andrade led a house band where musicians like Howard Johnson and Fats Green worked between better jobs, with no ambition beyond steady work.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Rent parties and Harlem's money and safety in the Depression
segments.summary: Holmes recalls Harlem as full of night life and cash during the Depression, safe at any hour with doors left unlocked.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Cotton Club celebrity nights and who could get in
segments.summary: The Cotton Club had a Black show and band but a White clientele, with Sunday celebrity nights, and Black patrons could get in if they could pay.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: The Savoy as a safe place for Harlem's youth
segments.summary: For about a dollar young people spent hours at the Savoy, and Holmes laments that nothing like it exists now.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Cost of the Nest, the Saratoga and the Cotton Club versus the Savoy
segments.summary: The Nest and Saratoga were small, expensive cabarets, while the Cotton Club catered to movie stars; Holmes wishes for a Savoy in every borough.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Subbing for Cab Calloway at the Cotton Club and unpaid rehearsals
segments.summary: The Blue Rhythm Band replaced Calloway, and producers called unpaid all-night rehearsals until the union forced pay.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Connie's Inn with Armstrong and the Fleischmann Yeast broadcasts
segments.summary: With Armstrong at Connie's Inn the band played three shows nightly, rehearsed after hours and for the radio program, and earned extra pay for rehearsals and broadcasts.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Willie Lynch's band, the Cotton Club and Edgar Hayes's 'Stardust'
segments.summary: Mills had Lynch form a substitute band to replace Cab Calloway at the Cotton Club, with Edgar Hayes's 'Stardust' solos a hit at the Lafayette, and Lynch took Holmes back.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Jobetus and Cass McCord, the supposed twins
segments.summary: Holmes replaced Jobetus McCord, doubting he and Cass were really twins, and Joe Garland took Cass's chair.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: A succession of leaders and dissension in the Blue Rhythm Band
segments.summary: Leaders ran from Carroll Dickerson to Baron Lee and Lucky Millinder, and several members wanted to lead, causing jealousy.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: The one tour with the band and being fired as spokesman
segments.summary: Touring was enough for him: he spoke for the men's pay demand and was replaced, with only nothing-to-speak-of recordings.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Armstrong forgets to introduce him at Boston's Symphony Hall
segments.summary: Armstrong usually introduced hometown players, but Russell had to remind him at Boston's Symphony Hall before he called Holmes 'Pickles'.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Armstrong gave Red Allen an hour of his own
segments.summary: Armstrong let Red Allen's own book fill an hour, then returned with one note that brought the house down.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Lee Collins fails as Allen's replacement
segments.summary: Russell brought in New Orleans trumpeter Lee Collins to replace Red Allen, but Collins was out of his depth with the tight band and Allen treated him graciously.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Red Allen the teaser and Holmes's friend
segments.summary: Red teased everyone to tears but never Holmes, who believes you only kid people you like.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: J.C. Higgenbotham as a trombonist and man
segments.summary: Higgenbotham was one of the best trombonists Holmes heard, instinctive rather than schooled, easy to work with and fond of a drink.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Pops Foster, bus seat-mate and old-looking young man
segments.summary: Pops Foster looked sixty-five but had young energy; Holmes was his bus seat-mate and later exchanged Christmas cards with his wife Alma.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Guitarist Bill Johnson
segments.summary: Bill Johnson was a quiet, college-educated guitarist and singer from Kentucky who was already at the Nest and liked a drink.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: The New Orleans beat and small-group sets at the Saratoga
segments.summary: Russell's rhythm section had a New Orleans beat, and he had the New Orleans players take over as a small band while downtown musicians packed the club.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Bechet and Benny Goodman battle at the Saratoga
segments.summary: After Bechet returned from Europe Goodman challenged him on clarinet in a friendly battle; Holmes played Jimmy Dorsey's 'Sensation' solo and still preferred Hodges.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Joe Steele, pianist who guarded his hands
segments.summary: Joe Steele, whose sister taught Holmes in Sunday School, played classical and dance piano, protected his fingers carefully, yet loved baseball.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: Joe Steele plays 'Rhapsody in Blue' for Gershwin
segments.summary: Holmes relates hearsay that Steele played the whole Rhapsody at an audition for the show 'Rhapsody in Black' and Gershwin said he needed no instruction.

segments.chapter: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
segments.title: How Willie Lynch's band became Irving Mills's Blue Rhythm Band
segments.summary: Mills put Ellington and then Calloway into the Cotton Club, then used Lynch's band as a substitute and renamed Lynch Earl Jackson to keep 'royal' names.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Cootie Williams and Alonzo Ross's band join Chick Webb
segments.summary: Webb enlarged to ten pieces by adding Holmes and Cootie Williams, who came from Alonzo Ross's broken-up Florida band that included Cass Carr.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Cass Carr's gigging band, his bass and musical saw
segments.summary: Cass Carr led ten-piece gig bands with a bass violin and a saw, used many New York musicians, paid reliably and later became a photographic-equipment seller.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Richard Fulbright, Edmond Hall and Cookie Mason of the Ross band
segments.summary: Holmes remembers Fulbright as a fine bassist, Hall as downtown-oriented, and Cookie Mason as a trumpeter he took for a gambler; touring bands faced jam sessions.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Wilton Crawley's clarinet and contortion act
segments.summary: Crawley was a Keith-circuit vaudeville single who took his clarinet apart, balanced a lit kerosene lamp and played upside down.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: The Crawley date with Jelly Roll Morton and Russell, retold
segments.summary: Morton and Russell both arrived to back Crawley, split the numbers, and traded barbs about the Lafayette versus the Paramount; Holmes recalls Morton's hard times.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Who was in the studio and Freddy Jenkins's precise playing
segments.summary: Holmes recognizes his solo on 'Keep Your Business to Yourself' and judges a sloppy trumpet solo to be someone other than Freddy Jenkins.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Freddy Jenkins, the showboat of Ellington's band
segments.summary: Jenkins was a neat, classy left-handed trumpeter with a big cigar who drew audiences in theatres, and may have briefly conducted Russell's band in 1936.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Leonard Feather and wealthy Bobby Burnet form a small group
segments.summary: At the Rhythm Club Feather asked him to join a mixed combination with trumpeter Bobby Burnet, a young millionaire who dressed like a tramp.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Nick's in the Village, February-March 1941
segments.summary: The Burnet-Feather group played two weeks at Nick's to little business, and Holmes says mixed bands were not unusual by then.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Cootie Williams's new band and the third saxophone part he wanted
segments.summary: Back from a machine shop job in Boston, Holmes joined Cootie Williams's new band, tired of Armstrong's noisy hard work, on condition of no solos.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Eddie Vinson arrives as the bald lead alto
segments.summary: Cootie's mystery lead player from Texas turned out to be Eddie 'Cleanhead' Vinson, a slow reader whom Holmes helped; he became the band's star.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Vinson's persecution complex and the New Year's Eve punch-up
segments.summary: At the Golden Gate Ballroom on New Year's Eve, half-drunk Vinson hit Lee Polk, thinking he was being talked about, and got knocked flat.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Opening in Chicago with a very loud band
segments.summary: Billed like a circus after leaving Goodman, Cootie's loud band opened in Chicago in a high-class nightclub where it was too much.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Cootie's veterans and youngsters, and how long at the Grand Terrace
segments.summary: He lists the older men (Walton, Walker, Perry, Sandy Williams, Bacon) and young wild ones, plus Kenon and Ballard, noting the band recorded in Chicago in April 1942.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Bud Powell joins and refuses to play 'that sad stuff'
segments.summary: Seventeen-year-old Bud Powell told Cootie he wouldn't play the theme as written; Holmes judges him a genius whose life was shortened.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Bud Powell borrowing five dollars and repaying seven
segments.summary: Bud borrowed money from Holmes between theatre shows and insisted on repaying with interest within twenty minutes.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: A White bandleader calls Bud a genius, and Cootie's string of pianists
segments.summary: A White orchestra leader on a train was amazed at Powell; Cootie kept changing piano players, all outstanding, and the band grew hard to handle.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Cootie cancels the tour; Vinson's cab ride to San Francisco
segments.summary: Cootie cancelled one-nighters in Chicago because he couldn't handle the young band, and Vinson once took a cab from Los Angeles to San Francisco.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Cootie's band beats Duke Ellington in a battle at the Savoy
segments.summary: Ellington arrived late and off form, and Cootie's loud, swinging band won the battle, which was rare for Ellington.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: The record-breaking package tour with the Ink Spots and Ella Fitzgerald
segments.summary: The Cootie band toured 27 theatres with the Ink Spots and Ella Fitzgerald, breaking records in 26, and Holmes calls them the happiest days of his life.

segments.chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
segments.title: Quitting Cootie Williams after his usher girlfriend's challenge
segments.summary: Embarrassed that his girlfriend had never heard him solo, Holmes asked Cootie for a feature; Cootie said nobody wanted to hear him, and Holmes walked out.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: First time stranded: a show in Leominster at sixteen
segments.summary: His first job offer, a small show band, collapsed when the Leominster theatre knew nothing of it; they sat overnight and a bandmate's father drove them home.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Stranded two weeks in Greenville, Mississippi with Armstrong
segments.summary: Cancelled engagements left Armstrong's band stuck in Greenville for two weeks without managers, until Glaser's people paid the bills.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Broke in Los Angeles after a crap game
segments.summary: While Armstrong filmed in Los Angeles, a storm cancelled the northern tour, and Holmes lost all his money at the chorus girls' party.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Alone on Christmas Day and the waitress who fed him
segments.summary: Penniless in a hotel three thousand miles from home he cried, until a waitress gave him free meals, recalling his mother's rule to be good to people.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Appearing in the film Sepia Cinderella with Kirby's band
segments.summary: With John Kirby's sextet in 1947 he shot a one-day cabaret scene in the Bronx for Sepia Cinderella.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Kirby calls him for a Washington nightclub job
segments.summary: Kirby's postwar band was rebuilt; he offered Holmes two weeks in a Washington club and Holmes describes the group's precise light-classics style.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: A first 'rehearsal' that was all whiskey
segments.summary: At the hotel the band, including Wallace Bishop, Billy Kyle and Jerry Blake, drank rather than rehearsed, with the alto book torn and dirty.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: The dark club, the first set and an instant raise
segments.summary: The club was too dark to read music; Holmes played two choruses on 'Sunny Side of the Street' and Kirby raised his pay from $140.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Kirby's expensive whiskey and the drunken pick-up band
segments.summary: Kirby bought whiskey inside the club at double price for his men, and the band, with a drunk trumpeter, was far from his original group.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Kirby's generous draws
segments.summary: Kirby insisted on giving him a hundred dollars as a draw and gave everything away, but his money was gone by payday.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Twenty dollars for whiskey, five for food
segments.summary: Kirby handed Holmes twenty-five dollars for three mornings in Chicago, then said he owed nothing at week's end.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Kirby's debts, Billy Kyle's sextet and personnel changes at the 845 Club
segments.summary: Kirby was in bad standing with the agents, Billy Kyle took over the Bronx 845 Club band with changes of bass, trumpet and clarinet.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Milwaukee and the free tray of whiskey
segments.summary: Kirby's band packed a Milwaukee bar owned by an old man's sons, where the band drank free and the boss turned his back at a rehearsal of bottles.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: The end of Kirby's band and Kirby's death
segments.summary: Kirby grew undependable, unpaid bills piled up and he left for California, dying on the way; Holmes was glad to leave before becoming an alcoholic.

segments.chapter: Stranded on the road and John Kirby
segments.title: Leaving full-time music for the Great American Insurance Company
segments.summary: From 1952 until the company moved to California in 1970 he worked in insurance and gigged with Joe Garland, having stopped traveling.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Signing up for the USO tour under Jesse Stone and manager Sylvester Lewis
segments.summary: After the war ended in 1945 he signed up for a USO tour; Jesse Stone was leader, but Sylvester Lewis, an ex-trumpeter, was manager.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: The USO band and trumpeter Nelson Williams
segments.summary: Holmes lists the USO band including Dave McRae and Louis Bacon, and trumpeter Nelson Williams, who had served in the Pacific.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Promised Spam, the greatest trip of his life
segments.summary: The six-month trip took them through the Philippines and Okinawa, where Spam was daily fare and supplies were short.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: News of Nelson Williams's death in Europe
segments.summary: The interviewer tells Holmes that Williams stayed in Europe and died about a year before; Holmes recalls him as a great trumpeter.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Nelson Williams asks Kirby for a raise and is finished
segments.summary: On Kirby's Milwaukee return Williams thought his own arrival made the band sound better and asked for a raise, ending his time in the band.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Closing the November 29 session; never getting to Europe
segments.summary: They plan to continue the USO story next time, and Holmes says he has never been to Europe, having once declined a USO tour with Noble Sissle.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Herbie Cowens and Jesse Stone: how he signed up for the USO
segments.summary: Holmes thought Herbie Cowens had invited him to Japan but ended up signing with Jesse Stone for a USO tour, rehearsing for pay.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Working at Small's Paradise with Gus Aikin while rehearsing
segments.summary: By night Holmes played with Aikin's six-piece band at Small's Paradise, a busy wartime club owned by the short, dumpy Ed Small.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: The USO show format and rehearsals at Noll Studios
segments.summary: The thirteen-person show ran an hour with an MC, three women and an eight-piece band, rehearsed at Noll Studios.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: USO show personnel and three months of rehearsal
segments.summary: He names the reeds, brass, rhythm and singers, and says the timed show could not be changed and was rehearsed for three months.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Leaving New York by train in USO uniforms, November 30, 1945
segments.summary: The show left Jersey by train for San Francisco in new Eisenhower-jacket uniforms with USO patches.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: The bucket-seat flight to Honolulu
segments.summary: They flew twelve or thirteen hours on a cargo plane with steel side seats to hot Honolulu in winter clothing.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Waikiki Beach disappoints, then shipped to Guam
segments.summary: Waikiki looked worse than Jones Beach to Holmes, and orders sent the show on to Guam.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Guam: missing his brother and Howard Johnson
segments.summary: On a stopover in Guam they visited a New York band and found that Holmes's brother and Howard Johnson had just left.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Arriving in Manila in rain and mud
segments.summary: The show landed at the back of Manila in thick mud and slept in tents with mosquito bars.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Weeks of waiting in the Manila staging area for instruments
segments.summary: Their instruments went missing for two or three weeks, during which about fifty shows lived like a family in the staging area without working.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: New Year's Eve in a quonset hut with White officers
segments.summary: Moved into a hut with drinking White officers, the Black performers were tense until an officer gave them whiskey and let Bacon fire a .45.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Pre-dawn orders and a rainy truck ride on Leyte
segments.summary: Woken at three after little sleep, the show flew to the island of Lahti in downpours and rode standing in an open truck.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Playing in the rain for soldiers who had waited for hours
segments.summary: Soldiers sat on stumps in the rain since afternoon, so Holmes agreed to perform on their homemade stage.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Sixteen days of rain and the whiskey he gave away
segments.summary: It rained fourteen of sixteen days; Holmes gave away his three bottles of stateside whiskey and disliked that others sold theirs.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Touring Philippine islands and crossing to Japan with Herbie Cowens
segments.summary: They played many islands; after a show's plane vanished at sea, shows went by boat, and Sylvester Lewis impressed him as manager.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Okinawa: bombed landscape and thirty days of Spam
segments.summary: Supplies failed so they ate C-rations and Spam on Okinawa among shot-off trees and empty highways, and he was eager to go home.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: First impressions of Tokyo, the Ginza and a surprise modern city
segments.summary: Tokyo amazed him with subways, steam trains run by children, stores and a theatre where he played the pipe organ.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Touring Japan but not performing in Tokyo
segments.summary: Troops weren't allowed in Tokyo, so the show played Kyoto and cities across Honshu.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: The mountain hotel at Kanazawa and Japan as the trip's best part
segments.summary: A hot-springs mountain hotel gave a sukiyaki dinner; Holmes liked Japan most, preferring not to be stationed in Tokyo like Herbie Cowens's group.

segments.chapter: USO tour to Japan, 1945-46
segments.title: Boat home to Seattle and news of his brother's burial
segments.summary: After eleven days at sea and a train to New York, his landlady told him to call his mother: his youngest brother had just been buried.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Deferring the Kirby story
segments.summary: The interviewer reminds him of joining Kirby in early 1947, and Holmes suggests saving it for another time.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Pearl Bailey as vocalist in Cootie Williams's band
segments.summary: Pearl Bailey was the band's only woman and not yet a star; Holmes credits a record with Hot Lips Page for launching her, though Vinson was the vocal star.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Retelling how he joined Kirby in Washington
segments.summary: Kirby offered a two-week Washington job; there was no rehearsal and the book was torn, and 'Sunny Side of the Street' won him a raise.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Fifteen-dollar whiskey and a drunken trumpeter
segments.summary: Kirby bought bar whiskey instead of using the shop next door, and a fresh bottle came every set until the trumpet player nearly fell off the stand.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Kirby band personnel and the changes before Milwaukee
segments.summary: The first band had Brereton, Jerry Blake, Kirby, Kyle and Bishop; Pete Clark and Rostelle Reese replaced two for the Milwaukee run.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Milwaukee success, then Kirby's five-hundred-dollar draw in Chicago
segments.summary: After a hit in Milwaukee, Kirby demanded a $500 draw from a gangster-run Chicago club and the band was let go after a week.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Charlie Ventura's bop band replaced by Kirby in Milwaukee
segments.summary: The Milwaukee club hated Ventura's bebop, which Holmes admired, and hired Kirby's popular-song band to finish the engagement.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: St. Louis hotel, Nelson Williams and Kirby's band breaking up
segments.summary: Nelson Williams replaced the trumpeter, a third Milwaukee stay followed, and Billy Kyle took the band into the 845 Club without Kirby.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Trying to remember the bass player
segments.summary: Holmes cannot recall the bassist's name, ruling out Al Hall and others.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Gigging with Sy Oliver's band
segments.summary: He did club dates with Oliver's band, including a two-week Jersey nightclub show, while Kirby had no work.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Joe and Moses Garland's society gigs
segments.summary: Garland's eight-piece band played lodge and fraternity dances, with Clyde Bernhardt on trombone singing one number a night.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Joe Garland's arrangements and 'In the Mood'
segments.summary: Garland avoided hard arrangements to suit his brother Moses, who always requested Joe's 'In the Mood', which Joe seldom played.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Garland band personnel and drummer Rick Harewood
segments.summary: The band had trumpeter Sleepy, Bernhardt, third altos and a drummer Holmes recommended, Rick Harewood.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Garland's pianist, bassists and guitarists
segments.summary: Freddie Gibbs played piano, Elbert Reynolds and John Williams bass, and various unnamed guitarists, as players came and went with gigs.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Taking a steady job with Great American Insurance
segments.summary: Because music wasn't steady he took an easy insurance job starting at noon, staying eighteen years until the company moved to California.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: How bop changed the music, and why he did not like it
segments.summary: He first heard bop in the early Forties at Minton's, found it 'for the birds', and preferred gutbucket jazz you can tap your foot to.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Garland's death and the end of his playing
segments.summary: Joe and Moses Garland died a day apart, ending the gigs; Holmes stopped playing after a foot operation and loss of sight in one eye.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Clyde Bernhardt's Saydisk record he did not realize was commercial
segments.summary: Clyde invited him to record and he didn't know it was commercial until handed an envelope of pay.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Personnel on the 'Blues and Jazz from Harlem' session
segments.summary: Holmes and the interviewer name the band: Jack Butler, Happy Caldwell, Jimmy Shirley, Earl Knight and Rick on drums, issued on Saydisk.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: The interviewer's own record with Doc Cheatham and Holmes
segments.summary: Vollmer recalls his 'More Blues and Jazz from Harlem' session with Cheatham, Bernhardt, Reuben Cole and Tommy Benford; Holmes says he was in poor shape.

segments.chapter: Kirby again, Garland gigs and later recordings
segments.title: Recording with Princess White and with a Swedish band
segments.summary: He did one more side with Princess White and added solos to tapes from a Swedish band that covered his 'Saratoga Shout'.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Making the Swedish band recording with earphones; no diary kept
segments.summary: The interviewer praises his bitey solos; Holmes recalls playing along to tapes with earphones in 1975, regrets not keeping a diary and agrees the interviews preserve history.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: A week with Fletcher Henderson at the Apollo
segments.summary: Drummer Alphonso Steele got him a one-week Apollo job with Henderson's pick-up band from Chicago, whose book was easy compared with Henderson's famous hard arrangements.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Good weeks and bad weeks at the theatre
segments.summary: Theatre houses varied; Holmes saw Armstrong pack the Apollo or play to empty seats, and Holy Week was always bad.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: The Ink Spots and Ella Fitzgerald show breaks records; Omaha is empty
segments.summary: Cootie's band toured with the Ink Spots and Ella Fitzgerald, broke records in 28 of 29 theatres, with a huge Regal Theatre crowd in a Chicago blizzard, but not in Omaha.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: The original Ink Spots
segments.summary: Holmes lists the Ink Spots members, Bill Kenney, Deek Watson and Hobby, and notes Charlie Fuqua had gone into the Army.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: A week in Lunceford's band under Eddie Wilcox
segments.summary: He sat in for a sick Simeon for a week in a Bronx theatre with the Lunceford band then led by pianist Wilcox, which was the whole show.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: David Nelson and Lee Collins fail with Russell; Red Allen shows how
segments.summary: Neither Nelson nor Collins, who was meant to replace Allen, had the drive for Russell's band, and Red Allen's playing one night made Collins quit.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Ready to pan Armstrong, who hit high F and called him Pickles
segments.summary: Russell's band was ready to pan Armstrong, but he dethroned Metcalf with big high notes; Armstrong always gave people nicknames, calling Holmes 'Pickles'.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Bill Dillard and the first, second and third trumpet parts
segments.summary: Dillard from Philadelphia played first trumpet, Red Allen was always the third hot man and Otis Johnson second in Russell's changing lineups.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Russell indulged him, in and out of the band like a spoiled child
segments.summary: Russell was easygoing and let Holmes come and go as he pleased, which Holmes now sees as taking advantage of him.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Depression days and landladies who trusted him with rent
segments.summary: He lived through the Thirties with little money, owing rent to people who believed in him, and he repaid every debt.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Bobby Neal and Lynn Pack
segments.summary: Neal was a bassist in taxi dance halls, and Pack was an altoist who left for Europe; Holmes never played with either.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Victoria Spivey, the studio house band and record executives
segments.summary: Russell's men served as house band in the studio, recording with anyone, including Spivey, Wilton Crawley and Bob Hope, with Russell handling the business.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Freddy 'Posey' Jenkins the showman
segments.summary: Jenkins posed, twirled his trumpet, smoked cigars, played left-handed after a childhood accident, and drew audiences before Ellington did.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Hodges's lack of showmanship against his applause
segments.summary: Hodges sat sullen and turned his back on audiences, yet won the biggest applause in Ellington's band.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: June Clark and Ed Swayzee
segments.summary: Holmes recalls trumpeters June Clark, who later boxed, and Ed Swayzee, a neat, clean player, but little detail about either.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Doc Cheatham, Ernest Elliott and Tommy Morris's records
segments.summary: He compares Cheatham to Swayzee and Mouse Randolph, and says Tommy Morris's records impressed him in Boston though he never met Morris.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Elmer James and O'Neil Spencer
segments.summary: James was a Chick Webb bassist; Spencer was young and wild drummer of the Blue Rhythm Band.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Henry 'Red' Hicks, the neat trombonist
segments.summary: Hicks came with Benny Carter's band, played sweet legit trombone and kept his suit unwrinkled on long bus rides; the nickname Red had nothing to do with red hair.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Andy Razaf hands out 'On Revival Day' in the studio
segments.summary: On May 19, 1930 Razaf brought the music, sang the vocal, and the band recorded it on the spot.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Jesse Crier sings 'Poor Little Me'
segments.summary: Crier was a singer brought in for one number at the same session and had worked at the Saratoga Club.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Telling the Ink Spots show tour again
segments.summary: He repeats the 29-theatre tour with Cootie, the Ink Spots, Ella and Vinson, the Regal Theatre blizzard and empty Omaha.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: The Ink Spots and Cootie gambling for big money
segments.summary: Bill Kenney, Deek Watson and Cootie each tried to break the others at gambling while the band nipped away at the pot.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Deek Watson's diamond ring and burning five-dollar bills
segments.summary: Kenney and Watson wore big diamond rings that flashed in the spotlight, and Watson lit cigars with five-dollar bills.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Rupert Cole joins Armstrong's band and loses at blackjack
segments.summary: Cole came from Don Redman's band, sight-read Armstrong's hard book as lead alto, won at blackjack on his first night and never again.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Rupert Cole the reed fanatic
segments.summary: Cole played beautifully but threw away reed after reed, never satisfied, which Holmes teased him about.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Holmes the mouthpiece freak
segments.summary: He never used the stock mouthpiece, tried every kind of metal and other mouthpiece, and sold two from a drawerful to a player from Machito's band.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Number-two reeds, and a trumpeter friend's too-stiff clarinet reed
segments.summary: Holmes used medium reeds to hear resonance, and a trumpet-playing friend's stiff reed gave no resonance on his new clarinet.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Oboe reeds and Rico number twos
segments.summary: Oboists make their own double reeds, but Holmes never learned to shave a reed, so he bought boxes of Rico number twos.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Slap-tonguing, instrument prices and Stradivarius violins
segments.summary: Holmes used to slap-tongue, remembers cheap altos, clarinets and sopranos at about a hundred dollars, and scoffs at thousand-dollar horns and expensive violins.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: The Lenox Club breakfast dance where Armstrong threw Rex Stewart's horn away
segments.summary: After Armstrong's Savoy appearance, musicians jammed at the Lenox Club's Sunday breakfast dances, and Armstrong outplayed Rex Stewart and Jack Teagarden.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Armstrong's broad tone and winning over unknowing Southern crowds
segments.summary: Armstrong's tone grew broader as he climbed, and he won over audiences who knew nothing of him while touring the South.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Armstrong the hardest-working leader
segments.summary: Armstrong sweated through each dance, changed with no dressing room, and worked harder than any leader Holmes knew, unlike Lionel Hampton.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Johnny Dunn and the French horn mix-up
segments.summary: Holmes remembers Johnny Dunn as a publicity-heavy trumpeter whose reign was over by 1927, and admits he is unobservant about how brass instruments are built.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Bobby Stark and Chick Webb's rehearsing band
segments.summary: Bobby Stark was his favorite hard-driving trumpeter; Webb loved rehearsing, hired only the best, and nearly had Ellington in his band.

segments.chapter: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
segments.title: Frankie Newton, Bill Coleman, Bubber Miley, Howard Scott and Cootie
segments.summary: He compares Newton and Coleman unfavorably to Stark's drive and praises Howard Scott's tone; the interview breaks off with Cootie Williams mentioned.
